step1.summary: Understand how computers run programs, write algorithms in pseudocode, and run your first JavaScript program.

slides.title: Welcome to Coding
slides.body:
In 26 steps, you will hand-build **Nhịp** — a social network for sharing short posts with a posting page and a profile page — from an empty HTML file to a PHP + MySQL product running live on the Internet.

Each step follows the same sequence: **introduction → illustration → academic → ideation → key knowledge → application to Nhịp → quiz**. To pass a step, the final quiz must achieve **at least 60%**.

slides.title: What this step teaches
slides.body:
Before writing any HTML line of code, you need to know **what programming actually is**:

- Computers only follow instructions exactly — they don't guess.
- An **algorithm** is a clear, finite sequence of steps that solves a problem.
- **Variables**, **conditions**, and **loops** are the three building blocks of every program.

At the end of this step, you will run your first JavaScript program and write the "post an article" algorithm for Nhịp.

slides.title: Preparation
slides.body:
You will need:

1. A modern browser (Chrome, Edge, or Firefox).
2. **Visual Studio Code** — download for free at code.visualstudio.com.
3. A folder named `nhip` on your computer — all project files will reside here.

No server or database is needed yet: the 1 stage runs entirely in the browser.

slides.title: Every program: input → process → output
slides.body: Keyboards, mice, and forms are **input**. Your code is the **process**. Screens, files, and outgoing data are **output**. Any application — including the social networks you use daily — is just many cycles of input → process → output connected together.

slides.title: Algorithm visualized as a flowchart
slides.body: Flowchart for the **post** operation: diamonds represent yes/no questions, rectangles represent actions. Following the arrows shows how the program runs before writing code.

slides.title: Variables are labeled boxes
slides.body: A variable holds a value and has a name for recall. Assigning a new value is like changing the contents of the box — the label remains. The data type indicates what the box contains: text, numbers, or true/false.

slides.title: Computational Thinking
slides.body:
Jeannette Wing (2006) calls this skill **computational thinking** and considers it a foundational skill like reading, writing, and arithmetic. Its four pillars are:

1. **Decomposition** — breaking down a large problem into smaller ones.
2. **Pattern Recognition** — identifying repetitions.
3. **Abstraction** — ignoring unnecessary details.
4. **Algorithms** — writing the steps to solve a problem.

> Wing, J.M. (2006) 'Computational thinking', *Communications of the ACM*, 49(3), pp. 33–35.

slides.title: Pólya's Four Steps to Problem Solving
slides.body:
Mathematician George Pólya proposed a process that programmers still use daily:

1. **Understand the problem** — what is the input, what is the required output?
2. **Devise a plan** — algorithm, flowchart, pseudocode.
3. **Carry out the plan** — write the code.
4. **Look back** — test, check edge cases, learn from experience.

> Pólya, G. (1945) *How to Solve It*. Princeton: Princeton University Press.

slides.title: What standards is this curriculum based on?
slides.body:
- **CS50 (Harvard)**: solves real problems from the first week, then delves into theory.
- **CS2023 (ACM/IEEE-CS/AAAI)**: international computer science curriculum framework; Coding adheres to the areas of *programming fundamentals*, *web development*, and *security*.
- **Original standard documentation**: MDN, WHATWG, W3C, IETF, PHP Manual, OWASP — no learning from anonymous blogs.

> Malan, D.J. (2025) *CS50's Introduction to Computer Science*. Harvard University. Available at: https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/
>
> Kumar, A.N. and Raj, R.K. et al. (2024) *Computer Science Curricula 2023*. ACM, IEEE Computer Society and AAAI.

slides.title: Decomposing Nhịp
slides.body:
Apply **decomposition** to the entire project. Nhịp includes:

- **Newsfeed page**: post composition box, list of latest posts.
- **Profile page**: photo, name, bio, user's own posts.
- **Each post**: author, content, timestamp, number of likes, number of replies.

Each bullet point will become a section of code. The problem "build a social network" is daunting; the problem "display a single post" can be done today.

slides.title: Understand the problem: posting an article
slides.body:
According to Pólya, start with these questions:

- **Input**: content typed by the user.
- **Constraints**: must not be empty; maximum 500 characters (this limit helps keep posts concise and readable).
- **Output**: new post appears at the top of the newsfeed, or an error message.

Writing these three lines means the hardest part is done.

slides.title: What is a program
slides.body:
**A program** is a sequence of instructions that a computer executes **in order**, from top to bottom, one instruction at a time.

Computers don't understand intent. If you issue a "print my name" command but forget to declare the name, the computer will report an error — it won't search for it itself. Programming is the art of writing instructions **so clear they cannot be misunderstood**.

slides.title: Pseudocode first, real code later
slides.body:
**Pseudocode** is an algorithm written in plain language, structured like code:

~~~text
nhận nội dung
nếu nội dung trống:
    báo "Hãy viết gì đó"
ngược lại nếu độ dài > 500:
    báo "Tối đa 500 ký tự"
ngược lại:
    thêm bài vào đầu bảng tin
~~~

Pseudocode cannot be executed, but it separates **thinking** from **typing syntax**.

slides.title: Variables and data types
Conditionals: branching
Loops: repeating multiple times
Functions: naming a task
Errors are normal
slides.body:
There are three types of errors:

- **Syntax errors** — typing mistakes against language rules (missing parentheses). The program won't run.
- **Runtime errors** — calling something that doesn't exist. The program stops midway.
- **Logic errors** — runs smoothly but produces incorrect results. The hardest to find.

How to find them: read error messages (they indicate line numbers), print variable values using `console.log`, and test with edge cases (empty string, exactly 500 characters, 501 characters).

slides.title: Create project folder
slides.body:
Open VS Code → **File → Open Folder** → select the `nhip` folder. Create a new file named `hello.html` and copy the code below into it.

The `<script>` tag allows writing JavaScript directly within the HTML page.

slides.title: Run and observe
slides.body:
Double-click `hello.html` to open it in your browser, press **F12**, and select the **Console** tab. You will see the line **Hello, Nhịp!**

Change the text in `console.log`, save the file (Ctrl+S), reload the page (F5). You will repeat this **edit → save → reload → view** cycle thousands of times.

slides.title: Write a post validation function
slides.body: Replace the `<script>` section with the algorithm written in the pseudocode part. Open the Console and read the results of the three calls — each time testing an edge case.

slides.title: Iterate through the list of posts
slides.body: Add this snippet to the end of `<script>`. It uses a loop and the function you just wrote to validate an entire list of posts — exactly what the newsfeed will do in step 6.

slides.title: Self-check
slides.body:
Before taking the quiz, ask yourself:

- If `.trim()` is removed, what does `checkPost("   ")` return? Why is that a logic error?
- If `MAX_LENGTH` is changed to 280 — how many places need to be fixed? (Answer: one. That's why constants are used.)
- The Console reports `checkPost is not defined` — where did you mistype a name?

quiz.q: What is an algorithm?
o: A clear, finite sequence of steps to solve a problem
quiz.why: Algorithms are language-independent: the same algorithm can be written in JavaScript, PHP, or pseudocode.

quiz.q: The computer automatically understands the writer's intent and corrects missing commands.
quiz.why: The computer executes each command precisely, without guessing intent — therefore, commands must be clear enough to prevent misinterpretation.

quiz.q: Arrange Pólya's four steps for problem-solving in the correct order.
quiz.why: Understand → plan → do → look back (Pólya, 1945).

quiz.q: What does the code snippet print?
quiz.why: Each assignment replaces the old value with the new value: 0 → 1 → 2.

quiz.q: What should you use to declare a variable when its value is NEVER reassigned?
quiz.why: const prevents accidental reassignment; only use let when a value truly needs to change.

quiz.q: Fill in the strict equality operator.
quiz.why: === compares both value and type; == performs type coercion and causes hard-to-find bugs.

quiz.q: Match error types with examples.
pairs: Runs smoothly but miscounts the number of posts
quiz.why: Logic errors are the hardest because the program doesn't report anything.

quiz.q: Which line allows a post consisting only of whitespace to still be published?
quiz.why: Missing .trim(): the string "   " is 3 characters long, so it's not considered empty.

quiz.q: What belongs to the four pillars of computational thinking (Wing, 2006)?
quiz.why: The four pillars: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithms.

quiz.q: Why should you define a constant MAX_LENGTH instead of typing the number 500 in multiple places?
o: Changing the limit only requires one edit
quiz.why: A single source of truth: change it in one place, and all places using it will update accordingly.

step1.title: 1. Programming mindset: algorithms, variables, and your first program

step2.summary: Understand the journey of a webpage from typing the address to its display, read requests/responses, and finalize the Nhịp project description.

slides.title: What happens when you open a social network?
slides.body:
You type an address, press Enter, and half a second later, the feed appears. In that half-second, at least four things happen: **finding the server address**, **opening a connection**, **sending a request**, **receiving and rendering the page**.

This step dissects each task. Once you understand it, everything that follows — PHP, SQL, security, deployment — will have a place to fit in.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
After this step, you will be able to:

- Distinguish between **client** and **server**, **static** and **dynamic** pages.
- Read the structure of a **URL** and the role of **DNS**.
- Read an **HTTP request/response** in DevTools: method, status code, header, body.
- Have the Nhịp project description and standard directory structure.

slides.title: Client and server
slides.body: **Client** (browser) sends requests. **Server** (host) receives, processes, and returns responses. Every click, every page load is a round of such requests and responses.

slides.title: Anatomy of a URL
slides.body: Each part of a URL has a function: the **protocol** specifies how to communicate, the **domain name** specifies who to talk to, the **path** specifies which page to request, and the **query string** sends additional parameters.

slides.title: DNS: The Internet's phonebook
slides.body: Computers don't know where "nhip.example" is — they only know IP addresses. DNS resolves domain names to IP addresses, like looking up a phone number in a directory. The result is cached to avoid looking it up again next time.

slides.title: A request and a response
slides.body: A request has **method + path + header (+ body)**. A response has **status code + header + body**. The body of a webpage is usually HTML.

slides.title: The Web originated from a proposal
slides.body:
In 1989, Tim Berners-Lee wrote a proposal at CERN for a networked hypertext system. His three inventions remain the backbone of today's web: **HTML** (document format), **URL** (address), **HTTP** (exchange protocol).

> Berners-Lee, T. (1989) *Information Management: A Proposal*. Geneva: CERN.

slides.title: HTTP is an open standard
slides.body:
HTTP is standardized by the IETF in RFC documents. RFC 9110 defines the meaning of methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE…) and status code groups (2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error).

> Fielding, R., Nottingham, M. and Reschke, J. (2022) *RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics*. IETF. Available at: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
>
> Mockapetris, P. (1987) *RFC 1034: Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities*. IETF.

slides.title: Stateless: HTTP doesn't remember you
slides.body:
According to Fielding (2000), the web architecture is intentionally **stateless**: each request must carry enough information on its own, and the server does not remember previous requests. This allows the web to scale to billions of users.

The consequence for Nhịp: if we want the server to know "who is posting," we must send proof with each request — that's **cookies and sessions** in stage 3.

> Fielding, R.T. (2000) *Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures*. PhD thesis. University of California, Irvine.

slides.title: Which pages does Nhịp need?
slides.body:
Sketch of two main pages:

- **Feed** (`index`): post composition box at the top, latest posts below.
- **Profile page** (`profile`): photo, name, bio, follower count, that person's posts.

Stage 1 builds these two pages using HTML/CSS/JS. Stage 2 transforms them into PHP reading real data.

slides.title: Static or dynamic page?
slides.body:
- **Static page**: the server sends the exact file available, everyone sees the same content (e.g., an 'About Us' page).
- **Dynamic page**: the server **builds the page for each request**, based on the viewer and the latest data (e.g., a news feed).

A news feed Nhịp must be a dynamic page: each person sees posts from those they follow, with the latest posts at the top. Therefore, we will need PHP and MySQL.

slides.title: The full journey of a page
slides.body:
1. You type `https://nhip.example/profile?u=lan`.
2. The browser asks **DNS** for the IP address.
3. Establishes a **TCP** connection, performs a **TLS** handshake (the 's' in https = encryption).
4. Sends a **request** `GET /profile?u=lan`.
5. The server runs code, reads data, and returns a **response** `200 OK` with HTML.
6. The browser reads HTML, downloads additional CSS, JS, images (each requiring another request), then **renders** the page.

slides.title: Main methods
slides.body:
| Method | Purpose | Example in Nhịp |
|---|---|---|
| GET | Read data | View feed |
| POST | Create new | Post an article |
| PUT/PATCH | Edit | Edit an article |
| DELETE | Delete | Delete an article |

Golden rule: **GET should never change data**. Browsers and search engines can call GET at any time.

slides.title: What status codes say
slides.body:
- **200 OK** — success.
- **201 Created** — successfully created (e.g., post created successfully).
- **301/302** — redirects to another address.
- **400 Bad Request** — incorrect data sent.
- **401 Unauthorized** — not logged in.
- **403 Forbidden** — logged in but no permission (e.g., deleting someone else's post).
- **404 Not Found** — this page does not exist.
- **500 Internal Server Error** — server-side code error.

slides.title: Header and body
slides.body:
**Header** contains accompanying information, in `Tên: giá trị` format:

~~~text
GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: nhip.example
Accept: text/html

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 1532

<!DOCTYPE html> ...
~~~

`Content-Type` specifies what the body is (HTML, JSON, image…). A blank line separates the header from the body.

slides.title: Frontend and backend
slides.body:
- **Frontend** — runs on the user's machine: HTML (structure), CSS (presentation), JavaScript (behavior).
- **Backend** — runs on the server: PHP (processing), MySQL (data storage).

The most important security rule of the entire course: **everything on the frontend can be modified by the user**. Frontend data validation is for convenience only; real validation **always happens on the backend**.

slides.title: Inspect real requests with DevTools
slides.body:
1. Open any page, press **F12** → **Network** tab.
2. Reload the page (F5).
3. Click the first row (HTML document). Look for: **Request Method**, **Status Code**, **Content-Type**.
4. Count how many requests the page loads to render completely.

Record these three numbers — you will compare them with Nhịp in stage 5 when optimizing performance.

slides.title: Set up directory structure
slides.body: In the `nhip` directory, create the following files and folders (leave content empty; steps 3–6 will fill them). Name them using **lowercase, no diacritics, connected by hyphens** — Linux servers are case-sensitive.

slides.title: Write the project description
slides.body: Every professional project starts with a README. Copy this template into `README.md` and fill in your part. The format is Markdown — the same format used to write this lesson.

slides.title: Draw the post creation process
slides.body:
On paper, draw the flow for the **post creation** operation once Nhịp has a backend:

1. User clicks "Post" → what request? (method, path)
2. What does the server check? (logged in, valid content)
3. What status is returned on success? What status if not logged in?

Keep the paper. In stage 3, you will code exactly this diagram.

quiz.q: In the client–server model, what role does the browser play?
quiz.why: The browser sends requests; the server processes and returns responses.

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
o: Resolve domain names to IP addresses
quiz.why: DNS is a directory: domain name → IP (Mockapetris, 1987).

quiz.q: Match parts of the URL https://nhip.example/profile?u=lan with their names.
quiz.why: Each part of a URL serves a distinct purpose.

quiz.q: Which method should be used for a new post operation?
quiz.why: Use POST to create new data. GET should never modify data.

quiz.q: Using GET to delete a post is acceptable because the path is concise.
quiz.why: Browsers and bots can automatically call GET (pre-fetching, crawling), leading to unintended data loss.

quiz.q: A logged-in user attempts to delete another user's post. Which status code should the server return?
quiz.why: 401 means unauthenticated; 403 means the server knows who you are but doesn't allow the action.

quiz.q: What runs on the backend of Nhịp?
quiz.why: CSS runs in the browser; permission checks must be on the server because anyone can modify the frontend.

quiz.q: Order the steps when opening an HTTPS page.
items: Look up DNS to get IP
Establish TCP connection and TLS handshake
quiz.why: You need to know the IP to connect; you need to connect to send a request.

quiz.q: HTTP is stateless: the server doesn't automatically remember your previous requests.
quiz.why: Therefore, cookies/sessions are needed for the server to recognize users (Fielding, 2000).

quiz.q: Why must the Nhịp news feed be a dynamic page?
o: Content changes based on the viewer and the latest data
quiz.why: Dynamic pages are rebuilt by the server for each request using real data.

step2.title: 2. How the web works: client, server, HTTP and the Nhịp project

step3.summary: Write meaningful HTML: document structure, semantic tags, post creation forms, and Nhịp's profile page layout.

slides.title: HTML is the skeleton
slides.body:
Every webpage has three layers: **HTML** is the skeleton (what's on the page), **CSS** is the skin (how it looks), **JavaScript** is the muscle (what it does).

This step focuses only on the skeleton — and getting it right. If the skeleton is crooked, no matter how beautiful the skin, it won't stand firm.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
- Write a standard HTML document structure.
- Choose the correct **semantic** tags: `header`, `nav`, `main`, `article`, `aside`, `footer`.
- Build a post **form** with labels and character limits.
- Complete the `index.html` (news feed) and `profile.html` (profile page) of Nhịp.

slides.title: A page is a tree
slides.body: Tags nested within tags form a **tree**: `html` is the root, `head` and `body` are two main branches. The browser builds this tree (called the DOM) from your HTML — JavaScript in step 6 will directly modify that tree.

slides.title: Semantic layout of the news feed
slides.body: Each region of the page has a tag that carries its correct meaning. Screen readers, search engines, and even you six months from now will be able to understand the page just by the tag names.

slides.title: Anatomy of a tag
slides.body: Opening tag, attributes (name="value"), content, closing tag. Some tags have no content and therefore no closing tag: `img`, `input`, `meta`, `br`.

slides.title: HTML is a living standard
slides.body:
HTML is currently maintained by WHATWG as a **Living Standard** — a standard that is continuously updated instead of being released in numbered versions. When in doubt about how to use a tag, the most accurate sources are the standard and MDN, not blogs.

> WHATWG (2025) *HTML Living Standard*. Available at: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/
>
> Mozilla (2025) *HTML: HyperText Markup Language*, MDN Web Docs. Available at: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML

slides.title: Accessibility is mandatory
slides.body:
A WebAIM survey of one million popular home pages (2024) found that **95,9%** pages had automatically detectable accessibility errors; the most common errors were low contrast text, missing alternative text for images, and missing form input labels.

All three of these errors can be fixed immediately with correct HTML: `alt` for images, `label` for input fields, and semantic tags for layout.

> WebAIM (2024) *The WebAIM Million*. Available at: https://webaim.org/projects/million/
>
> W3C (2023) *Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2*. Available at: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

slides.title: What makes up a post
slides.body:
Deconstructing a Nhịp post:

- **Profile picture + name** of the author (links to profile page)
- **Timestamp**
- **Content**
- **Actions**: like, reply

Each post is an `article` — because it makes sense on its own and can be shared independently.

slides.title: Profile page structure
slides.body:
A profile page consists of two blocks:

1. `header` of the profile: picture, display name, @username, bio, follower count, **Follow** button.
2. `section` of that person's posts — each post is still an `article` identical to those on the news feed.

The same post block is used on two pages: write it correctly once, reuse it everywhere.

slides.title: Standard document structure
slides.body:
~~~html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="vi">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Nhịp</title>
</head>
<body>
  ...
</body>
</html>
~~~

- `<!DOCTYPE html>` — enables the browser's standards mode.
- `lang="vi"` — screen readers pronounce Vietnamese correctly.
- `charset="UTF-8"` — displays accented characters correctly.
- `viewport` — displays correctly on mobile phones.

slides.title: Semantic tags
slides.body:
| Tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `header` | The header of a page or a section |
| `nav` | Main navigation links group |
| `main` | Main content — **only one** per page |
| `article` | Independent content: a post |
| `section` | A section with its own heading |
| `aside` | Supplementary content: follow suggestions |
| `footer` | Footer |

`div` carries no meaning — only use when none of the above tags are appropriate.

slides.title: Headings, paragraphs, links, images
slides.body:
~~~html

Bảng tin

Nội dung bài đăng.

lan.code 9:30 ~~~ - Headings follow a hierarchy h1 → h2 → h3, **do not skip levels** just to make text larger. - `alt` describes the image for those who cannot see it; for decorative images, use `alt=""`. - Declare `width`/`height` to prevent the page from jumping when images finish loading. - `time` has `datetime` that machines can read.

slides.title: Forms
slides.body:
~~~html
<form action="#" method="post">
  <label for="content">Có gì mới?</label>
  <textarea id="content" name="content" maxlength="500" required></textarea>
  <button type="submit">Đăng</button>
</form>
~~~

- `label for` correctly points to the `id` of the input field: clicking the text moves the cursor into the field.
- `name` is the field name the server will receive (2 stage).
- `maxlength`, `required` are convenient browser-side checks — **the server must still re-validate**.
- `method="post"` because posting is creating data.

slides.title: Button or link?
slides.body:
Simple rule:

- **Go to another place** → `<a href>` (to profile page).
- **Perform an action in place** → `<button>` (like, post).

Using `div` with a click event instead of a button is an accessibility error: it cannot be activated by keyboard, and screen readers don't recognize it as a button. `aria-label` names buttons that only have icons.

slides.title: Automated HTML checks
slides.body:
Browsers **do not report errors** when HTML is incorrect — they try to guess and render anyway. Therefore, you must use tools:

- **W3C Markup Validation Service** (validator.w3.org) — paste code, read errors.
- **Lighthouse** in DevTools → Accessibility section.

End-of-step goal: validator **0 errors**, Lighthouse Accessibility **from 90 points**.

slides.title: Write news feed: header section
slides.body: Open `index.html`, copy the boilerplate and navigation bar.

slides.title: Write news feed: post composition box
slides.body: Immediately below `header`, open `main` and add the post composition form.

slides.title: Write news feed: a post
slides.body: Add a list of posts and a sample post. In step 6, JavaScript will automatically generate `article` identical to this block.

slides.title: Write profile page
slides.body: Create `profile.html` with the same `head` and `header.topbar` structure as the news feed (change `aria-current` to the Profile page link), then replace `main` with the block below.

slides.title: Check and fix
slides.body:
1. Place any square image into `img/lan.jpg`.
2. Paste each file into **validator.w3.org/#validate_by_input**, fix until **0 errors**.
3. Open DevTools → **Lighthouse** → select only Accessibility → Analyze. Fix until **≥ 90**.
4. Try navigating the page **only with Tab and Enter keys**: all links, input fields, and buttons must be reachable.

The page looks crude at this point — as expected. CSS in step 4.

quiz.q: Which tag should each news feed post be wrapped in?
quiz.why: article is independent content, meaningful even when standing alone.

quiz.q: What is the lang="vi" attribute on the html tag for?
o: Screen readers and browsers know the page is written in Vietnamese
quiz.why: The correct language helps with proper pronunciation and correct spell-checking.

quiz.q: Fill in the attribute so the label points correctly to the input field.
quiz.why: label for = id of the input field; clicking the label moves the cursor into the field.

quiz.q: If maxlength="500" is already on the textarea, the server no longer needs to check the length.
quiz.why: Anyone can modify HTML or send direct requests; always perform actual validation on the server.

quiz.q: Which tags are semantic tags that describe regions of the page?
quiz.why: div carries no meaning, only use when no semantic tag is suitable.

quiz.q: Which tag should a 'like' button be written with?
quiz.why: Performing an action in place is a button; it can be clicked with a keyboard and understood by screen readers.

quiz.q: Which line violates the heading hierarchy rule?
quiz.why: After h1 must be h2; skipping levels to get smaller text is using the wrong tag — size is the job of CSS.

quiz.q: Match tags with roles.
quiz.why: Choose tags by meaning, not by appearance.

quiz.q: How should the alt attribute be for purely decorative images?
quiz.why: An empty alt tells screen readers to ignore it; missing alt makes it read the filename.

quiz.q: Why use a validator instead of just viewing the page in a browser?
o: The browser guesses and renders even if HTML is incorrect
quiz.why: Incorrect HTML can still be displayed but will break for screen readers, SEO, or other browsers.

step3.title: 3. Semantic HTML: build news feed and profile page structure

step4.summary: Understand how CSS selects and arranges elements: box model, cascade, flexbox, CSS variables, responsive — then apply a social media interface to Nhịp.

slides.title: From skeleton to face
slides.body:
The HTML in step 3 is semantically correct but looks like a document from 1995. CSS dictates **everything visible**: colors, font sizes, spacing, layout, and how the page adapts on mobile.

This step doesn't teach memorizing properties — it teaches **how CSS thinks**, so you can look up any property and understand it.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
- Write selectors and understand the **cascade**: when two rules conflict, which one wins.
- Grasp the **box model**: content, padding, border, margin.
- Build layouts using **flexbox**.
- Use CSS **variables** for colors and spacing.
- Make Nhịp **responsive** and achieve WCAG contrast standards.

slides.title: Box model
slides.body: Every element is a four-layered box: **content** → **padding** (inner spacing) → **border** → **margin** (space from other boxes). With `box-sizing: border-box`, the width you declare already includes padding and border — making calculations much easier.

slides.title: Flexbox: two axes
slides.body: Flexbox arranges children along the **main axis** (horizontal by default) and aligns them along the **cross axis**. `justify-content` handles the main axis, `align-items` handles the cross axis, `gap` handles spacing between children.

slides.title: A post card, deconstructed
slides.body: The Nhịp post card is two flex columns: a fixed profile picture on the left, and a flexible post body on the right. Within the post body, the header is another flex row: name on the left, timestamp on the right.

slides.title: Responsive design
slides.body:
Ethan Marcotte (2010) coined the term **responsive web design**: a single page that adapts to the screen thanks to flexible grids, flexible images, and media queries — instead of creating a separate page for mobile phones.

Today, most web traffic comes from mobile phones, so Nhịp designs **mobile-first**, then expands for larger screens.

> Marcotte, E. (2010) 'Responsive Web Design', *A List Apart*, 25 May. Available at: https://alistapart.com/article/responsive-web-design/

slides.title: Contrast and Touch Target according to WCAG
slides.body:
Two international standard numbers you must know:

- **Contrast 4,5:1** between normal text and background (WCAG 2.2, criterion 1.4.3); large text 3:1.
- **Minimum touch target 24×24 px** (criterion 2.5.8). Buttons on phones should be more generous, around 44 px.

Light gray text on a white background looks "subtle" but many people cannot read it.

> W3C (2023) *Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2*. Available at: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

slides.title: The CSS Standard
slides.body:
CSS is standardized by W3C into independent **modules**. The two most used modules in this step are:

> W3C (2024) *CSS Box Model Module Level 3*. Available at: https://www.w3.org/TR/css-box-3/
>
> W3C (2018) *CSS Flexible Box Layout Module Level 1*. Available at: https://www.w3.org/TR/css-flexbox-1/
>
> Mozilla (2025) *CSS: Cascading Style Sheets*, MDN Web Docs. Available at: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS

slides.title: Minimalist Design System for Nhịp
slides.body:
Before writing CSS, finalize a few decisions to ensure consistency across the entire page:

- **One background color, one text color, one accent color** (Post button, liked hearts).
- **Spacing scale** 4 – 8 – 12 – 16 – 24 px, no arbitrary odd numbers.
- **Font size** body 15–16 px, username bold.
- **Content column** max 620 px, centered — for comfortable reading.

All these values become **CSS variables** at the top of the file.

slides.title: Mobile First
slides.body:
Write CSS for narrow screens first — that's the most challenging case. Then just add a few rules in `@media (min-width: 700px)` to expand for desktops.

Conversely (desktop first then forcing it down to mobile) often requires overriding many rules.

slides.title: Selectors and Rules
slides.body:
~~~css
/* bộ chọn  { thuộc tính: giá trị; } */
.post { padding: 12px; }           /* class */
#composer { margin-bottom: 16px; } /* id */
.post-head a { font-weight: 700; } /* a nằm trong .post-head */
.like:hover { color: crimson; }    /* trạng thái */
~~~

Good practice: **style with classes**, avoid IDs (too strong, hard to override) and avoid styling by raw tag names (affects the entire page).

slides.title: Cascade and Specificity
slides.body:
When two rules set the same property, the browser considers them in order:

1. **Importance** — `!important` wins (avoid using).
2. **Specificity** — id > class > tag name.
3. **Order** — if specificity is equal, the later rule wins.

~~~css
.post p { color: black; }   /* 1 class + 1 thẻ */
p { color: red; }           /* 1 thẻ — thua dù viết sau */
~~~

slides.title: Units
slides.body:
- `px` — fixed, used for borders, shadows.
- `rem` — multiple of the root font size (usually 16 px). Used for font sizes to respect user's font size settings.
- `%` — relative to the parent element.
- `vw`, `vh` — viewport percentage.
- `max-width: 620px` + `width: 100%` — shrinks on small screens, stops at 620 px on large screens.

slides.title: Flexbox in Three Lines
CSS Variables
Media Queries
Foundation and Variables
slides.body: Open `css/style.css`, start with the foundation. `visually-hidden` hides text visually but screen readers still read it — use for `h1` of the news feed.

slides.title: Top Bar and Content Column
slides.body: The top bar sticks to the top when scrolling. The content column has a maximum width of 620 px and is centered.

slides.title: Compose Box
slides.body: `:focus-visible` shows a border when users navigate with the keyboard — never remove the focus outline without replacing it with something else.

slides.title: Post Card
slides.body: Two flex columns as illustrated. `overflow-wrap: anywhere` prevents long text from overflowing horizontally.

slides.title: Profile Page and Wide Screens
slides.body: Complete the profile page, then add media queries for screens from 700 px. Recheck with Lighthouse: Accessibility must still be **≥ 90**, and test the operating system's dark mode.

o: Adds a border to every box
Declared width includes padding and border

quiz.why: Order only resolves ties when specificity is equal; .post p (class + tag) is stronger than p.

quiz.why: justify-content handles the main axis, align-items handles the cross axis.

quiz.why: Criterion 1.4.3: 4,5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text.

quiz.q: Should remove the outline of input fields on focus because it looks bad.
quiz.why: Keyboard users lose their position; if removed, it must be replaced with another clear indicator.

quiz.q: Which options help make Nhịp responsive?
quiz.why: A large fixed width forces phones to scroll horizontally.

o: IDs have too high specificity, are hard to override, and cannot be reused
quiz.why: Classes are reusable and maintain low specificity, making cascade control easier.

step4.title: 4. CSS and Layout: Turning a Frame into a Social Media Interface

step5.summary: JavaScript deep enough for product development: data types, strings, arrays, objects, functions, scope, and map/filter/find methods — applied to Nhịp's post data model.

slides.title: The Language of the Browser
slides.body:
JavaScript is the only programming language that runs natively in all browsers. In step 1 you used variables, conditionals, loops, and functions. This step goes deep enough to **build a real product**: describe a post with data, then filter, count, and sort an entire list of posts.

We haven't touched the interface yet — step 6 will connect this data to the page.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
- Distinguish **data types** and avoid type coercion pitfalls.
- Handle **strings**: slice, find, concatenate with template literals.
- Use **arrays** and **objects** to model posts.
- Write pure **functions**, understand variable **scope**.
- Use `map`, `filter`, `find`, `sort` instead of manual loops.

slides.title: Arrays: cells numbered from 0
slides.body: An array is a sequence of contiguous cells, the first cell has index **0**. `posts.length` is the number of cells; the last cell is `posts[posts.length - 1]`. Accessing a non-existent cell does not throw an error — it returns `undefined`.

slides.title: Objects: a post
slides.body: An object groups information about **one thing** as key-value pairs. A post has an ID, author, content, timestamp, and number of likes. An array of objects is essentially a data table — identical to the MySQL table in milestone 2.

slides.title: Filter → Sort → Map Chain
slides.body: Each method takes an array and returns a **new array**: filtered, sorted, transformed. The original array is not modified. Chaining them together is the clearest way to process lists.

slides.title: JavaScript is an international standard
slides.body:
Brendan Eich created JavaScript in 1995 at Netscape. The language is standardized by Ecma International under the name **ECMAScript** (ECMA-262 standard), with a new version each year. All browsers implement this same standard, so your code runs identically everywhere.

> Ecma International (2025) *ECMA-262: ECMAScript 2025 Language Specification*. 16th edn. Geneva: Ecma International.
>
> Mozilla (2025) *JavaScript Guide*, MDN Web Docs. Available at: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide

slides.title: Functions are tools of abstraction
slides.body:
In MIT's classic textbook, Abelson and Sussman treat **naming a computation** as the most powerful tool for managing complexity: you use a function without needing to remember what it does inside.

A **pure** function — same input always gives the same output, with no changes to anything outside — is the easiest to test and to combine. The data-handling functions in Nhịp will be written in this style.

> Abelson, H. and Sussman, G.J. (1996) *Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs*. 2nd edn. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.

slides.title: Post data model
slides.body:
What fields does a post need? Start small:

| Field | Type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| id | number | 1 |
| author | string | "lan.code" |
| text | string | "Hello Nhịp" |
| createdAt | ISO string | "2026-10-27T09:30:00" |
| likes | number | 3 |
| likedByMe | boolean | false |

This table will become the `posts` table in MySQL at stage 2 — almost unchanged.

slides.title: What operations does the feed need?
slides.body:
- Sort posts with the **newest first**.
- Get **one person's posts** (for their profile page).
- **Count** the total likes for one person.
- **Like / unlike** a post by id.
- Show time as **"5 min"** instead of an ISO string.

Each line is one function. Once these five functions are written, step 6 only needs to connect them to the UI.

slides.title: Data types and coercion traps
slides.body:
The seven primitive types you'll meet most often: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null`, `bigint`, `symbol`; everything else is `object` (including arrays and functions).

~~~js
typeof "5"        // "string"
"5" + 1           // "51"  — ghép chuỗi!
"5" - 1           // 4     — ép sang số
Number("5") + 1   // 6     — ép tường minh: an toàn
"5" === 5         // false
~~~

Data from an input field is **always a string**. To calculate with it, convert explicitly using `Number()`.

slides.title: Strings and template literals
slides.body:
~~~js
const name = "Lan";
const text = "  Học Coding vui lắm  ";

text.trim()                 // "Học Coding vui lắm"
text.includes("Coding")     // true
text.trim().slice(0, 7)     // "Học Cod"
text.toUpperCase()          // "  HỌC CODING VUI LẮM  "
`Xin chào ${name}!`        // "Xin chào Lan!"
~~~

A template literal (backtick) embeds expressions with `${...}` and can span multiple lines. It is more concise than concatenating strings with `+`.

slides.title: Arrays: add, remove, find
slides.body:
~~~js
const tags = ["html", "css"];
tags.push("js");            // thêm cuối → ["html","css","js"]
tags.unshift("intro");      // thêm đầu
tags.includes("css");       // true
tags.indexOf("js");         // 3
const copy = [...tags];     // sao chép (spread)
~~~

`push`/`unshift` **modify the original array**. When you need to keep the old data intact, create a new array with spread: `[newPost, ...posts]`.

slides.title: Objects: read, update, copy
slides.body:
~~~js
const post = { id: 1, author: "lan.code", text: "Chào", likes: 0 };

post.author                       // "lan.code"
post["likes"]                     // 0
const { author, likes } = post;   // tách trường (destructuring)
const liked = { ...post, likes: post.likes + 1 };  // bản sao đã sửa
~~~

Copy with `{ ...post }`, then change the fields you need — the original stays intact, which is easier to control than editing in place.

slides.title: Arrow functions and scope
filter, map, find, sort
Dates and times
Sample data
slides.body: Open `js/app.js`. Start with sample data — this is the temporary "database" for stage 1.

slides.title: Sorting and filtering functions
slides.body: Two pure functions: they don't modify `posts` and always return a new array.

slides.title: Liking doesn't mutate existing data
slides.body: `toggleLike` returns a **new array** in which exactly one post is replaced by an updated copy. This lets step 6 re-render the UI safely.

slides.title: Create a new post and show the time
slides.body: Reuse `checkPost` from step 1. `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` is the browser's built-in standard library — nothing extra to install.

slides.title: Self-check with console.assert
slides.body: Add this to the end of the file. `console.assert` stays silent when the check passes and only shows red when it fails — a minimal built-in way to test in the browser. Open `index.html` and check the Console: no red lines means it passed.

quiz.why: The + operator concatenates when it meets a string. Explicitly convert with Number() before adding.

quiz.why: Array JavaScript is indexed starting from 0.

quiz.why: Accessing a nonexistent slot returns undefined without an error, so you must check for it yourself.

quiz.why: filter keeps the elements that meet the condition and returns a new array.

quiz.why: sort mutates the original array; copy it with [...posts] before sorting.

quiz.why: Spread copies every field, and fields written later override earlier ones.

quiz.why: map transforms each element and returns a new array of the same length.

quiz.why: Prefer the platform's standard library: correct grammar in every language, with no added download.

step5.title: 5. JavaScript fundamentals: conditionals, loops, functions, arrays and objects

step6.summary: Connect data to the interface: select and create DOM elements, handle events, re-render the feed, save to localStorage — and meet XSS for the first time.

slides.title: Make Nhịp move
slides.body:
You already have the interface (steps 3–4) and the data with its handler functions (step 5). Those two still live apart. This step connects them: type a post → click Post → the post appears at the top of the feed; click like → the like count changes; reload the page → the post is still there.

This is the final step of stage 1: once it's done, Nhịp is a **working prototype**.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
- Select elements with `querySelector`, create elements with `createElement`.
- Handle events with `addEventListener`; use **event delegation**.
- Write one `render()` function that re-renders the feed from data.
- Save and read data with `localStorage` + JSON.
- Know why you must **not** put user text into `innerHTML`.

slides.title: The loop of a user interface
slides.body: An event (click, type) → updates the **data** → calls **render** to redraw the interface from that data. The interface is never the place where truth is kept — the data is. This is also the core idea behind React, Vue, and every modern UI library.

slides.title: Event bubbling
slides.body: When you click the like button, the event **bubbles** up through each parent element: button → article → section → body. So a single listener placed at `section#posts` catches the like click on every post, including posts created just now.

slides.title: textContent and innerHTML
slides.body: Given the same string typed by a user: `textContent` displays it literally as text; `innerHTML` treats it as **HTML code** and runs it. User text that runs as code is an XSS vulnerability.

slides.title: DOM is a standard
slides.body:
DOM (Document Object Model) is the programming interface browsers provide for JavaScript to read and modify pages. WHATWG standardizes it — `querySelector`, `addEventListener`, and `createElement` behave the same across browsers because they follow this standard.

> WHATWG (2025) *DOM Living Standard*. Available at: https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/
>
> Mozilla (2025) *Introduction to events*, MDN Web Docs. Available at: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Core/Scripting/Events

slides.title: XSS according to OWASP
slides.body:
OWASP ranks **Injection** (including Cross-Site Scripting) among the top risks for web applications. The first recommendation from OWASP for the browser side is to insert untrusted data into the page using **safe properties** such as `textContent`, not `innerHTML`.

The 4 stage will attack and patch XSS on the server side. Today you only need the right habit from the first line.

> OWASP Foundation (2021) *OWASP Top 10:2021*. Available at: https://owasp.org/Top10/
>
> OWASP Foundation (2025) *Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html

slides.title: Browser storage
slides.body:
`localStorage` (part of the Web Storage spec in the HTML Living Standard) stores key–value pairs **as strings**. They persist after reloading or closing the browser, but **only on that device**. Switch devices and they're gone; a user clearing browser data also erases them.

This is exactly why the 2 stage needs a server and a database.

> WHATWG (2025) 'Web storage', in *HTML Living Standard*. Available at: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webstorage.html

slides.title: A single source of truth
slides.body:
Design for the feed:

1. The `state` variable holds the array of posts — the **only source of truth**.
2. Every action (posting, liking) only **creates new state** using the functions from step 5.
3. After each action: `save()`, then `render()`.

Never edit a like count directly on the button and forget to update the data — that is how the interface and the data drift apart.

slides.title: One drawing function for two pages
slides.body:
The feed and the profile page both show a list of posts, differing only in **which posts**:

- Feed: all posts, newest first.
- Profile page: only `ME`'s posts.

Write one `renderPosts(container, list)` function that serves both. Whichever page has `#composer` also attaches the post-creation event.

slides.title: Select elements
slides.body:
~~~js
const form = document.querySelector("#composer");   // phần tử đầu tiên khớp
const buttons = document.querySelectorAll(".like"); // mọi phần tử khớp
const box = document.getElementById("posts");
~~~

`querySelector` takes **CSS selectors** — exactly the selectors you wrote in step 4. If nothing is found it returns `null`, so check before using: `if (form) { ... }`.

slides.title: Create and attach elements
slides.body:
~~~js
const p = document.createElement("p");
p.textContent = userText;          // an toàn: luôn là chữ
p.className = "post-text";
container.append(p);               // gắn vào cuối
container.replaceChildren();       // xoá hết con
~~~

`textContent` never runs HTML. For complex markup, use a `<template>` tag in HTML and then `cloneNode(true)` — both concise and safe.

slides.title: Events
Event delegation
JSON and localStorage
slides.body:
~~~js
localStorage.setItem("nhip.posts", JSON.stringify(state));
const saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("nhip.posts") || "null");
~~~

- `JSON.stringify` turns data into a string. `JSON.parse` does the reverse.
- Saved data can be corrupted or edited by the user. Wrap `JSON.parse` in `try/catch` and provide a default value.
- JSON is also the format Nhịp will use to talk to the PHP server in step 3.

slides.title: State for screen readers
slides.body: The like button is a **toggle**. Report its state with `aria-pressed`: ~~~html ~~~ CSS in step 4 already turns `.like[aria-pressed="true"]` red. One attribute handles both accessibility and appearance.

slides.title: Post template in HTML
slides.body: In `index.html` and `profile.html`, delete the hand-written sample post in `#posts` and add this `template` card right before `</main>`. JavaScript will clone it for each post.

slides.title: Save, load, and render
slides.body: Add to `js/app.js`, below the functions of step 5. Delete the old test `console.log` lines and keep `console.assert`.

slides.title: Render the right page and catch the like click
slides.body: A page that has `.profile` renders only the posts of `ME`. A single listener on `#posts` handles every like button.

slides.title: Publishing posts and the character counter
slides.body: Only the feed has a composer, so check that `composer` exists before attaching events. Errors are shown with `setCustomValidity`, the browser's standard error message, which is accessible by default.

slides.title: Attack yourself
slides.body: Publish a post with this content: ~~~text ~~~ With `textContent`, the post shows that string **verbatim**. That's safe. Now temporarily change the `.post-text` line to `innerHTML` and publish again: a dialog pops up. That's XSS. **Change it back to `textContent`** before continuing.

slides.title: Step 1 acceptance
slides.body:
**Source code for step 1 (HTML/CSS/JS):** [download nhip-chang1-html-css-js.zip](/downloads/coding/nhip-chang1-html-css-js.zip). Unzip it to compare with your work. The code and the course material are in sync.

A working Nhịp passes when:

- [ ] Publishing: the new post appears at the top of the feed. Empty posts or posts over 500 characters are blocked.
- [ ] Liking and unliking changes the count and color. Both work with the keyboard.
- [ ] Reloading the page keeps the data.
- [ ] The profile page shows only your posts.
- [ ] The console shows no red errors, and all `console.assert` are silent.
- [ ] Lighthouse Accessibility is ≥ 90 on both pages.

Once all six lines pass, take the quiz to unlock step 2.

quiz.why: You must check for null before attaching events, like in the if (composer) block.

quiz.q: Assigning user-typed text to innerHTML is safe if you've checked the length.
quiz.why: Length doesn't matter. Even a short string can contain a tag that runs code. Use textContent.

quiz.q: What does event.preventDefault() do in a submit event?
o: Stops the browser from submitting the form and reloading the page
quiz.why: The feed handles it with JavaScript, so the browser doesn't need to reload the page.

quiz.q: Order the steps that run when the like button is clicked.
items: The click event bubbles up to #posts
Create a new state with toggleLike
quiz.why: Event → data → save → render. The UI is always drawn from the data.

quiz.q: Why is one listener on #posts enough instead of one on each like button?
o: The event bubbles up to the parent element, including from posts created later
The browser only allows one listener
quiz.why: Event delegation: newly created posts don't need a listener attached.

quiz.q: The article has data-id="7". What is the result?
quiz.why: dataset always returns the string "7", so === with the number 7 is false. Use Number().

quiz.q: Call the function that converts the data to a string before saving.
quiz.why: localStorage only stores strings. Read it back with JSON.parse.

quiz.q: What limitation of localStorage requires Nhịp to need a server in step 2?
o: It only exists on one device
If the user clears browser data, it's lost
Other people can't see your posts
It can't store accented Vietnamese text
quiz.why: localStorage can store accented text, but the data only lives in one browser.

quiz.q: Which line creates the XSS vulnerability?
quiz.why: innerHTML runs HTML in post.text. Use textContent.

quiz.q: Which attribute tells screen readers whether the like button is on or off?
quiz.why: aria-pressed="true"/"false" describes an on/off button.

step6.title: 6. DOM and events: the feed Nhịp runs in the browser

step7.summary: Install XAMPP, enable Apache and MySQL, understand htdocs and localhost, run your first PHP file, get familiar with phpMyAdmin, and put Nhịp on the server.

slides.title: Why does Nhịp need a server?
slides.body:
In step 1, every post lives in `localStorage` of **one** browser. If you post on your laptop, your phone can't see it, and friends never will.

A real social network needs a **shared** place to keep data, and a program **running in that shared place** to receive posts, check them, save them, and send them back to everyone. That shared place is the **server**.

Step 2 builds that server right on your machine. It's called **localhost**.

slides.title: Goal of the step
slides.body:
By the end of this step you will:

1. Install **XAMPP** and know what's inside it (Apache, MariaDB/MySQL, PHP, phpMyAdmin).
2. Start and stop Apache and MySQL, and read the error when a service fails to start.
3. Understand **htdocs** and how a folder becomes a `http://localhost/...` address.
4. Write and run your **first PHP file**, and explain why the browser doesn't see PHP code.
5. Open **phpMyAdmin** and read the main information on the home page.
6. Move the `nhip/` folder of stage 1 into the server.

Suggested duration: 120 minutes, of which 40 minutes is installation.

slides.title: The Four Layers of a PHP Page
slides.body:
You type an address → the browser sends a request HTTP to **Apache** (the web server) → Apache sees the `.php` extension, so it hands the file to **PHP** to run → PHP asks **MySQL** for data when needed → PHP prints HTML → Apache sends HTML back to the browser.

This group of four is commonly called **LAMP** (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP). XAMPP is a prepackaged installer of all four for Windows and macOS — the X means it runs on multiple operating systems.

slides.title: Dashboard XAMPP
slides.body:
After installing, you control the server with **XAMPP Control Panel** (Windows) or **manager-osx** (macOS, *Manage Servers* tab). Two important lines:

- **Apache**: the web server, listening on port **80** by default (and 443 for HTTPS).
- **MySQL**: actually **MariaDB**, the continued development of MySQL, listening on port **3306**.

When a service starts successfully, it turns green and shows its PID; if it won't start, read the *Log* panel below right away.

slides.title: From Folder to Address
slides.body:
Apache serves everything in the document root directory (DocumentRoot), where XAMPP is **htdocs**:

| Operating system | htdocs path |
|---|---|
| Windows | `C:\xampp\htdocs` |
| macOS | `/Applications/XAMPP/xamppfiles/htdocs` |

The file `htdocs/nhip/hello.php` is at the address `http://localhost/nhip/hello.php`. Any folder that contains `index.php` (or `index.html`) only needs its folder name typed: `http://localhost/nhip/`.

slides.title: Client–Server Model and CGI
slides.body:
From the early 1990s, web servers only returned static files. To make a page **change according to the viewer**, people had the server run a program and send back its output — standardized as **CGI** (Common Gateway Interface, RFC 3875). PHP was born in 1994 precisely from this need, and today it runs behind most websites that use the server-side languages you know.

The idea hasn't changed: **the code runs on the server, and only the result travels over the network.**

> Robinson, D. and Coar, K. (2004) *RFC 3875: The Common Gateway Interface (CGI) Version 1.1*. IETF. Available at: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3875
>
> The PHP Group (2025) *History of PHP*, PHP Manual. Available at: https://www.php.net/manual/en/history.php.php

slides.title: Why Learn on localhost First
slides.body:
Major introductory courses such as CS50 (Harvard) all have learners run the server **right on their own machine** before putting anything online. The reasons:

- **Short feedback loop**: edit a file, reload the page, see the result in a second.
- **Safety**: your mistakes don't leak out, and nobody can attack a test server.
- **Free and no network needed**.

The XAMPP publisher itself warns that the default configuration *is only for development* and is not safe to expose to the Internet. You will see this warning on the welcome page.

> Malan, D.J. (2025) *CS50's Web Programming with Python and JavaScript*. Harvard University. Available at: https://cs50.harvard.edu/web/
>
> Apache Friends (2025) *XAMPP FAQs*. Available at: https://www.apachefriends.org/faq_windows.html

slides.title: Plan for Nhịp
slides.body:
Stage 2 turns Nhịp from a "static page + localStorage" into a "PHP page + database":

| Step | What Nhịp adds |
|---|---|
| 7 (this lesson) | The server runs, `nhip/` folder in htdocs |
| 8 | `.php` pages, shared header/footer, post form that submits to the server |
| 9 | `nhip` database schema |
| 10 | SQL queries for the feed and profile page |
| 11 | PHP reads/writes MySQL using PDO |

Stage rule: **everything users submit is re-validated by the server**, even when JavaScript has already checked it.

slides.title: Which XAMPP version to choose
slides.body:
- **Windows**: download the latest version from the Apache Friends site (the 2026 year is 8.5.x, 8.4.x, 8.3.x, where the first number is the PHP version). Pick **8.4** unless you have other requirements: it is recent enough and stable.
- **macOS**: Apache Friends has stopped releasing new versions for macOS; the last one is **8.2.4** (PHP 8.2), available under *More Downloads → XAMPP Mac OS X* on SourceForge. Every lesson in this course runs on PHP 8.2.
- **Linux**: use your distribution's packages (`apache2`, `php`, `mariadb-server`, `phpmyadmin`).

Equivalent alternatives: **MAMP** (macOS/Windows), **Laragon** (Windows). The root folder name may differ (`htdocs` or `www`), but everything else is the same.

slides.title: Step 1 · Download XAMPP

image.alt: The Download page of Apache Friends lists XAMPP for Windows, the 8.5.12, 8.4.27 and 8.3.36 builds, with a Download button for 64-bit
image.caption: apachefriends.org/download.html, screenshot taken on 27/10/2026. Each line is one PHP version; click Download (64-bit).

slides.body:
1. Open **apachefriends.org** → the **Download** section.
2. Choose your operating system, then click **Download (64-bit)** on the 8.4.x line (about 190 MB).
3. Download only from the project's official site or SourceForge. "Repackaged" installers on unknown sites may contain malware.
4. (Advanced) Compare the **sha1** checksum of the downloaded file with the one on the site to make sure the file was not altered.

slides.title: Step 2 · Install
slides.body:
**Windows**

1. Run the `xampp-windows-x64-...-installer.exe` file. If Windows shows a UAC prompt, click *OK*. XAMPP recommends **not** installing into `C:\Program Files` because write permissions are restricted.
2. On the *Select Components* screen, keep **Apache, MySQL, PHP, phpMyAdmin**; uncheck FileZilla Server, Mercury, Tomcat and Perl if you don't use them.
3. Install folder: leave the default `C:\xampp`.
4. Windows Firewall asks whether to allow Apache network access: choose **Private networks**, not Public.

**macOS**

1. Open the `.dmg` file and drag **XAMPP** into *Applications*.
2. On first launch, macOS may block the app because it "cannot verify the developer": go to *System Settings → Privacy & Security* → **Open Anyway**.

slides.title: Step 3 · Turn on Apache and MySQL
slides.body:
- **Windows**: open *XAMPP Control Panel* → click **Start** on the Apache line, then the MySQL line. Green-background text and numbers in the *PID(s)* and *Port(s)* columns mean success.
- **macOS**: open `manager-osx` → **Manage Servers** tab → select *Apache Web Server* → **Start**; do the same for *MySQL Database*. The status changes to **Running** with a green dot.

Quick check: open a browser and type `http://localhost`. Seeing the *Welcome to XAMPP* page means Apache is running.

Each time you restart your computer, you need to turn these two services back on (or tick *Autostart* under *Config* in the Control Panel on Windows).

slides.title: Localhost welcome page

image.alt: The Welcome to XAMPP page, titled XAMPP Apache + MariaDB + PHP + Perl, with links to FAQs, HOW-TO Guides, PHPInfo, phpMyAdmin
image.caption: http://localhost/dashboard/ on a machine running XAMPP. The second line reads: XAMPP is for development only.

slides.body:
This page is `htdocs/dashboard/index.html` — just one file in htdocs like any other. The top bar has:

- **PHPInfo**: the full PHP configuration (version, extensions, `php.ini` in use).
- **phpMyAdmin**: the web interface for managing databases.

When you put a product on the Internet, you **never** expose the PHPInfo page: it reveals paths, versions and configuration to attackers.

slides.title: When Apache won't start
slides.body:
The most common error is a **port already in use**. The log shows something like `Port 80 in use by ...` or *Apache shutdown unexpectedly*.

1. Find what is holding the port: on Windows run `netstat -ano | findstr :80`; on macOS run `sudo lsof -iTCP:80 -sTCP:LISTEN`.
2. It is usually IIS/World Wide Web Publishing Service, an old Skype, or another copy of Apache. Stop that program if you can.
3. If you can't stop it, change the Apache port: Control Panel → Apache → **Config → httpd.conf**, change `Listen 80` to `Listen 8080`; also change `ServerName localhost:8080`. After that the address becomes `http://localhost:8080/`.

If MySQL won't run because port **3306** is busy, it is usually because another MySQL is installed: stop that service in *Services* (Windows) or change `port=3306` in `my.ini`/`my.cnf`.

slides.title: Your first PHP file
slides.body:
Create a folder `htdocs/nhip/`, and inside it create `hello.php`. Things to know before typing:

- PHP code goes between `<?php` and `?>`. Anything outside those tags is sent as-is, like HTML.
- `<?= $bien ?>` is shorthand for `<?php echo $bien; ?>` — it prints the value to the page.
- Each statement ends with a `;`. Variables always start with `$`.
- `date_default_timezone_set` sets the time zone; without this line, the printed time may be UTC.
- Save the file with **UTF-8** encoding (VS Code already defaults to this) so Vietnamese characters don't break.

slides.title: The server runs; the browser only sees the result

image.alt: The source view of hello.php contains only HTML: Hello, Nhịp! and the line The server is running PHP 8.2.4 at 08:55, 27/10/2026, with no php tags left
image.caption: Right-click → View Page Source (Ctrl/Cmd + U). All <?php ?> tags are gone.

slides.body:
Open `http://localhost/nhip/hello.php` and view the page source. You only see HTML already containing the time and version — no `$name`, no `date(...)`.

This is the biggest difference from JavaScript in stage 1: JS code is sent to the browser and **anyone can read it**; PHP code stays on the server. That way, later the database password can sit in PHP where users cannot see it.

If you see the raw PHP code shown on the page, it means you're opening the file directly (`file:///...`) rather than through `http://localhost` — Apache isn't being used.

slides.title: Getting to know phpMyAdmin

image.alt: The phpMyAdmin home page 5.2.1 is in English: the left column lists the databases information_schema, mysql, performance_schema, test; the right panel, "Database server", shows MariaDB 10.4.28, server collation UTF-8 Unicode utf8mb4
image.caption: http://localhost/phpmyadmin — the interface can be switched to Vietnamese under the Language menu.

slides.body:
Three areas to remember:

- **Left column**: list of databases. `mysql`, `information_schema`, `performance_schema` are system ones — **don't edit, don't delete**.
- **Top tab bar**: *Databases* (create new), *SQL* (type commands), *Export/Import* (back up, restore), *User accounts*.
- **"Database server" panel**: version (MariaDB 10.4 on XAMPP 8.2), the logged-in user (`root@localhost`) and **server collation must be utf8mb4** to store Vietnamese and emoji in full.

slides.title: Root account with no password
slides.body:
XAMPP ships with a preset account MySQL **`root` with an empty password**, and phpMyAdmin logs in automatically with it. On a personal machine that only you can access, this is acceptable for learning.

Keep three things in mind for the later steps:
1. Never use `root` for a real application. Step 24 will create a separate account with a strong password on hosting.
2. Never let Apache of XAMPP listen on public networks (coffee shop, dormitory) — that's why *Private networks* was chosen when the firewall asked.
3. Database connection info will live in **a single config file** (step 11), not scattered through the code.

slides.title: Folder structure from now on
slides.body:
~~~text
htdocs/
└── nhip/
    ├── hello.php        ← tệp thử, xoá được sau step 8
    ├── index.html       ← từ chặng 1 (đổi thành index.php ở step 8)
    ├── profile.html
    ├── css/style.css
    ├── js/app.js
    └── img/
~~~

Naming convention: **lowercase, no diacritics, no spaces** (`profile.php`, not `Trang Cá Nhân.php`). Linux servers are case-sensitive: `Style.css` and `style.css` are two different files. It runs on Windows but breaks when uploaded to hosting at step 24.

slides.title: Write hello.php
slides.body: Create `htdocs/nhip/hello.php` with the content below, save it as UTF-8, then open `http://localhost/nhip/hello.php`. Reload the page a few times: the time changes because PHP runs again on every request.

slides.title: Expected result

image.alt: The browser shows the heading Hello, Nhịp! and the line Server is running PHP 8.2.4 at 08:55, 27/10/2026
image.caption: The PHP version and the time on your machine will differ. That is exactly the proof that the code is really running.

slides.body:
Try three changes and reload the page after each one:

1. Change `$name` to your name.
2. Delete the `;` after `$name = 'Nhịp'` → the page reports **Parse error** with a line number. Read the message carefully and fix it.
3. Misspell the variable name `<?= $nam ?>` → **Warning: Undefined variable $nam**. PHP still keeps running but prints nothing — this kind of error is easy to miss, so always keep an eye on warnings.

slides.title: Deploy Nhịp to the server
slides.body:
1. Copy the entire `nhip/` folder of stage 1 into `htdocs/` (keep the `hello.php` you just created).
2. Open `http://localhost/nhip/` — Apache chooses `index.html` automatically.
3. Publish a test page: the stage 1 sample still runs, because HTML/CSS/JS runs on any web server.
4. Open *DevTools → Network* and reload the page: each file (`style.css`, `app.js`) is one HTTP request with status **200**. This is the same flow you learned in step 2, now answered by Apache on your machine.

slides.body:
- [ ] `http://localhost` shows the Welcome to XAMPP page.
- [ ] `http://localhost/phpmyadmin` opens, and the server collation is utf8mb4.
- [ ] `hello.php` prints the correct time and version PHP; view the page source and no PHP code remains.
- [ ] You have caused and fixed a *Parse error*.
- [ ] `http://localhost/nhip/` opens the template for step 1.
- [ ] You know how to change the Apache port if port 80 is already taken.

Step 8 will change `index.html` to `index.php` and let PHP draw the feed itself.
