quiz.why: Apache is the web server; it hands .php files to PHP to run, then sends the result back.

quiz.q: What address does the file htdocs/nhip/hello.php have?
quiz.why: htdocs is the root folder, so it does not appear in the address.

quiz.q: Users can view your PHP code using View Page Source.
quiz.why: PHP runs on the server; the browser only receives its HTML output.

quiz.q: Apache reports that port 80 is already in use. What is the correct way to handle it?
o: Find and stop the program holding the port, or change Listen to 8080 in httpd.conf
quiz.why: Two servers cannot listen on the same port; free the port or use a different one.

quiz.q: What does the page display?
quiz.why: <?= $x ?> is shorthand for echo $x.

quiz.q: Which databases in phpMyAdmin belong to the system and must not be deleted?
quiz.why: Nhịp is the database you build yourself at step 9.

quiz.q: You open hello.php and see the raw <?php ... ?> text on the page. What is the most likely cause?
o: Opening the file via file:/// instead of http://localhost
quiz.why: Without Apache, no one runs PHP; the browser shows the file as plain text.

quiz.q: Fill in the name of the document root directory of XAMPP.
quiz.why: The Apache of XAMPP serves everything in htdocs.

quiz.q: Why not use a root account with no password for a real website?
o: root has full access; if it leaks, the entire database server is lost
quiz.why: Principle of least privilege: an application should have only the permissions it needs.

quiz.q: Which line causes PHP to report a Parse error?
quiz.why: Missing ; at the end of the assignment statement.

step7.title: 7. Set up localhost: XAMPP, Apache, PHP and phpMyAdmin

step8.summary: PHP basics through Nhịp itself: variables, strings, arrays, typed functions, shared includes, reading forms with $_POST, server-side validation, htmlspecialchars, and the Post/Redirect/Get pattern.

slides.title: To let PHP draw the feed
slides.body:
In stage 1, JavaScript draws the feed **in the browser**. From this step, **PHP draws the feed on the server** and sends back the complete HTML. Users who turn off JavaScript can still read it; search engines can read it; and most importantly, posts are sent **to the server**, no longer stuck in one browser.

You already know programming (step 1, 5). PHP is just new syntax for old ideas: variables, conditions, loops, functions, arrays.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Read and write PHP syntax: variables, types, strings, indexed arrays and associative arrays.
2. Write functions **with type declarations** using `declare(strict_types=1)`.
3. Split the shared header and footer using `require`.
4. Receive form data via `$_POST`, and address parameters via `$_GET`.
5. **Validate again on the server** and print user text safely using `htmlspecialchars`.
6. Apply the **Post/Redirect/Get** pattern so that reloading the page does not resubmit it.
7. Temporarily save posts to a JSON file, and understand why this approach is not enough for social media.

slides.title: One request, one run
slides.body:
Each time the browser calls `index.php`, PHP **runs the file from the first line to the last**, prints HTML, and then **forgets everything**: variables do not carry over to the next load. Anything that must be remembered longer than one request has to live elsewhere: a file, a database (step 11), or a login session (step 12).

This is the "stateless" model of HTTP that you learned at step 2, now seen from the server side.

slides.title: Post/Redirect/Get
slides.body:
If you submit a form with POST and return HTML directly, then when the user presses F5 the browser asks *"Resubmit form?"* and the post is published **twice**.

The standard approach: after handling the POST, return **303 See Other** with the `Location: index.php` header; the browser then sends a GET to that page itself. Reloading now only repeats the GET, which is harmless.

slides.title: The canonical source for PHP
slides.body:
The official documentation of PHP is the **PHP Manual** maintained by The PHP Group. Each function has its own page stating its parameter types, return values, and the version it was introduced in. Habit of professional developers: when you meet an unfamiliar function, open `php.net/tên_hàm` (for example `php.net/htmlspecialchars`).

On coding style, the PHP community agrees on **PSR-12** from the PHP-FIG: 4-space indentation, function braces on their own line, and `strict_types` declarations right after `<?php`. The code in this course follows PSR-12.

> The PHP Group (2025) *PHP Manual*. Available at: https://www.php.net/manual/en/
>
> PHP Framework Interop Group (2019) *PSR-12: Extended Coding Style*. Available at: https://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-12/

slides.title: Do not trust data from the client
slides.body:
The `required` attribute, `maxlength` in HTML, and all checks done with JavaScript are **only for the user's benefit**. An attacker who sends a HTTP request directly (with `curl`, Postman, or DevTools) bypasses all of them. OWASP places input validation **on the server side** at the top of its list of proactive controls.

The Post/Redirect/Get pattern was first described as a web design pattern in 2003, and it is now the default approach of every framework.

> OWASP Foundation (2024) *OWASP Top 10 Proactive Controls: C3 Validate all Input & Handle Exceptions*. Available at: https://top10proactive.owasp.org/
>
> Fielding, R., Nottingham, M. and Reschke, J. (2022) *RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics*, §15.4.4 303 See Other. IETF. Available at: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

slides.title: From One HTML File to Many Pieces
slides.body:
`index.html` and `profile.html` in step 1 repeat the same `<head>` and navigation bar. Fixing the menu means fixing it in two places. The plan:

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `includes/helpers.php` | Shared functions: `e()`, `time_ago()`, `check_post()`, `redirect()` |
| `includes/header.php` / `footer.php` | Header and footer |
| `includes/post.php` | Template for **one** post card |
| `includes/storage.php` | Read/write posts (temporarily with JSON) |
| `index.php`, `profile.php` | Each page keeps only its own part |

The `includes/` folder holds code that is **not** opened directly in a browser; step 5 will move it fully out of the public area.

slides.title: Variables and Types
slides.body:
~~~php
<?php
$name   = 'lan.code';     // string
$likes  = 3;              // int
$ratio  = 0.75;           // float
$liked  = true;           // bool
$avatar = null;           // null: "chưa có giá trị"

var_dump($likes);         // int(3) — xem kiểu và giá trị khi gỡ lỗi
echo gettype($ratio);     // double
~~~

- Variable names start with `$` and are case-sensitive (`$Name` ≠ `$name`).
- PHP automatically changes type under loose comparison `==`: `"1" == 1` is `true`, `"abc" == 0` is `false` (from PHP 8). Always use **`===`** as in JavaScript.

slides.title: Strings
slides.body:
~~~php
$user = 'lan.code';
echo 'Xin chào $user';         // Xin chào $user   — nháy đơn: không thay biến
echo "Xin chào $user";         // Xin chào lan.code — nháy kép: thay biến
echo 'Xin chào ' . $user;      // nối chuỗi bằng dấu chấm, không phải dấu +
echo "Bài số {$post['id']}";   // phần tử mảng trong nháy kép: bọc {}

strlen('Nhịp');      // 6  — đếm BYTE, chữ "ị" chiếm 3 byte
mb_strlen('Nhịp');   // 4  — đếm KÝ TỰ, luôn dùng cho tiếng Việt
trim("  hi  ");      // "hi"
~~~

The limit of 500 characters per post must be measured with `mb_strlen`; otherwise, Vietnamese posts would be blocked earlier than English ones.

slides.title: Arrays: Lists and Dictionaries
slides.body:
~~~php
$tags = ['php', 'sql', 'css'];          // mảng chỉ số: 0, 1, 2
$tags[] = 'js';                          // thêm vào cuối
echo count($tags);                       // 4

$post = [                                // mảng kết hợp: khoá => giá trị
    'id' => 1,
    'author' => 'lan.code',
    'likes' => 3,
];
echo $post['author'];                    // lan.code
$post['likes']++;                        // 4

foreach ($tags as $i => $tag) { echo "$i: $tag\n"; }
foreach ($post as $key => $value) { /* ... */ }
~~~

A post is an **associative array**, and the feed is an **array of associative arrays**, like the array of objects in step 5 and also the shape that PDO returns in step 11.

slides.title: Typed Functions and strict_types
include, require and __DIR__
slides.body:
~~~php
require __DIR__ . '/includes/helpers.php';
~~~

| Command | File not found |
|---|---|
| `include` | Warning, keeps running |
| `require` | Fatal error, stops entirely |

A missing function file or configuration file means the page cannot work correctly, so always use **`require`**. `require_once` loads only once even when called many times, which is needed when several files load the same library.

`__DIR__` is the directory containing the file **currently running that line**. Writing `__DIR__ . '/includes/...'` keeps the path correct no matter where the page is called from; writing bare `'includes/...'` will break when the folder structure changes in stage 5.

slides.title: Alternative syntax for views
slides.body:
In a file with several HTML, write the loops and conditionals **interleaved** so you don't get lost between the `{ }` delimiters: ~~~php

~~~ A rule to keep the code tidy: **process at the top of the file, print at the bottom**. The top part computes the variables (`$posts`, `$error`), and the bottom part contains only HTML, ``, `foreach` and `if`. This is the seed of the MVC architecture in step 20.

slides.title: $_GET, $_POST and $_SERVER
slides.body:
PHP puts the request data into **superglobal** arrays:

| Variable | Contains | Example in Nhịp |
|---|---|---|
| `$_GET` | Parameters in the `?u=lan.code` address | `profile.php?u=lan.code` |
| `$_POST` | Fields of the `method="post"` form | the content of the `$_POST['body']` post |
| `$_SERVER` | Request information | whether `$_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD']` is `GET` or `POST` |

A key may **not exist** (someone submitted the form without a field). Always read safely:

~~~php
$body = (string) ($_POST['body'] ?? '');
~~~

`??` returns the right-hand operand when the left is unset or null; `(string)` casts to a string even when an attacker sends an array `body[]=...`.

slides.title: htmlspecialchars: e() of Nhịp
Temporarily saved in a JSON file
slides.body:
There is no database yet, so we store posts in `data/posts.json`:

~~~php
$posts = json_decode(file_get_contents($file), true);  // true: ra mảng kết hợp
file_put_contents($file, json_encode($posts, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE), LOCK_EX);
~~~

- `JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE` keeps the text "Nhịp" instead of `"Nh\u1ecbp"`.
- `LOCK_EX` locks the file while writing so two people posting at the same time don't overwrite each other halfway.

This is only a stopgap: it **can't be searched, can't be paginated, reads the whole file every time**, and has no relationship between users and posts. Steps 9–11 replace it with MySQL.

slides.title: helpers.php
slides.body: Create `nhip/includes/helpers.php`. The return type `never` of `redirect()` (PHP 8.1+) makes clear this function never returns — `exit` stops every line after it.

slides.title: Header, footer, post card
slides.body: `header.php` uses two variables, `$title` and `$active`, which the page that calls it assigns beforehand. `post.php` prints one post from the `$post` variable. The username in the address goes through `urlencode`, and in HTML it goes through `e()`.

slides.title: storage.php
slides.body: Three functions: read, write, add a post, and `newest_first` replacing `newestFirst()` from stage 1. `usort` sorts in place; `strcmp` can compare dates because the `Y-m-d H:i:s` format sorts alphabetically in the same order as chronologically.

slides.title: index.php: feed + posting
slides.body: Delete `index.html`, create `index.php`. The top of the file handles POST, the bottom prints the interface. When there's an error, the compose box keeps the text the user typed (via `e($body)`) so they don't have to retype it.

slides.title: profile.php reads ?u=
slides.body: The profile page filters posts by the username in the address. Try `profile.php?u=minh.dev`, then `profile.php?u=x` — thanks to `e()` the `` tag shows up as plain text.

slides.title: Result: the feed drawn by PHP

image.alt: The Nhịp feed with the compose box What's new? and three posts: First post sent to the server PHP! just now, Box model 11 hours ago, CSS flexbox 17 hours ago
image.caption: http://localhost/nhip/ after posting. Reload the page: the post is still there, not duplicated.

slides.title: The server blocks empty posts

image.alt: An empty compose box with the red line Write something. above the Post button
image.caption: Type only spaces and click Post: the HTML required attribute lets it through, and check_post() on the server blocks it.

slides.body: Try bypassing the browser check: in DevTools → Elements, delete the textarea's `maxlength` attribute, paste 600 characters, then post. The server still returns *"Maximum 500 characters."* — that's why the check **must** live on PHP.

slides.title: The vulnerability you just created

image.alt: The browser opens http://localhost/nhip/data/posts.json and shows the entire contents of the JSON file, including all the posts
image.caption: Anyone who knows the address can download all the data — because data/ sits inside htdocs.

slides.body:
Open `http://localhost/nhip/data/posts.json`: the whole temporary database is shown. Everything in htdocs is **public**. Temporarily block it with a one-line `data/.htaccess` file:

~~~apache
Require all denied
~~~

Reload: Apache returns **403 Forbidden**. This lesson comes back in step 20 (only keep the `public/` folder in the public area) and step 24 (the config file on hosting).

slides.title: Acceptance check for step 8

step8.title: 8. PHP foundations: syntax, arrays, functions, include and forms

step9.summary: Relational model, primary keys, foreign keys, 1–many and many-to-many relationships, normalization 1NF–3NF, data types and utf8mb4 — then create the database nhip using phpMyAdmin.

slides.title: Data needs a shape
slides.body:
The JSON file in step 8 keeps each post as a separate block: the author's name repeats in every post, the heart count is just a number (it doesn't know **who** liked it), and there's no place for "who follows whom".

A social network is really **entities and the relationships between them**: users write posts, users like posts, users follow users. Relational databases exist precisely to describe and query such relationships.

This step **doesn't write any PHP lines yet**. Designing the right schema is the hardest decision to reverse in the whole project — so do it carefully first.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Read and draw an entity–relationship (ER) diagram for Nhịp.
2. Distinguish **primary keys, unique keys, and foreign keys**, and know which error each type prevents.
3. Represent **1-to-many**, **many-to-many**, and **self-referencing** relationships.
4. Apply the three normal forms **1NF, 2NF, 3NF** to remove repeated data.
5. Choose the right data types, and understand why it must be **utf8mb4**.
6. Create databases and tables in phpMyAdmin using both the interface and `schema.sql` files.

slides.title: Relationship diagram of Nhịp
slides.body:
Four tables are enough for the whole 3 stage:

- **users** — one row per person.
- **posts** — one row per post, pointing to its author via `user_id`. A reply is also a post, pointing to the original post via `parent_id`.
- **likes** — one row per like: *who* liked *which post*.
- **follows** — one row per follow relationship: *who* follows *whom*.

Crow's foot notation: a single line means "one", and a three-pronged fork means "many".

slides.title: Tables, rows, columns
slides.body:
A **table** (relation) is a set of **rows** (tuples, records) that share the same **columns** (attributes). Each column has a **type** and **constraints**.

Two foundational rules of the relational model:

1. Each cell holds **only one value** (don't cram a list into a single cell).
2. Each row must be **distinguishable** from every other row, using the primary key.

slides.title: Codd's relational model
slides.body:
In 1970, Edgar F. Codd (IBM) proposed storing data as **relations** (mathematical tables) and querying them with relational algebra, instead of having programs follow pointers through files. That idea became SQL and underlies every relational database system today: MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle.

Chen (1976) added the **entity–relationship model** for designing on paper before creating tables. That is the very diagram you just looked at.

> Codd, E.F. (1970) 'A relational model of data for large shared data banks', *Communications of the ACM*, 13(6), pp. 377–387. doi:10.1145/362384.362685
>
> Chen, P.P. (1976) 'The entity-relationship model — toward a unified view of data', *ACM Transactions on Database Systems*, 1(1), pp. 9–36. doi:10.1145/320434.320440

slides.title: Normalization and MySQL references
slides.body:
Codd (1971) defined **normal forms** to avoid *update anomalies*: fixing one fact in one place but forgetting another, which leaves the data contradicting itself. The classic database textbook by Silberschatz and colleagues still teaches the sequence 1NF → 2NF → 3NF.

For details on data types, character sets and foreign keys, see the official documentation of MySQL. MariaDB is compatible with every part used in this course.

> Silberschatz, A., Korth, H.F. and Sudarshan, S. (2019) *Database System Concepts*. 7th edn. New York: McGraw-Hill.
>
> Oracle (2025) *MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: Data Types; Character Sets; FOREIGN KEY Constraints*. Available at: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/

slides.title: Find entities from a user story
slides.body:
Write down what users can do, underlining **nouns** (entities) and **verbs** (relationships):

- A **user** *signs up* with an email and a username.
- A user *writes* many **posts**, each up to 500 characters.
- A user *replies* to a post with another post.
- A user *likes* anyone's post, at most once per post.
- A user *follows* other users, but cannot follow themselves.

Each sentence implies a constraint: "at most once per post" → the composite primary key of `likes`; "cannot follow themselves" → the `CHECK` constraint. Constraints that live **inside the database** cannot be bypassed by any code.

slides.title: A flawed design to avoid
slides.body:
The "quick" approach that beginners often take:

| id | author | author_email | body | liked_by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | lan.code | lan@vd.vn | Hello Nhịp | minh.dev,an.ui |
| 2 | lan.code | lan@vd.vn | Learning SQL | minh.dev |

Three problems:

1. `liked_by` stores a **list** in one cell → violates 1NF, and it can't be counted or searched with SQL.
2. Lan's email is repeated in every post → changing the email means editing hundreds of rows, and missing one leaves the data contradictory.
3. A user who hasn't written any posts has **nowhere** to be stored.

Normalization is the systematic fix for these three problems.

slides.title: Primary key and AUTO_INCREMENT
slides.body:
A **primary key** (PRIMARY KEY) uniquely identifies a row: no duplicates, no NULLs, and each table has exactly one primary key.

~~~sql
id INT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
PRIMARY KEY (id)
~~~

- `AUTO_INCREMENT`: the database assigns numbers 1, 2, 3… automatically. Never compute `max(id) + 1` in PHP as in step 8; two people posting at the same time would get the same number.
- `UNSIGNED`: non-negative, range 0 → 4.294.967.295.
- The primary key should be a **surrogate key** (a meaningless number), not an email or username, since users can change those.

slides.title: Unique key and foreign key
slides.body:
~~~sql
UNIQUE KEY uq_users_username (username),
CONSTRAINT fk_posts_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
  REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE
~~~

- **UNIQUE**: no two users may share the same `username` or `email`. Checking only in PHP is not enough, because two sign-up requests at the same time can still slip through. A constraint in the database cannot be bypassed this way.
- **FOREIGN KEY**: `posts.user_id` may only contain an id that **currently exists** in `users`. Inserting a post for a user 999 that does not exist → a 1452 error.
- `ON DELETE CASCADE`: deleting a user automatically deletes their posts, likes and follow relationships. Alternatives: `RESTRICT` (forbid deletion while posts exist) or `SET NULL`.

Foreign keys only work with the **InnoDB** storage engine, the default since MySQL 5.5, and the reason every table explicitly specifies `ENGINE=InnoDB`.

slides.title: 1-to-many, many-to-many, self-referencing
slides.body:
| Relationship | Example | How to store it |
|---|---|---|
| 1-to-many | One person writes many posts | Foreign key column on the **many** side: `posts.user_id` |
| Many-to-many | Many people like many posts | A **junction table** `likes(user_id, post_id)` |
| Self-referencing 1-to-many | A reply to a post | `posts.parent_id → posts.id` |
| Self-referencing many-to-many | People following people | Junction table `follows(follower_id, followee_id)` |

A junction table uses a **composite primary key** `PRIMARY KEY (user_id, post_id)`: the pair (person, post) cannot appear twice, so each person can like a given post at most once, guaranteed by the database itself.

slides.title: Three normal forms
slides.body:
- **1NF** — each cell holds one atomic value, with no repeating groups. Fix `liked_by` by moving it into a separate `likes` table.
- **2NF** — satisfies 1NF, and every non-key column depends on the **whole** primary key. If `likes` has an extra `post_body`, this column depends only on `post_id` (half the key), which is wrong. It must move to `posts`.
- **3NF** — satisfies 2NF, and no non-key column depends on another non-key column. `posts.author_email` depends on `user_id`, not on the lesson, so move it to `users`.

The classic mnemonic: every column must depend on *"the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key"*.

When do you **deliberately** break the rule? When you measure a real slowdown, for example storing the heart count in `posts` so you don't have to count it. Step 21 covers that. For now, keep the standard.

slides.title: Choosing data types
slides.body:
| Data | Type | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| id | `INT UNSIGNED` | Enough for 4 billion rows, 4 bytes |
| Username | `VARCHAR(30)` | Short, with a clear limit |
| Post content | `VARCHAR(500)` | Limit of 500 **characters**, matching Nhịp's rule |
| Email | `VARCHAR(255)` | Enough for every real-world valid email |
| Password hash | `VARCHAR(255)` | PHP recommends leaving 255 for future hashing algorithms |
| Timestamp | `DATETIME` | Not limited to the year 2038 like `TIMESTAMP` |
| Optional | `NULL` | `avatar`, `parent_id`, `updated_at` |

`VARCHAR(n)` in MySQL counts **characters**, not bytes, matching `mb_strlen` at step 8. Only unlimited-length text (articles) needs `TEXT`.

slides.title: utf8mb4 and Collations
slides.body:
In MySQL, the old `utf8` (`utf8mb3`) stores at most **3 bytes** per character, so an emoji that needs 4 bytes gets truncated or throws an error. Always use **`utf8mb4`**, which is the full UTF-8.

**Collation** determines how characters are compared and sorted:

- `utf8mb4_unicode_ci`: follows the Unicode standard; `ci` is *case-insensitive*, so `Lan` and `lan` count as **duplicates** under a UNIQUE check, which is exactly what we want for usernames.
- MySQL 8 also has `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci` (Unicode standard 9.0). MariaDB's 10.4 of XAMPP isn't available yet, so this course uses `utf8mb4_unicode_ci` so it runs on both.

Set the character set at the **database** level, and every table will inherit it.

slides.title: Naming conventions
slides.body:
- Table names: **plural, lowercase, underscores**: `users`, `posts`, `likes`.
- Foreign keys: `<bảng số ít>_id` → `user_id`, `post_id`.
- Timestamps: suffix `_at` → `created_at`, `updated_at`.
- Constraint names with prefixes: `uq_` (unique), `idx_` (index), `fk_` (foreign key), `chk_` (check). When an error occurs, the message contains this exact name, so you know right away which constraint was violated.
- **Don't** use the reserved word SQL as a column name (`order`, `group`, `user`).

Passwords **never** get a `password` column. Only `password_hash` (step 12).

quiz.why: Many-to-many always needs a junction table holding two foreign keys.

quiz.q: What does the PRIMARY KEY (user_id, post_id) of likes guarantee?
o: Each person can like a given post at most once
Deleting a post deletes its likes
quiz.why: The combination of primary-key values must not repeat.

BCNF only if there is a trigger

step9.title: 9. Relational databases: schema design for a social network

step10.summary: Load sample data, then write every query Nhịp needs: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, JOIN, LEFT JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING, subqueries, pagination, safe UPDATE/DELETE, and transactions.

slides.title: Ask the data one question
slides.body:
The feed of Nhịp must answer the question: *"What are the 20 newest original posts, each with its author's name and like count?"*

At stage 1, you answer with `filter`, `map`, and `sort` over an array. With SQL, you **describe the result you want** and let the database work out the fastest way to get it, whether the table has 10 rows or 10 million rows. That is **declarative** language, unlike the **imperative** language you have written so far.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Load sample data using `INSERT` and the **Import** feature of phpMyAdmin.
2. Write `SELECT … FROM … WHERE … ORDER BY … LIMIT`.
3. Join tables using `JOIN` and `LEFT JOIN`; know when LEFT is needed.
4. Count and group using `COUNT`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`.
5. Use a subquery for the "Following" feed.
6. Paginate using `LIMIT/OFFSET` and understand its limits.
7. Edit/delete safely: **never** `UPDATE`/`DELETE` without `WHERE`; group multiple statements into one **transaction**.

slides.title: JOIN combines two tables
slides.body:
`JOIN users AS u ON u.id = p.user_id`: for each row of `posts`, find the row of `users` whose `id` equals `user_id`, then **paste the two rows into one**.

- **INNER JOIN** (abbreviated `JOIN`): keeps only rows that have a match on both sides.
- **LEFT JOIN**: keeps **every** row on the left; where the right side has no match, it fills in `NULL`.

A post that nobody has liked has no row in `likes`. With `JOIN`, that post **disappears** from the feed; with `LEFT JOIN`, the post stays and its like count is 0.

slides.title: The actual execution order of SQL
slides.body:
You write `SELECT` first, but the database processes clauses in logical order:

**FROM / JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT**

Practical consequences:

- `WHERE` cannot use an alias defined in `SELECT` (the column doesn't exist yet at that point).
- Filter **each row** with `WHERE`; filter **each group** after counting with `HAVING`.
- `ORDER BY` can use aliases, because it runs after `SELECT`.

slides.title: SQL: from SEQUEL to the ISO standard
slides.body:
Chamberlin and Boyce (IBM) designed SEQUEL in 1974 so that non-programmers could query data with near-English sentences; the name was later shortened to SQL. Since 1987, SQL has been the international standard ISO/IEC 9075 and is still being updated (latest edition SQL:2023).

Because it is a standard, the queries in this course run almost unchanged on MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL or SQLite; the differences lie in each system's own extensions.

> Chamberlin, D.D. and Boyce, R.F. (1974) 'SEQUEL: A structured English query language', *Proceedings of the 1974 ACM SIGFIDET Workshop*, pp. 249–264. doi:10.1145/800296.811515
>
> ISO/IEC (2023) *ISO/IEC 9075-2:2023 Information technology — Database languages SQL — Part 2: Foundation (SQL/Foundation)*. Geneva: ISO.

slides.title: Safe queries per the MySQL documentation
slides.body:
The MySQL documentation recommends enabling `sql_safe_updates` mode when working by hand: this mode **rejects** `UPDATE` and `DELETE` statements that have no `WHERE` using a key, exactly the kind of command that has wiped out real data at many companies.

On pagination, the MySQL optimization manual notes that `LIMIT n OFFSET m` must still **read and skip** the first m rows; the deeper the page, the slower. Keyset pagination fixes this.

> Oracle (2025) *MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: Using Safe-Updates Mode (--safe-updates)*. Available at: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/mysql-tips.html
>
> Oracle (2025) *MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: LIMIT Query Optimization*. Available at: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/limit-optimization.html

slides.title: Each screen is one query
slides.body:
Before writing SQL, list each screen and its **question**:

| Screen | Question |
|---|---|
| Feed | 20 latest root posts + author + likes count |
| Profile | User info + follower / following counts |
| Post detail | The replies to one post, oldest first |
| Following tab | Posts from people I follow |
| Leaderboard | Who posts the most |

Write and **run each query in phpMyAdmin** first. Once it is correct, move it into PHP at step 11. Errors in SQL are much easier to spot before PHP wraps them.

There are two ways to run `seed.sql`:

1. **Import**: choose `nhip` → **Import** tab → *Choose File* → `database/seed.sql` → **Import** at the bottom of the page.
2. **SQL**: open the file in VS Code, copy everything, paste it into the **SQL** tab → **Go**.

Syntax to insert multiple rows at once:

~~~sql
INSERT INTO users (username, display_name, email, password_hash)
VALUES ('lan.code', 'Lan Nguyễn', 'lan@example.com', '$2y$10$…'),
       ('minh.dev', 'Minh Trần',  'minh@example.com', '$2y$10$…');
~~~

Do not write `id` — `AUTO_INCREMENT` assigns it automatically. To reload from scratch: run `schema.sql` again (after dropping the database), then `seed.sql`.

slides.title: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT
slides.body:
~~~sql
SELECT id, body, created_at          -- lấy cột nào (tránh SELECT * trong mã thật)
FROM posts                           -- từ bảng nào
WHERE user_id = 1                    -- lọc dòng
  AND parent_id IS NULL              -- NULL phải so bằng IS / IS NOT
ORDER BY created_at DESC             -- mới nhất trước
LIMIT 5;                             -- tối đa 5 dòng
~~~

Common operators in `WHERE`: `=`, `<>`, `<`, `>=`, `BETWEEN a AND b`, `IN (1, 2, 3)`, `LIKE '%php%'` (`%` matches any string), `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`.

**NULL trap**: `parent_id = NULL` **always** returns an empty result, because NULL means "unknown" and comparing with "unknown" also gives "unknown". Always write `IS NULL`.

slides.title: Aliases and fully qualified column names
slides.body:
When joining several tables, some share column names (`id`, `created_at`). Set **table aliases** and always write `bảng.cột`:

~~~sql
SELECT p.id, u.username, p.created_at
FROM posts AS p
JOIN users AS u ON u.id = p.user_id;
~~~

Without the prefix, MySQL reports *Column 'id' in field list is ambiguous* (#1052).

Column aliases: `COUNT(l.user_id) AS likes` — the name `likes` is exactly the array key that PHP receives at step 11 (`$post['likes']`), so name it clearly, in lowercase.

slides.title: Counting hearts: LEFT JOIN + GROUP BY
slides.body:
~~~sql
SELECT p.id, p.body, COUNT(l.user_id) AS likes
FROM posts AS p
LEFT JOIN likes AS l ON l.post_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.body;
~~~

- `LEFT JOIN` multiplies each post into multiple rows: one row per heart (or one NULL row if there are no hearts).
- `GROUP BY p.id` collapses the rows of the same post into one.
- `COUNT(l.user_id)` counts the **non-NULL** values, so a post with no hearts shows **0**. If you write `COUNT(*)`, a post with no hearts shows **1** (it counts the NULL row too), a classic mistake.

Every column in `SELECT` that is not inside an aggregate function must appear in `GROUP BY`; MySQL 8 with `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` enabled will raise an error if one is missing.

The yellow warning *"does not contain a unique column"* only means phpMyAdmin does not allow direct editing of results that have `GROUP BY` — it is not an error.

slides.title: HAVING and subqueries
slides.body:
**HAVING** filters **after** grouping:

~~~sql
SELECT u.username, COUNT(*) AS post_count
FROM posts AS p JOIN users AS u ON u.id = p.user_id
GROUP BY u.username
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;      -- WHERE không làm được: lúc WHERE chạy chưa đếm
~~~

**Subquery** is a `SELECT` nested inside another statement:

~~~sql
-- Bài của những người user 1 theo dõi
WHERE p.user_id IN (SELECT followee_id FROM follows WHERE follower_id = 1)

-- Đếm ngay trong SELECT (truy vấn con tương quan)
(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM follows WHERE followee_id = u.id) AS followers
~~~

A correlated subquery re-runs for **every** outer row. That's fine for a personal page, but don't use it on a list of thousands of rows.

slides.title: Pagination
slides.body:
**OFFSET**: easy to write, fits "page 1, 2, 3":

~~~sql
-- trang n (bắt đầu từ 1), mỗi trang 20 bài
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20 * (n - 1);
~~~

**Keyset** (cursor): fits infinite scrolling like a social feed:

~~~sql
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-10-27 04:05:59', 7)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
~~~

Always add `id` to `ORDER BY` as a **tiebreaker key**. When two posts share a timestamp, their order stays fixed, so no post is repeated or skipped across pages.

slides.title: Safe INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
slides.body:
~~~sql
INSERT INTO likes (user_id, post_id) VALUES (2, 4);

UPDATE posts
SET body = 'Nội dung mới', updated_at = NOW()
WHERE id = 3 AND user_id = 1;          -- chỉ sửa khi ĐÚNG chủ bài

DELETE FROM likes WHERE user_id = 2 AND post_id = 4;
~~~

Three habits of people who do this for real:

1. Write the `WHERE` **first**, then write the `SET`/`DELETE`.
2. Run the `SELECT` with that exact `WHERE` first to see **which rows** will be affected.
3. Read the "*N rows affected*" count after running. Expect 1 and get 0? The condition is wrong (for example, not the post owner). Get 8? Stop immediately.

`WHERE id = 3 AND user_id = 1` is **an ownership check right inside the SQL**, the main technique of step 13.

step11.summary: Connect PHP to MySQL using PDO: DSN string, three required options, prepared statements with named parameters, fetch, lastInsertId, transactions and error handling — the Nhịp feed reads and writes a real database.

slides.title: Connecting the two halves of stage 2
slides.body:
Step 8 has PHP that render pages but save data to a JSON file. Steps 9–10 have a database and queries but only run in phpMyAdmin. This step **joins the two halves**: PHP sends the exact SQL statements you wrote to MySQL and gets the results back as an array.

The tool is **PDO** (PHP Data Objects), a database access layer built into PHP that uses one syntax for MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, and more. At the end of this step, the `posts.json` file and the `data/` folder are **deleted outright**.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Open a PDO connection with the DSN and the **three options** every serious project sets.
2. Store the connection details in **a separate config file** with a template.
3. Run queries as **prepared statements** with `?` and `:ten` parameters.
4. Fetch data with `fetch`, `fetchAll`, and `fetchColumn`; get the new id with `lastInsertId`.
5. Group multiple statements into a **transaction** starting with PHP.
6. Read PDO error messages and know why they must never be exposed.
7. Move every SQL into `includes/posts.php`, `includes/users.php`.

slides.title: Prepared statements: the template and the data travel separately
slides.body:
With prepared statements, the SQL statement is sent to MySQL **first**, with placeholders `?` or `:body`. MySQL parses the statement and "locks" it into a fixed template. The user's data is sent **afterward** and fills only the placeholders, as **values**.

Even if the user types `'); DROP TABLE posts; --`, that string is just the content of a post. It cannot become a SQL command, because the command template was fixed beforehand. This is how you stop **SQL Injection** at the root (step 17 will try attacking it).

slides.title: From Request to Data Flow
slides.body:
One load of `index.php` passes through all four layers:

1. Apache receives `GET /nhip/index.php`.
2. PHP runs `bootstrap.php` → `db()` opens **one** TCP connection to MySQL on port 3306.
3. `feed_posts()` sends the feed query and gets back an array of associative arrays.
4. The `foreach` loop prints each post via `includes/post.php`.
5. PHP ends → the connection closes automatically.

One connection per request; don't open a new connection inside the loop.

slides.title: PDO in the PHP documentation
slides.body:
PDO has been available since PHP 5.1 (2005) and is the database access method that the PHP Manual recommends for new code, along with `mysqli`. The old `mysql_*` function has been **completely removed** from PHP 7 — any guide that still uses `mysql_query` is outdated.

From PHP 8.0 onward, the default error mode of PDO is `ERRMODE_EXCEPTION`; we still state it explicitly so the code also runs correctly on older servers.

> The PHP Group (2025) *PHP Data Objects*, PHP Manual. Available at: https://www.php.net/manual/en/book.pdo.php
>
> The PHP Group (2025) *Prepared statements and stored procedures*, PHP Manual. Available at: https://www.php.net/manual/en/pdo.prepared-statements.php

slides.title: OWASP: parameterization is the first line of defense
slides.body:
The OWASP SQL Injection prevention guide ranks **prepared statements (parameterized queries)** as defense number 1, ahead of stored procedures and allowlist-based input validation. Manual "escaping" is explicitly marked as **not recommended**.

OWASP also notes one exception: parameters can only replace **values**, not **table names, column names, or sort direction**. For those, choose from an allowlist written in the code.

> OWASP Foundation (2025) *SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
>
> OWASP Foundation (2025) *Query Parameterization Cheat Sheet*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Query_Parameterization_Cheat_Sheet.html

slides.title: Each layer does one job
slides.body:
Design the code for PHP of Nhịp from now on:

| File | Knows | Doesn't know |
|---|---|---|
| `config.php` | Password, database name | Everything else |
| `db.php` | How to open the connection | Which tables, which SQL statements |
| `posts.php`, `users.php` | SQL statements | HTML, `$_POST` |
| `index.php`, `profile.php` | `$_GET`/`$_POST`, which functions to call | SQL |
| `header.php`, `post.php` | HTML | SQL, `$_POST` |

Easy rule: **pages never write SQL, and functions SQL never print HTML.** To change how lives are counted, edit one place only; to change the card look, also one place only. Step 20 gives the official name for this split: Model – View – Controller.

slides.title: DSN and three options
slides.body:
~~~php
$dsn = 'mysql:host=127.0.0.1;dbname=nhip;charset=utf8mb4';
$pdo = new PDO($dsn, 'root', '', [
    PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE            => PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION,
    PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE => PDO::FETCH_ASSOC,
    PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES   => false,
]);
~~~

- **DSN** (Data Source Name): database type, server, database name and, very importantly, `charset=utf8mb4`. Without the charset, Vietnamese text turns into `Nh?p`.
- `ERRMODE_EXCEPTION`: if SQL is wrong, it **throws an exception** instead of silently returning `false`.
- `FETCH_ASSOC`: each row is `['id' => 1, 'body' => '…']`, with no extra numeric keys.
- `EMULATE_PREPARES => false`: use MySQL's **real** prepared statements, and numbers come back as the correct `int` type.

`127.0.0.1` instead of `localhost`: on macOS/Linux, `localhost` makes PDO try to connect through a file socket; use an IP to force TCP through port 3306 like phpMyAdmin.

slides.title: Configuration files and templates
slides.body:
`config.php` **returns** an array (`return [...]`), so read it with:

~~~php
$config = require __DIR__ . '/config.php';
echo $config['db_name'];   // nhip
~~~

Two files come as a pair:

- `config.sample.php`: sample values, **included** in the shared source code so others know what to fill in.
- `config.php`: your machine's real values, **never** pushed to Git or shared with anyone (step 20 adds it to `.gitignore`).

When deploying to hosting at step 24, you only edit `config.php` on the server: the database server name, account, password, and `debug => false`.

slides.title: prepare, execute, and two kinds of placeholders
Get the result
slides.body:
| Method | Returns | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `fetchAll()` | Array of all rows (empty if none) | List of posts |
| `fetch()` | One row, or `false` | Find one user |
| `fetchColumn()` | Value of the first column of the first row | `SELECT COUNT(*)` |
| `rowCount()` | Number of rows affected by `UPDATE`/`DELETE` | Check whether an update/delete had any effect |
| `db()->lastInsertId()` | id just assigned by `AUTO_INCREMENT` | After `INSERT` |

`fetch()` returns `false` when there are no rows. The `find_user_by_username` function converts it to `null`, so the return type `?array` is clear and the calling page only needs to check `=== null`.

slides.title: Transactions in PHP
Reading PDO errors

image.alt: Blank page with the line Fatal error: Uncaught PDOException: SQLSTATE[HY000] [1049] Unknown database 'nhipp' in .../includes/db.php:14, followed by Stack trace through PDO->__construct, db(), feed_posts()
image.caption: Typed db_name wrong as nhipp. Read from left to right: exception type → error code MySQL → message → file:line → call path.

slides.body:
How to read it:

- `[1049] Unknown database` means the database name is wrong. Other common ones: `[1045] Access denied` (wrong username or password), `[2002] Connection refused` (MySQL not enabled in XAMPP), `[1146] Table doesn't exist`, `[1064] syntax error`.
- Read a *stack trace* from the bottom up: `index.php` line 20 calls `feed_posts()`, which calls `db()`, and `db()` fails at line 14.
- PHP 8.2 masks the password automatically as `SensitiveParameterValue`, but the server path and account name are still exposed. So `debug` must be `false` on hosting (step 19 builds a friendly error page).

slides.title: Reading numbers from the database
slides.body:
Results from PDO always need casting when passed into a typed function:

~~~php
$user = find_user_by_username('lan.code');
posts_by_user((int) $user['id']);       // strict_types: phải là int
echo (int) $post['likes'];              // số in thẳng, không cần e()
~~~

With `EMULATE_PREPARES => false`, MySQL returns column `INT` as `int` of PHP, but `COUNT()` in a subquery, or values on hosting with a different configuration, can come back as a `"4"` string. Casting `(int)` at the point of use is a cheap, safe habit.

MySQL recognizes that `u.username` depends on `p.id` through the primary key, so `GROUP BY p.id` is all it needs; if your hosting reports the error `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY`, list all the columns as in step 10.

slides.body: `bootstrap.php` is the shared entry point: every page only needs one line of `require`. It also turns error display on or off according to `debug` in the config.

step11.title: 11. PDO: join PHP with MySQL using a prepared statement

step12.summary: Accounts for Nhịp: sign-up with validation, hash passwords with password_hash, log in with password_verify, sessions and secure cookies, regenerate the session ID, log out via POST and flash messages.

slides.title: Who is using Nhịp?
slides.body:
Up to step 11, every post is published by "user number 1", a hard-coded `CURRENT_USER_ID = 1`. A social network must know **who** is sending the request, because every later permission (editing your own post, following, liking) depends on that answer.

But HTTP remembers nothing between two requests (see step 8). This step solves that: how does the server **recognize the same person** across hundreds of requests without ever storing their password.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Understand the difference between **authentication** (who you are) and **authorization** (what you are allowed to do).
2. Hash passwords with `password_hash`, verify with `password_verify`, and know why **not** to use `md5`/`sha1`.
3. Use **sessions**: the cookie carries a session ID, and the server holds the session data.
4. Set the cookie flags `HttpOnly`, `SameSite`; regenerate the session ID on login.
5. Write a sign-up page that validates each field and catches duplicate errors from the database.
6. Log in with username **or** email, with errors that reveal no information.
7. Log out with **POST**; show a one-time message (flash).

slides.title: Session: the cookie carries only one ID
slides.body:
1. Log in correctly → PHP creates a session and writes `$_SESSION['user_id'] = 1` to a **file on the server**.
2. The response includes `Set-Cookie: nhip_session=k3f9…`, which is just a long random string.
3. On every later request, the browser automatically sends that cookie back.
4. `session_start()` uses the token to open the exact session file → PHP knows this is user 1.

The user **cannot** edit `user_id`, because it isn't stored in the browser. The only thing that must be protected is the session token. Whoever holds the token "becomes" you.

slides.title: One-way, salted hashing
slides.body:
`password_hash('nhip-demo-2026', PASSWORD_DEFAULT)` produces a string like this:

~~~text
$2y$10$h0dW2ml77LkJMSpa1YcEbu…
 │   │  └─ muối (22 ký tự) + kết quả băm
 │   └──── chi phí: 2^10 vòng lặp
 └──────── thuật toán: bcrypt
~~~

- **One-way**: no function can "reverse" the hash back into the password.
- **Random salt**: two people with the same password still get two different hashes.
- **Deliberately slow**: each attempt takes a few tens of milliseconds. That is negligible for a legitimate user logging in, but it turns brute-forcing billions of passwords into decades.

slides.title: NIST and OWASP recommendations
slides.body:
NIST's digital identity guidelines (SP 800-63B) require passwords to be stored with a **salted, cost-intensive** hash, allow passwords at least 64 characters long, and **do not** impose rules like "must include a special character" or periodic password changes. Length matters more than complexity.

OWASP places bcrypt among acceptable algorithms (along with Argon2id and scrypt), and notes that bcrypt only uses the **first 72 bytes** of a password, so Nhịp caps 72.

> National Institute of Standards and Technology (2024) *SP 800-63B-4: Digital Identity Guidelines — Authentication and Authenticator Management*. Gaithersburg: NIST. doi:10.6028/NIST.SP.800-63b-4
>
> OWASP Foundation (2025) *Password Storage Cheat Sheet*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html

slides.title: Cookies and sessions according to the standard
slides.body:
Cookies are defined in RFC 6265 by the IETF. The `HttpOnly` attribute prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie (reducing damage when XSS occurs); `SameSite` determines whether the cookie is sent with cross-site requests, the foundation of defense against CSRF at step 18.

OWASP recommends **changing the session ID immediately after login** to prevent *session fixation* attacks: an attacker plants a session ID in the victim's browser, waits for the victim to log in, then reuses that ID.

> Barth, A. (2011) *RFC 6265: HTTP State Management Mechanism*. IETF. Available at: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265
>
> OWASP Foundation (2025) *Session Management Cheat Sheet*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html

slides.title: Designing the account flow
slides.body:
| Page | GET | POST |
|---|---|---|
| `register.php` | Empty form | Validate → create account → sign in right away → feed |
| `login.php` | Form | Check password → rotate session ID → feed |
| `logout.php` | **405** | Delete session + cookie → feed |
| `index.php` | Anyone can view | Must be signed in to post |

The four functions in `includes/auth.php` encapsulate all session details: `start_session()`, `current_user()`, `require_login()`, `login_user()`/`logout_user()`. Pages only call these functions — no page touches `$_SESSION['user_id']` directly.

slides.title: What NOT to do
slides.body:
- **Don't** store plaintext passwords, even "temporarily", even in log files.
- **Don't** write your own hashing algorithm, and **don't** use `md5()`/`sha1()`/`hash('sha256', …)` for passwords: they are designed to be **fast**, so a graphics card can try billions of guesses per second.
- **Don't** report "email does not exist" or "wrong password" separately. Use one generic message so attackers can't discover who has an account.
- **Don't** store `user_id` in a plain cookie: if a user changes `1` to `2`, they become someone else.
- **Don't** log out via a GET link.

slides.title: password_hash and password_verify
session_start and cookie flags
Regenerate the session ID on login
current_user and require_login
slides.body:
~~~php
$me = current_user();          // mảng người dùng hoặc null — trang công khai
$me = require_login();         // chưa đăng nhập → chuyển login.php — trang riêng tư
~~~

`current_user()` does not trust stale session data: it **re-reads from the database** via `user_id`. If the account has been deleted, the next load automatically turns the user into a guest. The `static` variable holds the result so the whole page queries only once.

Place `require_login()` **inside the POST branch** of `index.php`: guests can still read the feed, but the server blocks posting, even if someone builds a form and submits it directly.

slides.title: Registration validation
slides.body:
| Field | Rule | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| `username` | 3–30 characters `a-z 0-9 . _` | `preg_match('/^[a-z0-9._]{3,30}$/', …)` |
| `display_name` | 1–60 characters, diacritics allowed | `mb_strlen` |
| `email` | Valid format | `filter_var(…, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)` |
| `password` | 8–72 bytes | `strlen` (bcrypt counts bytes) |
| `password_confirm` | Unique `password` | `!==` |

Usernames are `strtolower` before being checked: `Lan.Code` and `lan.code` are the same.

**Duplicate** name/email checks must not be done with `SELECT` first and then `INSERT`: two people signing up at the same time would slip through. Just `INSERT`, let the unique constraint `UNIQUE` (step 9) reject it, then require `PDOException` with the code **23000**.

slides.title: Report errors in the right place, easy to reach

image.alt: The Create Account page Nhịp with three red-bordered fields: the username 'hoa test' says only lowercase unaccented letters, digits, dots, and underscores are allowed; the email 'hoa@' says it is invalid; the password says it must be 8–72 characters
image.caption: Submitting an invalid form: each error sits directly under its own field, and the value already typed is kept (except for the password).

slides.body:
Three details make the form easy to use, including for screen readers:

- The error field has `aria-invalid="true"` (CSS outlines it in red based on exactly this attribute).
- `aria-describedby` links the field to its error line, so the screen reader announces the error when the user enters the field.
- `autocomplete="new-password"` / `"current-password"` so the browser's password manager suggests a strong password and autofills it in the right place.

The form sets `novalidate` so the **server's** validation is visible; the production version may remove this attribute.

slides.title: Login reveals nothing

image.alt: The login page showing lan.code in the username field and the red error line "Username or password is incorrect."
image.caption: A wrong password and a wrong username both get the same single message.

slides.body:
Beyond the error text itself, the **response time** can also leak information. If the username does not exist and the reply comes back instantly, while a real username takes 60 ms to `password_verify`, an attacker can measure the timing and learn which accounts exist.

So `verify_login` still hashes once when the user is not found. Step 19 adds a **limit on attempts** to block password guessing.

slides.title: Real hashes in the database

image.alt: Result of SELECT id, username, password_hash FROM users: lan.code and hoa.test have different $2y$10$ strings, while minh.dev, an.ui, khoa.data and mai.sec share the same $2y$12$N5Wu3hqguk6TTH…
image.caption: The four sample accounts share one string because seed.sql copies in ONE precomputed hash. lan.code was rehashed when it logged in on PHP 8.2.

slides.body:
Observations:

- Every string starts with `$2y$` — bcrypt. No password can be read back.
- `lan.code` at load time is `$2y$12$…`; after one successful login it becomes `$2y$10$…` with a **new salt**: that is the `password_needs_rehash` at work.
- `hoa.test` (signed up through the site) gets its own salt. If you sign up another account with the same password, the hash string still comes out completely different.

slides.body: New file. Add `require __DIR__ . '/auth.php';` and `start_session();` to the end of `bootstrap.php`. The session must start before `header.php` prints anything.

slides.body: Add three functions to `includes/users.php`. `find_user_by_id` is used for `current_user()`. `validate_registration` returns errors keyed by field name, so the page prints each one under the right input.

image.caption: Log in as lan.code / nhip-demo-2026: the menu changes and the compose box appears.

2. *Application → Cookies*: `nhip_session` has the **HttpOnly ✓** and **SameSite Lax** columns.

- [ ] The `users` table has only `password_hash` of the form `$2y$…`.
- [ ] Log in with username **or** email; on a wrong entry, one generic error message.

step13.summary: Complete CRUD for posts: detail page, edit, delete; check ownership inside the SQL statement; distinguish 403, 404, 405; read IDs safely and ask for confirmation before deleting.

slides.title: From "can post" to "can manage"
slides.body:
Nhịp already has **C** (Create — publish a post) and **R** (Read — the feed). A real product also needs **U** (Update — fix a typo) and **D** (Delete — remove a post published by mistake).

These two operations are much more dangerous: they **change existing data**. If the check is wrong, anyone can edit or delete someone else's post — the authorization bug ranks number 1 in the OWASP Top 10. This step teaches how to write U and D so that bug cannot happen.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Map CRUD ↔ HTTP method ↔ SQL statement.
2. Write the `post.php?id=` detail page and the `edit.php?id=` edit page.
3. Delete via **POST** to `delete.php`, with a confirmation prompt.
4. Check ownership **inside the SQL statement** (`WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?`) and read `rowCount()`.
5. Read the id from the address using `filter_var` and return exactly **403 / 404 / 405**.
6. Show the "edited" mark using the `updated_at` column.

slides.title: CRUD, HTTP and SQL
slides.body:
| Action | Page Nhịp | HTTP | SQL |
|---|---|---|---|
| Create | `index.php` | POST | `INSERT` |
| Read | `index.php`, `post.php?id=3` | GET | `SELECT` |
| Update | `edit.php?id=3` | GET (form) → POST | `UPDATE … WHERE id AND user_id` |
| Delete | `delete.php` | POST | `DELETE … WHERE id AND user_id` |

General rule: **GET is read-only**. Every write operation uses POST, because browsers, search engines and caches may re-issue a GET at any time.

slides.title: Two-layer permission checks
slides.body:
**UI layer**: only the post's author sees the Edit/Delete buttons. This is for **usability**, not security. Anyone can type `edit.php?id=2` into the address bar.

**Server layer**: `edit.php` compares the post's `user_id` with the currently logged-in user. `UPDATE`/`DELETE` add the extra condition `user_id = ?`. If the user is not the author, **no row matches**, even if the PHP code above has a mistake.

Two layers, but only the second one is security.

slides.title: Broken Access Control — OWASP A01
slides.body:
In the OWASP Top 10 **2025**, *Broken Access Control* ranks **#1** (as in the 2021 edition): **100%** of the applications tested had at least one form of this flaw, and it is the category with the most occurrences in the entire dataset. The most common form is **IDOR** (Insecure Direct Object Reference): changing the id in the address to view or edit another person's object.

OWASP recommends: **deny by default**, enforce authorization checks in trusted server-side code for **each** request, implement the authorization mechanism **once** and reuse it across the application, and bind operations to the record's owner.

> OWASP Foundation (2025) *A01:2025 – Broken Access Control*, OWASP Top 10:2025. Available at: https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A01_2025-Broken_Access_Control/
>
> OWASP Foundation (2025) *Authorization Cheat Sheet*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html

slides.title: Method semantics and status codes
slides.body:
RFC 9110 defines GET as a **safe** method (it does not change server state) and specifies the meaning of the error codes:

- **403 Forbidden**: the server understands the request but **refuses** to fulfil it.
- **404 Not Found**: the resource was not found, *or* the server **does not want to reveal** that it exists.
- **405 Method Not Allowed**: the resource exists, but does not accept this method.

Note the second clause of 404: the standard HTTP allows 404 to be returned instead of 403 to avoid leaking information. Nhịp uses exactly this at `delete.php`.

> Fielding, R., Nottingham, M. and Reschke, J. (2022) *RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics*, §9.2.1, §15.5.4–15.5.6. IETF. Available at: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

slides.title: Three pages, three functions
slides.body:
| File | Task |
|---|---|
| `post.php?id=` | One post + its answers (step 15). Linked from each post's timestamp. |
| `edit.php?id=` | GET: pre-filled form. POST: validate → `update_post` → back to `post.php`. |
| `delete.php` | POST only: `delete_post` → back to the feed. |

Three new functions in `posts.php`: `find_post`, `update_post`, `delete_post`. Two helpers in `helpers.php`: `abort()` renders the error page with a status code, and `id_param()` reads a safe id.

The `includes/post.php` post card decides for itself whether to show the Edit/Delete buttons, based on `current_user()`.

slides.title: Safe id parsing
Owner-conditioned UPDATE
slides.body:
~~~php
$stmt = db()->prepare('
    UPDATE posts SET body = :body, updated_at = NOW()
    WHERE id = :id AND user_id = :user_id');
$stmt->execute(['body' => $body, 'id' => $id, 'user_id' => $me['id']]);
return $stmt->rowCount() === 1;
~~~

- `user_id` comes from the **session** (`require_login()`), never from the form.
- `rowCount()` reports how many rows changed: 1 means success, 0 means “none of your posts has this id”.
- `updated_at = NOW()` records when the edit happened; the post card shows “· edited” when this column is not NULL.

A small caveat of MySQL: if the new content is **identical** to the old content, `body` does not change but `updated_at` still does → `rowCount()` is still 1.

slides.title: DELETE and CASCADE
403, 404 or 405?
slides.body:
| Situation | Nhịp returns | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `edit.php?id=abc` | 404 | malformed id = no resource |
| `edit.php?id=999` (doesn't exist) | 404 | |
| `edit.php?id=2` (someone else's post) | **403** | Public post, everyone knows it exists → be honest: no permission |
| `POST delete.php` someone else's post id | **404** | Doesn't distinguish "doesn't exist" from "not yours": one sentence, one code |
| `GET delete.php` | 405 | Delete accepts only POST |
| Not logged in | 303 → `login.php` | `require_login()` |

The `abort()` function consolidates this: it sets the status code, renders the error page inside the shared Nhịp layout, then `exit`.

slides.title: Confirm before deleting
slides.body:
Delete forms with data attributes:

~~~html
<form method="post" action="delete.php" data-confirm="Xoá bài này? Không hoàn tác được.">
~~~

`js/app.js` has **one** `submit` listener for the whole page (event delegation — step 6): any form that has `data-confirm` asks `confirm()` before submitting.

Why not write `onsubmit="return confirm(...)"` directly in HTML? Step 18 turns on a **Content Security Policy** that forbids any JavaScript code written inside HTML attributes. Today's approach is already ready for that.

With JavaScript turned off, the form still submits (without asking again). The feature doesn't depend on JavaScript; JavaScript only improves the experience.

slides.title: The vulnerability is still pending at step 18
slides.body:
Try building a HTML page in another folder, containing:

~~~html
<form method="post" action="http://localhost/nhip/delete.php">
  <input type="hidden" name="id" value="3">
</form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>
~~~

If Lan is logged in to Nhịp and opens that page, would the post 3 get deleted? This is called **CSRF** (Cross-Site Request Forgery). The cookie `SameSite=Lax` at step 12 already blocks this case in modern browsers, but you shouldn't rely on a single layer. Step 18 adds an **anti-CSRF token** to every POST form.

step14.summary: Full profile page: edit your profile, safely upload an avatar (content check, random renaming, blocking code execution), follow / unfollow, and a "Following" feed.

slides.title: One corner for everyone
slides.body:
Social networks differ from forums in one way: you **choose whom to listen to**. This step gives Nhịp three things that make that possible:

1. **Profile** for each person: display name, bio, avatar.
2. **Follow**: one click creates a relation in the `follows` table (designed in step 9).
3. **Following feed**: only posts from the people you chose.

It also includes the most dangerous feature of the course so far: **receiving files from strangers** and storing them on the server.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Write the `settings.php` profile-edit page, validating each field as in step 12.
2. Send files using `enctype="multipart/form-data"` and read `$_FILES`.
3. Check uploaded files **by content** (finfo, getimagesize), limit size, rename randomly.
4. Forbid the upload directory from running code using `.htaccess`.
5. Follow / unfollow via POST; use `INSERT IGNORE` for harmless repeated operations.
6. Query the "Following" feed with a subquery `IN`.
7. Represent button state with `aria-pressed`.

slides.title: Follow Graph
slides.body:
The `follows` table is a **directed graph**: each row is an arrow from the follower to the followed user.

- Lan's number of **followers** = number of arrows **pointing into** Lan: `COUNT(*) WHERE followee_id = 1`.
- Number **following** = number of arrows **pointing out**: `COUNT(*) WHERE follower_id = 1`.
- Two arrows in opposite directions between two people = **mutual follow** (friends).

Large social networks suggest "people you may know" precisely by walking these arrows two steps.

slides.title: The Path of an Uploaded File
slides.body:
1. The browser sends the file in the body of the request `multipart/form-data`.
2. PHP saves it temporarily to the system temp directory under a random name, recording the info in `$_FILES['avatar']`.
3. Nhịp checks: whether there was an upload error, whether it exceeds 2 MB, whether the **content** is an image.
4. `move_uploaded_file` moves the file to `uploads/avatars/` with a **new name assigned by the server**.
5. The relative path is saved to `users.avatar`.

If the 3 step is skipped, the temp file is automatically deleted when PHP finishes running.

slides.title: OWASP on File Upload
slides.body:
The *File Upload* guidance from OWASP lists the required measures:

- Allow only an **approved list of extensions/types**, not block by a blacklist.
- **Do not trust** `Content-Type` sent by the client; check the **file signature** (magic bytes).
- **Rename** the file with a value generated by the application.
- **Limit file size**.
- Store files outside the web root if possible; otherwise, **forbid execution** in the storage directory.

File upload vulnerabilities fall under *Injection* and *Security Misconfiguration*: a `.php` file that gets into the web directory lets an attacker run commands on your server.

> OWASP Foundation (2025) *File Upload Cheat Sheet*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html

slides.title: Social Networks Are a Graph
slides.body:
Research on online social networks models the "follow" relationship as a directed graph and identifies a pattern that repeats across every platform: the distribution of follower counts is **highly skewed** (a few accounts have enormous numbers, most have few), and the rate of mutual follows is much lower than in two-way friend networks.

The technical implication for Nhịp: never load the **entire** follower list onto the page, since a famous account can have millions of rows. Always `COUNT`, and paginate when you need to list them.

> Kwak, H., Lee, C., Park, H. and Moon, S. (2010) 'What is Twitter, a social network or a news media?', *Proceedings of the 19th International Conference on World Wide Web*, pp. 591–600. doi:10.1145/1772690.1772751

slides.title: Designing the New Parts
slides.body:
| File | Task |
|---|---|
| `settings.php` | Edit display name, bio, avatar |
| `follow.php` | POST `user_id` + `action=follow/unfollow` → back to profile page |
| `includes/follows.php` | `is_following`, `follow`, `unfollow`, `following_feed` |
| `includes/uploads.php` | `save_avatar`, `delete_avatar` |
| `uploads/avatars/` + `uploads/.htaccess` | Where images are stored, forbid code execution |
| `profile.php` | "Edit profile" button (own profile) or "Follow"/"Following" |
| `index.php?tab=following` | Following feed |

The follow button is **a POST form**, not a link: following is a write action.

slides.title: multipart/form-data and $_FILES
slides.body:
~~~html
<form method="post" action="settings.php" enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <input id="avatar" name="avatar" type="file" accept="image/jpeg,image/png,image/webp">
~~~

Without `enctype`, the browser only sends the file **name**, not its content. `accept` filters files in the picker dialog — convenient for users, **not** a security check.

PHP fills in `$_FILES['avatar']`:

| Field | Example | Trusted? |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `anh-cua-toi.jpg` | No — set by user |
| `type` | `image/jpeg` | No — browser guesses, can be edited |
| `tmp_name` | `/tmp/phpA1b2C3` | Yes — PHP sets it |
| `error` | `UPLOAD_ERR_OK` (0) | Yes |
| `size` | `2688` | Yes |

slides.title: Check Files by Content
Random Names and Banning Code Execution
slides.body:
~~~php
$name = bin2hex(random_bytes(16)) . '.' . AVATAR_TYPES[$mime];
// 55c8bcc37640e1719e9b88c0b31d6ee1.jpg
move_uploaded_file($file['tmp_name'], AVATAR_DIR . $name);
~~~

The server generates the name with `random_bytes` (a cryptographically secure random source): it won't overwrite others' files, can't be guessed, and carries no odd characters such as `../` or `shell.php.jpg`.

The last line of defense — `uploads/.htaccess`:

~~~apache
<FilesMatch "\.(php|phtml|phar|php[0-9])$">
  Require all denied
</FilesMatch>
Options -Indexes
~~~

Even if a `.php` file somehow gets in, Apache also refuses to serve it. `-Indexes` forbids listing the directory's files.

slides.title: Follow: INSERT IGNORE
slides.body:
~~~php
db()->prepare('INSERT IGNORE INTO follows (follower_id, followee_id) VALUES (?, ?)')
    ->execute([$me, $target]);
~~~

If a user taps "Follow" twice (slow network, double-click), the second request violates the compound primary key. `INSERT IGNORE` turns that duplicate error into a silent no-op. The end result is still correct: **one** row. An operation that produces the same result whether it runs once or many times is called **idempotent**.

`DELETE` for unfollow is already idempotent: deleting a row that doesn't exist does nothing.

Self-following is blocked three ways: the button is hidden, `follow()` returns early, and the table's `CHECK` constraint (step 9).

slides.title: Following Feed
slides.body:
~~~sql
WHERE p.parent_id IS NULL
  AND (p.user_id = :me
       OR p.user_id IN (SELECT followee_id FROM follows WHERE follower_id = :me2))
~~~

- Include the user's **own** posts too, so a post they just published still shows up in this tab.
- `:me` and `:me2` carry the same value but must be two names: with a real prepared statement (`EMULATE_PREPARES => false`), each placeholder can be used only **once**.
- `bindValue(..., PDO::PARAM_INT)` for every parameter, because `LIMIT` requires an integer.

The tab is selected via `?tab=following`. Guests (not logged in) always see the Newest tab. The `$tab` variable accepts only the two valid values; anything else falls back to the default.

slides.title: Nhịp more lively
slides.body:
Up to step 14, every action reloads the whole page. For "Follow" that's acceptable, but not for liking: users tap the heart dozens of times while scrolling the feed, and jumping back to the top each time is a broken experience.

This step reconnects the **event → data → re-render** loop from step 6, but the data now lives on the server: JavaScript sends a background request using **Fetch**, PHP returns **JSON**, and JavaScript only re-renders the button that was just pressed.

Added alongside are two features that make a social network: **conversation** (nested replies) and **search**.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Send a background POST request using `fetch` + `FormData`, read JSON and the status code.
2. Write one PHP file that serves **both** JSON and HTML depending on the `Accept` header. Features still work with JavaScript turned off.
3. Toggle the like with `INSERT IGNORE` + `rowCount()`.
4. Mark "liked" for the whole list with **one** `IN (?, ?, …)` query.
5. Fetch the entire multi-level reply chain with `WITH RECURSIVE`, build the tree in PHP, and print it with a **recursive function**.
6. Search with `LIKE`, escape `%` and the user's `_`.

slides.title: Fetch: the page doesn't reload
slides.body:
1. User clicks ♥ → the small form's `submit` event around the button.
2. `app.js` calls `event.preventDefault()`, then `fetch('like.php', { method: 'POST', body: FormData, headers: { Accept: 'application/json' } })`.
3. `like.php` sees `Accept: application/json` → returns `{"liked": true, "likes": 5}`.
4. `app.js` updates `aria-pressed` and the count.

Without JavaScript: step 2 doesn't happen, the form submits normally, and `like.php` doesn't receive the `Accept` JSON header, so it redirects back to the lesson page. One file, two modes of use: this is called **progressive enhancement**.

slides.title: From a flat list to a tree
slides.body:
The database stores only **one** pointer per post, `parent_id`. To draw the conversation, Nhịp:

1. Use `WITH RECURSIVE` to fetch **all** descendants of the root post in a single query.
2. Group by `parent_id`: `$byParent[5] = [bài 6, bài 9]`, `$byParent[6] = [bài 14]`…
3. The function `$build(5)` fetches the children of 5, then calls itself on `$build(6)`, `$build(14)`… until there are no children left.
4. `render_replies()` renders each level as a `<ol>` nested inside the level above.

The data structure (a tree) determines the code structure (recursion) and the HTML structure (nested lists).

slides.title: Fetch and progressive enhancement
slides.body:
The Fetch API has been standardized by WHATWG as the *Fetch Living Standard*, replacing the old `XMLHttpRequest`. All modern browsers support it. `fetch` returns a **Promise**: `await` waits for the response without blocking the interface.

The concept of *progressive enhancement* (Champeon, 2003) proposes building core functionality with HTML that works everywhere first, then adding JavaScript as a better experience. The GOV.UK team applies this principle to all public services because a significant share of users **cannot run** JavaScript (unstable networks, failed file loads, old browsers), even though they never turned it off.

> WHATWG (2025) *Fetch Living Standard*. Available at: https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/
>
> Government Digital Service (2024) *Building a resilient frontend using progressive enhancement*, GOV.UK Service Manual. Available at: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/using-progressive-enhancement

slides.title: Recursive queries in SQL
slides.body:
The *recursive common table expression* was added to the SQL standard:1999. MySQL has supported it since 8.0, MariaDB since 10.2 — XAMPP 8.2 (MariaDB 10.4), and most hosting today can run it.

A recursive CTE has two parts joined by `UNION ALL`: the **anchor member** (the first level) and the **recursive member** (joins the base table with the CTE's own result). The database repeats the recursive member until it returns no more rows.

> Oracle (2025) *MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: WITH (Common Table Expressions) — Recursive Common Table Expressions*. Available at: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/with.html
>
> MariaDB Foundation (2025) *Recursive Common Table Expressions Overview*. Available at: https://mariadb.com/kb/en/recursive-common-table-expressions-overview/

One PHP file, two kinds of response
Toggling a like in two statements SQL
IN with a dynamic number of placeholders
WITH RECURSIVE
slides.body:
~~~sql
WITH RECURSIVE thread AS (
    SELECT id, 1 AS depth FROM posts WHERE parent_id = 5      -- neo: con trực tiếp
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.id, t.depth + 1
    FROM posts AS c JOIN thread AS t ON c.parent_id = t.id    -- đệ quy: con của con
)
SELECT … FROM posts AS p … JOIN thread AS t ON t.id = p.id
~~~

Iteration 1: `{6, 9}`. Iteration 2: children of 6 and 9 → `{14}`. Iteration 3: children of 14 → `{15}`. Iteration 4: empty → stop.

Because of the foreign key, a post cannot be its own ancestor through the loop (it must exist before its child), so the recursion always stops. For data that might contain cycles, MySQL caps it at `cte_max_recursion_depth` (default 1000).

slides.title: Recursion in PHP
Searching with LIKE
slides.body:
~~~php
$pattern = '%' . addcslashes($query, '%_\\') . '%';
$stmt = db()->prepare(FEED_SQL . ' WHERE p.body LIKE :pattern …');
~~~

In `LIKE`, `%` means "any string" and `_` means "any single character". If users search for `50%` without escaping, their `%` matches everything. `addcslashes` adds a backslash before `\`, `%`, `_` and `\` itself so they become literal characters.

Prepared statements are still **required**: escaping wildcards only changes their meaning within `LIKE`; it does not prevent SQL Injection.

- The `utf8mb4_unicode_ci` collation makes `LIKE` **case-insensitive** and treats `a` ≈ `á`: searching "join" finds "JOIN".
- `LIKE '%…%'` cannot use an index, which is fine for a few thousand lessons. For large data, use a `FULLTEXT` index and `MATCH … AGAINST`.

slides.title: Search forms use GET
slides.body:
~~~html
<form method="get" action="search.php" role="search">
  <input id="q" name="q" type="search" minlength="2" required>
~~~

Search **doesn't change data** → use **GET**: results get their own address (`search.php?q=JOIN`), can be shared with friends, can be bookmarked, and the Back button works correctly.

- `type="search"`: the phone keyboard shows a "Search" button, and there's a quick clear button.
- `role="search"`: screen readers jump straight to the search area.
- The sentence “4 results for “JOIN”” carries `role="status"` so it gets read aloud after the search.
- At least 2 characters in **both** HTML and PHP: searching for a single character scans the whole table and returns meaningless results.
