step16.summary: Security theory background: the CIA triad, authentication, authorization and accountability, secure design principles, the STRIDE threat model, OWASP Top 10:2025, and the ethics and law of testing. Output: the SECURITY.md file of Nhịp.

slides.title: Nhịp is running. Now who will break it?
slides.body:
At the end of 3, Nhịp can do everything a small social network does. But "running" only means **well-meaning users** can use it. The 4 step changes the perspective: you play the **attacker** against your own product, find every way to break it, then patch it at the root.

Security is not a feature added at the end, but **a way of thinking**. This step does not write any PHP lines yet. It gives you the thinking framework and a risk map of Nhịp, the `SECURITY.md` file that the next three steps will mark complete one by one.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Explain the **CIA** triad and map each asset of Nhịp onto it.
2. Distinguish **authentication, authorization, accountability** (AAA).
3. State and apply the classic **secure design principles**.
4. Build a **threat model** with STRIDE: assets, trust boundaries, entry points, threats, countermeasures.
5. Read the **OWASP Top 10:2025** and identify which part of Nhịp each item corresponds to.
6. Know the **ethical and legal boundaries**: only test your own system, or systems you are authorized to test in writing.

slides.title: The CIA triad
slides.body:
- **Confidentiality (Secrecy)**: only authorized people can read the data. *Leaking password hashes or emails* is a violation.
- **Integrity**: data is not modified without authorization. *Someone editing Lan's post* is a violation.
- **Availability**: the system works when needed. *Someone sending a million posts that crashes Nhịp* is a violation.

Every vulnerability breaks at least one of the three. When assessing a bug, the first question is always: *which part of the CIA does it break, and how badly?*

slides.title: Trust boundaries of Nhịp
slides.body:
Data flow diagram (DFD) of Nhịp with the **trust boundaries** (dashed lines):

1. **Browser ↔ Apache/PHP**: everything passing through here is controlled by the user: parameters, forms, cookies, headers, files.
2. **PHP ↔ MySQL**: PHP is the only component allowed to query the database.
3. **PHP ↔ upload directory**: the only place where users can send files to the server.

Vulnerabilities almost always sit **right at the boundary**, where untrusted data enters the trusted zone without being checked.

slides.title: OWASP Top 10:2025

image.alt: The OWASP Top 10:2025 page lists A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Security Misconfiguration, A03 Software Supply Chain Failures, A04 Cryptographic Failures, A05 Injection, A06 Insecure Design, A07 Authentication Failures, A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures, A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures, A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
image.caption: top10.owasp.org/2025 — © OWASP Top 10 Team, licensed under CC BY 3.0. Captured on 27/10/2026.

slides.body: The 2025 edition replaces the 2021 edition. Two new categories: **A03 Software Supply Chain Failures** (flaws in libraries and build tooling) and **A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions** (improper error handling that leaves the system "fail-open" when abnormal conditions occur). Injection drops from #3 to #5, but still has **the most CVEs** of any category.

slides.title: Saltzer and Schroeder's Principles
slides.body:
In 1975, Saltzer and Schroeder (MIT) published eight design principles for information-protection systems, which remain the foundation of every security course. Five of these principles Nhịp apply directly:

- **Economy of mechanism** — the simpler the mechanism, the easier it is to verify: one function `e()`, one function `require_login()`.
- **Fail-safe defaults** — the default is **deny**: if `$tab` is invalid, fall back to "Newest"; if `action` is unknown, do nothing dangerous.
- **Complete mediation** — check permissions on **every** access, not just the first.
- **Least privilege** — each part gets only the permissions it needs (a separate MySQL account in step 24).
- **Open design** — security does not rely on hiding the code; assume the attacker has read all of the source code.

> Saltzer, J.H. and Schroeder, M.D. (1975) 'The protection of information in computer systems', *Proceedings of the IEEE*, 63(9), pp. 1278–1308. doi:10.1109/PROC.1975.9939

slides.title: Modeling Threats
slides.body:
Shostack (Microsoft) organizes threat modeling around **four questions**: *What are we building? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good enough job?* He also popularized the **STRIDE** framework for answering the second question systematically.

The OWASP Top 10:2025 shows that in the test data, **100%** applications have at least one form of access control flaw (A01), and **100%** were tested for Injection (A05). XSS alone had over 30 thousand CVEs; SQL Injection had over 14 thousand.

> Shostack, A. (2014) *Threat Modeling: Designing for Security*. Indianapolis: Wiley.
>
> OWASP Foundation (2025) *OWASP Top 10:2025*. Available at: https://top10.owasp.org/2025/

slides.title: Ethics and the Law
slides.body:
The techniques in this stage are **double-edged**: the same `' OR 1=1 --` chain used to test your own system can be used to break into someone else's. The line is **permission**.

- Only test attacks on **Nhịp on your own localhost**, or on systems the owner has allowed **in writing**.
- In Vietnam, unauthorized intrusion into other people's computer networks or electronic devices is a **crime** under the Penal Code 2015 (amended 2017), and the Law on Cybersecurity 2018 strictly prohibits cyberattacks.
- If you find a vulnerability in someone else's product, report it privately to them (**responsible disclosure**). Do not exploit it, and do not make it public before it is patched.

> National Assembly (2017) *Penal Code No. 100/2015/QH13, amended and supplemented by Law No. 12/2017/QH14*. Hanoi.
>
> National Assembly (2018) *Law on Cybersecurity No. 24/2018/QH14*. Hanoi.

slides.title: Four Questions for Nhịp
slides.body:
1. **What are we building?** A PHP + MySQL application: users register, post, edit and delete their own posts, like, reply, follow, upload avatars, and search.
2. **What can go wrong?** Walk through each **entry point** (each 12 PHP file that receives data) using the six letters of STRIDE.
3. **What are we going to do about it?** Each threat gets a countermeasure and a step that implements it.
4. **Is it good enough?** At the end of step 19, go back through each row of the table and attack it again.

The output of the four questions is `SECURITY.md`, a **living document**. Adding a new feature means adding a row to the entry point table.

slides.title: Authentication, Authorization, Accounting
slides.body:
| | Question | Where Nhịp happens |
|---|---|---|
| **Authentication** | Who are you? | `login.php`, `password_verify`, session (step 12) |
| **Authorization** | What are you allowed to do? | `require_login()`, `AND user_id = ?` (step 13) |
| **Accounting** | Who did what, and when? | Activity log (step 19) |

A classic mistake: *"once logged in, you may do anything."* Logging in only answers the first question. Lan, who is logged in, still must not delete Minh's post. That is the second question, and it must be asked separately for **every** write operation.

In the OWASP Top 10:2025, the first-question flaw is **A07 Authentication Failures**, the second-question flaw is **A01 Broken Access Control**, and the gap on the third question is **A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures**.

slides.title: STRIDE: Six Types of Threats
slides.body:
| Letter | Threat | Violates | Example on Nhịp |
|---|---|---|---|
| **S** | Spoofing | Authentication | Stealing session cookies, guessing passwords |
| **T** | Tampering | Integrity | Changing `id` to edit someone else's post; SQL Injection |
| **R** | Repudiation | Accountability | "I didn't delete that post", with no log to check against |
| **I** | Information disclosure | Confidentiality | Error page prints file paths and database account names |
| **D** | Denial of service | Availability | Sending thousands of posts per second |
| **E** | Elevation of privilege | Authorization | An uploaded `.php` file that runs |

How to use: for **each entry point**, ask the six questions in turn: "Can S happen here? What about T?…". This mechanical method is deliberate, so nothing gets missed.

slides.title: The attack surface of Nhịp
slides.body:
Attack surface = **every place where data from outside comes in**. For Nhịp:

- **12 file PHP** receives `$_GET`/`$_POST` (listed in `SECURITY.md`).
- **1 file intake points**: `settings.php`.
- **Cookies** `nhip_session`.
- **HTTP headers**: `Accept` (read in `like.php`), `User-Agent`, `Referer`…
- **phpMyAdmin** on localhost. Never expose it publicly on real hosting.

Every feature you add widens the surface. The *economy of mechanism* principle suggests: if a feature isn't needed, **don't build it**; if an entry point isn't used, **delete it** (like `hello.php` from step 7; it's time to delete it).

slides.title: Risk = likelihood × impact
slides.body:
Can't patch everything at once. Rank by two axes:

| | Low impact | High impact |
|---|---|---|
| **Easy to exploit** | Post spam | **SQL injection, XSS storage, editing others' posts** |
| **Hard to exploit** | Guessing the next post id | Session hijacking over an unencrypted network |

The top-right cell is priority number 1, which is exactly the content of step 17. The table in OWASP follows the same logic: each item has *Avg Weighted Exploit* (ease of exploitation) and *Avg Weighted Impact* (severity of harm).

Recording the risk scores in `SECURITY.md` helps the whole team agree on **what to do first**, instead of patching by gut feeling.

slides.title: Defense in depth
slides.body:
No single layer is perfect, so Nhịp should stack several **independent** layers against the same threat. Example with a *malicious file upload*:

1. `accept` on the file picker, which helps well-meaning users.
2. Limit the size to 2 MB.
3. `finfo` + `getimagesize` read the **content**.
4. Server-generated random name, with the extension taken from an allowlist.
5. `.htaccess` forbids running `.php` in `uploads/`.
6. (Step 18) Redraw the image with GD to strip any extra data hidden in the file.

An attacker must get through **all** of them; we only need **one** layer to hold. Note that the 1 layer is not a security measure. Any layer that runs on the client is only a convenience.

slides.title: What is Nhịp exposing?
slides.body:
Type `curl -I http://localhost/nhip/index.php` (or DevTools → Network → click the request → *Headers*):

~~~text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.2.4
Set-Cookie: nhip_session=kb5gvl…; path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate
Content-type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
~~~

Read it like an attacker:

- `X-Powered-By: PHP/8.2.4` — states the PHP version outright, which helps look up known vulnerabilities for that exact version (*Information disclosure*).
- No `Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy` — the browser's defensive layers are left empty.
- Cookies already have `HttpOnly`, `SameSite` (step 12) — good.

Step 18 adds security headers; step 24 turns off `X-Powered-By` on hosting (`expose_php = Off`).

slides.title: OWASP Top 10:2025 in Nhịp
slides.body:
| Category | In Nhịp | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| A01 Broken Access Control | Editing/deleting others' posts, CSRF | Step 13, 18 |
| A02 Security Misconfiguration | `debug = true` on hosting, exposed `X-Powered-By` | Step 19, 24 |
| A03 Software Supply Chain | Libraries downloaded from untrusted sources | Nhịp uses no external libraries; step 20 covers Composer |
| A04 Cryptographic Failures | Passwords stored with md5, no HTTPS | Step 12, 24 |
| A05 Injection | SQL Injection, XSS | **Step 17** |
| A06 Insecure Design | No limit on login attempt rate | Step 19 |
| A07 Authentication Failures | Session ID not regenerated, error messages reveal accounts | Step 12, 18 |
| A08 Data Integrity Failures | Uploaded files disguised as images | Step 14, 18 |
| A09 Logging & Alerting Failures | No record of who deleted what | Step 19 |
| A10 Exceptional Conditions | Error PDO exposes details; mid-operation failures leave data half-written | Step 11, 19 |

slides.body: Create a `nhip/SECURITY.md`. Markdown is the default documentation format for every code repository. GitHub also displays the `SECURITY.md` file in the project's *Security* tab.

step16.title: 16. Security theory: threat modeling, CIA, and OWASP Top 10

step17.summary: Understand and prevent the two most common injection flaws: SQL Injection and XSS. Attack a deliberately flawed Nhịp copy in the localhost lab, then confirm that prepared statements, e() and Content-Security-Policy block these attacks in the real version.

slides.title: Why you should attack your own code
slides.body:
You wrote Nhịp correctly from the start: prepared statements (step 11), `e()` (step 8). But "believing it is safe" is different from "knowing it is safe". The only way to be sure a fix works is to **reproduce the exact attack it must block**.

This step does that in a controlled way: in the `lab/` folder (opened only from localhost, step 16) there are three **deliberately flawed** copies of the Nhịp feature. You attack them to see that the vulnerability is **real**, compare with the real version to see that it is safe, and finally add one more layer of defense.

Everything runs only on your machine, with your sample data — that is the ethical and legal condition in step 16.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Explain **injection**: data gets interpreted as commands.
2. Reproduce **SQL Injection**: pull data using `UNION`, bypass login — on the lab copy.
3. Confirm that Nhịp's **prepared statement** is immune, and understand why.
4. Reproduce **XSS storage**: user content runs as code in someone else's browser.
5. Confirm that `e()` (htmlspecialchars) blocks XSS, and add **Content-Security-Policy** as a second layer.
6. Add `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`; mark A05 and part of A01/A07 in `SECURITY.md`.

slides.title: Injection: when data becomes commands
slides.body:
Every injection flaw has the same shape: user data is **concatenated directly** into a string that a **parser** then reads — the database reads SQL, the browser reads HTML/JavaScript.

If the boundary between "the developer's command" and "the user's data" disappears, the attacker writes data so that their part **crosses the boundary** and becomes a command.

The root fix is always the same: **keep data and commands in two separate channels** — parameterize with SQL, encode output with HTML. "Filtering bad characters" only patches the symptom.

slides.title: What SQL Injection looks like
slides.body:
Lab on a string-concatenated search:

~~~php
$sql = "SELECT id, body FROM posts WHERE body LIKE '%$q%'";
~~~

If the user types `q` normally, nothing goes wrong. But if they type a single quote, the statement **breaks** right there: the part after the quote is no longer search text and becomes **SQL**. Adding `UNION SELECT` appends the result of another query, and adding `-- ` (two dashes and a space) **comments out** the rest of the original statement.

slides.title: Injection according to OWASP
slides.body:
In the OWASP Top 10:2025, **A05 Injection** is one of the most tested categories (100% of applications) and has **the most CVEs** of any category — including XSS (high frequency, low impact, more than 30 thousand CVEs) and SQL Injection (low frequency, high impact, more than 14 thousand CVEs).

OWASP defines it: an application is flawed when *user data is not validated or filtered* and *a dynamic, non-parameterized query is passed directly to the interpreter*. The number-one defense is still **parameterized queries**.

> OWASP Foundation (2025) *A05:2025 – Injection*, OWASP Top 10:2025. Available at: https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A05_2025-Injection/
>
> OWASP Foundation (2025) *SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet*; *Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/

slides.title: Origins and defensive standards
slides.body:
The term *SQL injection* was first publicly described in 1998 (Rain Forest Puppy, *Phrack* 54). *Cross-site scripting* was warned about by CERT in 2000. More than two decades later they still top the list — not because they are hard to fix, but because every new developer repeats the same string-concatenation mistake.

Content-Security-Policy, the defense-in-depth layer against XSS, was standardized by W3C (CSP Level 3) and is supported by every modern browser.

> Howard, M. and LeBlanc, D. (2003) *Writing Secure Code*. 2nd edn. Redmond: Microsoft Press.
>
> West, M. (2024) *Content Security Policy Level 3*, W3C Working Draft. Available at: https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/

slides.title: The lab process
slides.body:
For each vulnerability, follow three steps:

1. **Attack the lab copy** (`lab/*.php`, deliberately flawed) → see the attack succeed and understand how it works.
2. **Repeat the same attack on the real version** (`search.php`, `login.php`, `index.php`) → see it fail.
3. **Explain why** the real version is safe, then add one more layer of defense if there is one.

The `lab/` folder contains `.htaccess` holding `Require local`: only your machine can open it, and nobody from the network can reach it. Once this step is done, **delete the whole `lab/` folder** — vulnerable code never lives alongside the real code.

slides.title: 1 attack — UNION pulls hidden data

image.alt: Search lab page: the input contains zzz' UNION SELECT username, password_hash FROM users --, the dark panel shows the SQL query as assembled, and the results table lists each account's username and its $2y$ hash string
image.caption: lab/search-unsafe.php — a post-search query is turned into a query that dumps all password hashes.

slides.body:
On the **lab version**, enter the following into the search box:

~~~text
zzz' UNION SELECT username, password_hash FROM users --
~~~

The SQL that actually runs becomes: find posts containing the text `zzz` (nothing) **UNION** the list of usernames and password hashes. `UNION` works because the original query returns exactly **two** columns. Result: the entire `users` table appears on the search page.

This is why password hashing must be strong (step 12): even if the table is stolen, bcrypt makes recovering the original passwords take decades. But the best option is to **not let it be stolen**.

slides.title: 2 attack — bypassing login

image.alt: Lab login page: the username field contains lan.code' --, the password is anything. The concatenated SQL has its password check commented out, and a red banner shows Logged in: lan.code
image.caption: lab/login-unsafe.php — gets into lan.code's account without knowing the password.

slides.body:
The lab login checks the password **directly inside the SQL** using string concatenation. Enter the username:

~~~text
lan.code' --
~~~

and any password. The `-- ` part turns the rest of the `AND password_hash = '…'` into a comment, so the statement becomes only `WHERE username = 'lan.code'` — it returns Lan, and the "login" succeeds.

This is an **A07 Authentication Failures** issue layered on top of **A05 Injection**. The real Nhịp never compares passwords in SQL: it fetches the hash and uses `password_verify` in PHP (step 12).

slides.title: Why the real version is immune

image.alt: The real Nhịp search page with the same attack string in the box returns 0 results for zzz' UNION SELECT username, password_hash FROM users --
image.caption: search.php (real) with the exact attack string: it's treated as search text and returns 0 results.

slides.body:
Paste the **exact attack string** into the real `search.php`: no hash is leaked, only "0 results". Because:

~~~php
$stmt = db()->prepare('… WHERE p.body LIKE :pattern');
$stmt->bindValue(':pattern', '%' . $query . '%');
~~~

The SQL statement is sent to MySQL **first**, with a placeholder `:pattern`. When the data arrives later, MySQL treats the **entire** string, including `' UNION SELECT …`, as **a single value** to compare in `LIKE`, not as SQL. The query template is fixed, so data cannot cross the boundary (step 11).

That is the root fix: not "blocking the word UNION", but **separating the command channel from the data channel**.

slides.title: 3 attack — stored XSS

image.alt: Lab feed page with a pink background. The title has changed to Nhịp has been hijacked! hoa.test's post now shows only the text Ảnh đẹp nè and a broken image icon
image.caption: lab/feed-unsafe.php prints the body without e(): the code inside the post runs, changing the page title and background.

slides.body: Post a **normal** message through the real Nhịp with this content: ~~~text Ảnh đẹp nè ~~~ The post is stored verbatim in the database (correct, since it's user content). But `lab/feed-unsafe.php` prints `body` **without `e()`**. The browser sees a broken `` and runs `onerror` — the attacker's code executes in the session of **every** viewer of the feed. It's called **stored** (persistent) because the code lives in the database and runs automatically for everyone who opens the page — far more dangerous than an attack limited to a single link.

slides.title: 1 layer — e() in the real version

image.alt: The real Nhịp feed: Hoa's post displays the literal string Ảnh đẹp nè as plain text. Nothing runs, and the background is white as usual
image.caption: index.php (real) shows that same post: all the tags appear as plain text, and nothing runs.

slides.body:
Open the same post on the **real** feed: it shows the string `` **verbatim** as plain text, and nothing happens. Because `includes/post.php` prints it through `e()`: ~~~php

~~~ `htmlspecialchars` converts `<` into `<`, and `"` into `"`… so the browser treats this as **text to display**, not as a tag to build. This is **output encoding**: separating the channels once more, this time at the PHP → HTML boundary.

slides.title: 2 layer — Content-Security-Policy

image.alt: Lab feed page after enabling CSP: the background is white again, the title still reads Lab feed forgot e(), and Hoa's post shows only text and a broken image icon — the onerror code does not run
image.caption: The same lab page after adding CSP: the Console shows 'The action has been blocked', and the title and background no longer change.

slides.body:
Humans forget. One day someone adds a spot that prints without `e()`. As a defense-in-depth layer, use **Content-Security-Policy** — a HTTP header that tells the browser *"only run scripts from this same domain; forbid any code written inside HTML"*.

~~~php
header("Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; "
    . "img-src 'self' data:; object-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'");
~~~

Now even if `feed-unsafe.php` still prints without `e()`, `onerror=` **does not run** — DevTools → Console logs *"inline event handler violates… Content Security Policy"*. For CSP to be this strict, the Nhịp **must not** have `<script>` or `style=` mixed inside HTML — everything is placed in `js/app.js` and `css/style.css` (reason in step 13).

slides.title: Adding two more headers
slides.body:
~~~php
header('X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff');
header('Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin');
~~~

- `nosniff`: tells the browser **not to guess** the file type. If an attacker tricks an uploaded `.txt` file into containing HTML, the browser won't "helpfully" render it as HTML — this blocks a XSS path through uploaded files.
- `Referrer-Policy`: does not send the full address (which may contain `?id=`, tokens) to other sites when the user clicks an outbound link — reduces information leaks (A01).

All three are grouped into `send_security_headers()` and called once in `bootstrap.php` **before** `session_start()` (headers must come before content).

slides.title: Approaches NOT to use
slides.body:
Common wrong approaches newcomers try:

- **Blocking keywords** (`UNION`, `SELECT`, `<script>`): attackers get around it with mixed case, encoding, or odd whitespace. The blocklist is always incomplete.
- **`addslashes` by hand**: misses many cases and still breaks with some character encodings. A prepared statement does it correctly and more simply.
- **`mysql_real_escape_string`**: memorizing API `mysql_*` that has been **removed** from PHP 7.
- **Testing only at JavaScript**: passes in one second using `curl`.
- **`htmlspecialchars` at SAVE time**: wrong timing. Encode when **outputting**, not on input. The same data can be output to HTML, JSON, or email, and each one needs different encoding.

Rule: **parameterize when talking to the database, encode when outputting to the target context.**

slides.title: includes/security.php
slides.body: Create a new file, add `require` to `bootstrap.php`, and call `send_security_headers()` right before `start_session()`.

slides.title: Append to bootstrap.php
slides.body: Order matters: the HTTP header must be sent before the page outputs its first character, and before `start_session()` (this function also sends `Set-Cookie` headers).

slides.title: Attack it yourself, following the list
slides.body: Do these in order on your own machine (the lab version first, then the real one): 1. `lab/search-unsafe.php?q=` + `' UNION SELECT username, password_hash FROM users -- ` → get the hash. Then paste it into the real `search.php` → 0 results. 2. `lab/login-unsafe.php` with the username `lan.code' -- ` → you get in. Try the same thing on the real `login.php` → "Invalid username or password". 3. Publish a post containing `` through the real Nhịp. View it on the real `index.php` → it shows verbatim. View it on `lab/feed-unsafe.php` → the code runs. Add CSP → reopen the lab → the code is blocked (see Console).

slides.title: Clean up the lab
slides.body: Once that's done, **erase the traces**: 1. Delete the entire `nhip/lab/` folder. 2. Delete the CSS `.lab-*` blocks in `style.css` (marked "only used in step 17"). 3. In phpMyAdmin, delete the post containing `` that you published to test it. 4. In `SECURITY.md`, mark **A05 Injection** as handled, and note clearly: SQL Injection is blocked by prepared statements, XSS is blocked by `e()` + CSP. Vulnerable code must not remain anywhere, and must not be pushed to Git (step 20) or to hosting (step 24).

slides.title: Step 17 acceptance
slides.body:
- [ ] Reproduce all three attacks on the lab version and explain how each SQL/HTML input gets altered.
- [ ] Confirm these attacks fail on the real version, and explain why (separating the command and data channels).
- [ ] Nhịp sends `Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy` (checked with `curl -I` or DevTools).
- [ ] The real Nhịp still works fully under CSP: liking, replying, switching tabs. The Console reports no CSP violations.
- [ ] The `lab/` folder and CSS `.lab-*` have been deleted, and the test post XSS has been deleted.
- [ ] `SECURITY.md` marks A05 as complete.

quiz.why: The boundary between commands and data is erased; the fix is to separate the two channels again.

quiz.q: The original query is SELECT id FROM posts WHERE body LIKE '%$q%'. With $q = ' UNION SELECT password_hash FROM users -- what happens?
quiz.why: UNION appends the results of a second query; -- comments out the rest.

The command template is sent first, and the data arrives later as a value only, so it cannot become a command

quiz.q: Blocking keywords like UNION and SELECT is not a reliable way to prevent SQL injection.
quiz.why: Blocklists are always incomplete; attackers get around them with mixed case, encoding, and so on. Use parameterization.

quiz.q: How is XSS stored different from XSS reflected?

quiz.why: Stored code attacks everyone who opens the page, which is more dangerous than the kind that works through a single link.

quiz.q: How does e() (htmlspecialchars) protect against XSS?

step17.title: 17. SQL Injection and XSS: attack it first, then patch at the root

step18.summary: Patch the three remaining vulnerabilities of stage 4: CSRF with a synchronizer token on every POST form, harden session cookies, and re-render uploaded images with GD to strip code hidden in the files.

slides.title: The vulnerability that gets you even without typing anything
slides.body:
SQL Injection and XSS require the attacker to **enter** something into Nhịp. CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) is different: the victim only needs to be **logged in to Nhịp** and accidentally open another page from the attacker. That page silently sends a request to Nhịp **using the victim's identity**.

In step 13 we already saw this threat: a rogue page builds a form pointing to `delete.php`. The `SameSite=Lax` cookie (step 12) blocks most cases, but "most" isn't enough. This step adds the official defense layer, then cleans up the last two risks: session cookies and uploaded images.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Understand how CSRF works and why automatic cookies are the root cause.
2. Install a **synchronizer token**: each session gets a secret token, and every POST must carry the exact one.
3. Compare tokens safely with `hash_equals`; return the **419** code on mismatch.
4. Harden the session cookie: `HttpOnly`, `SameSite`, `Secure` (for HTTPS).
5. Re-render uploaded images with **GD** to strip extra data, which blocks "polyglot" files that are both an image and code.
6. Check off A01 (CSRF) and A08 in `SECURITY.md`.

slides.title: CSRF: borrowing the browser's hands
slides.body:
1. Lan logs in to Nhịp. The browser stores the session cookie of Nhịp.
2. Lan opens another page (`trang-xau.com`) that contains a hidden form pointing to `nhip/delete.php`, which submits itself using JavaScript.
3. On command, the browser sends a POST request to Nhịp, and **automatically attaches the cookie of Nhịp** (cookies always travel with the destination, no matter who starts the request).
4. If Nhịp only checks the cookie, it assumes this is Lan and deletes the post.

The key point: the attacker **cannot** read anything from Nhịp (the same-origin policy blocks that), but can still **trigger** the action. You need a proof that only the genuine Nhịp page has.

slides.title: Synchronizer token
slides.body:
That proof is the **CSRF token**: a random string stored in Lan's session.

- Every POST form of Nhịp embeds this token in the hidden field `_token`.
- The server compares the submitted token with the one in the session. Only a match is processed.
- `trang-xau.com` **cannot read** the token (it sits inside the HTML of Nhịp, a different origin), so it cannot fill it in correctly, and the forged request is rejected.

A token differs from a cookie in one way: the browser **sends cookies automatically**, but the token must be **deliberately embedded** in the form, which only the genuine Nhịp page can do.

slides.title: CSRF per OWASP
slides.body:
CSRF falls under the **A01 Broken Access Control** category of the OWASP Top 10:2025 (CWE-352). The OWASP prevention guidance ranks the measures:

1. Use a framework with built-in anti-CSRF protection, or a **synchronizer token** as Nhịp does.
2. Additional layer: cookies with the **`SameSite`** attribute (Lax or Strict).
3. For sensitive requests: re-verify the user (password entry, OTP).

OWASP stresses that tokens must be **cryptographically random, bound to the session, and compared in constant time**, exactly the three things `bin2hex(random_bytes(32))`, stored in `$_SESSION`, and `hash_equals` does.

> OWASP Foundation (2025) *Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
>
> MITRE (2025) *CWE-352: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)*. Available at: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/352.html

slides.title: SameSite and Safe File Uploads
slides.body:
The `SameSite` cookie attribute (RFC 6265bis) determines whether a cookie is sent with requests initiated from other sites. `Lax`, the default in modern browsers, blocks cookies on cross-origin POSTs and mitigates most of CSRF. Tokens are still needed, though, because not every browser behaves this way, and safety should not rest on a single layer.

For uploaded images, OWASP recommends **re-encoding** the image instead of only validating it. Reading the pixels and writing them to a new file strips any stray data blocks, where code can be hidden in a polyglot file.

> Barth, A. and West, M. (2025) *Cookies: HTTP State Management Mechanism (draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis)*. IETF. Available at: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis/
>
> OWASP Foundation (2025) *File Upload Cheat Sheet*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html

slides.title: One checkpoint for every form
slides.body:
Instead of checking the token on each page (easy to forget), Nhịp places **one** checkpoint in `bootstrap.php`: the function `csrf_check()` runs on **every** POST request, before any page handles it.

- `csrf_token()` — creates (on first use) or returns the session's token.
- `csrf_field()` — prints the hidden field, embedded in every `<form method="post">`.
- `csrf_check()` — blocks POST requests missing or carrying a wrong token, using `abort(419, …)`.

The code **419** is not part of the original HTTP standard, but many frameworks (Laravel…) use it for "token expired", clearly distinguished from 400/403. Fail-safe defaults (step 16): without a valid token, **deny** the request; there is no need to list which pages require protection.

slides.title: Generating and embedding the token
Checking the token safely
Fetch also carries the token itself
slides.body:
The like button sends via `fetch` (step 15). Anything else to do? **No**, because the button sits inside a `<form class="like-form">` that already has `csrf_field()`:

~~~js
body: new FormData(form),   // FormData gói MỌI input của form, gồm _token
~~~

`FormData` automatically collects the entire hidden field `_token`, so the fetch request carries the token just like a regular form. This is the benefit of wrapping the button in a form instead of attaching loose data in JavaScript.

An endpoint that returns JSON like `like.php` when given a wrong token will land on the 419 HTML page; with Nhịp that rarely happens since the token is always present. Large applications typically return an error 419 in the form JSON for API calls.

slides.title: Hardening the session cookie
slides.body:
Revisit the cookie flags set in step 12; now you understand their security meaning:

~~~php
session_set_cookie_params([
    'httponly' => true,    // JS không đọc được → XSS khó trộm phiên (step 17)
    'samesite' => 'Lax',   // lớp 2 chống CSRF, bổ sung cho token
    'secure'   => false,   // ĐỔI THÀNH true khi có HTTPS (step 24)
]);
~~~

- When `Secure` is on, the cookie is sent **only** over HTTPS, so someone eavesdropping on public Wi-Fi cannot capture it. On localhost (HTTP) it must be left `false`, otherwise the browser drops the cookie and you cannot log in. Turn it on in hosting.
- The session ID still changes on login (`session_regenerate_id`, step 12), which prevents session fixation.

These three flags plus the CSRF token cover all four corners of session protection.

slides.title: Redraw the image with GD
slides.body:
Step 14 checks the image with `finfo`. But an attacker can create a file that is **both a valid image and contains PHP code** in its metadata block (a "polyglot" image). `finfo` sees a real image and lets it through.

Final layer: **re-draw** the image using the GD library of PHP:

~~~php
$image = imagecreatefromjpeg($file['tmp_name']);   // đọc PIXEL vào bộ nhớ
imagejpeg($image, $path, 85);                       // ghi ra tệp MỚI từ pixel
imagedestroy($image);
~~~

The new file contains only the image's pixels. Every foreign data block (including hidden code) is **not copied over**. Verification: append `<?php … ?>` to the end of a `.jpg` file, upload it, then `grep` the saved file. The code string is gone.

slides.title: Why not rely on SameSite alone
slides.body:
You already have `SameSite=Lax`, so why do you still need a token? Because of **defense in depth** (step 16):

- Very old browsers don't understand `SameSite` → only the token protects them.
- `Lax` still sends cookies with **top-level GET navigations**. If some action changes data via GET (Nhịp doesn't have one, but just in case), the token is the checkpoint.
- Cookie settings may be changed by mistake later. The token is an independent layer that doesn't depend on cookie flags.

Two independent layers guard against the same threat: an attacker must break **both**. This is also why we keep both `finfo` and GD for images, and both `e()` and CSP for XSS.

slides.title: includes/csrf.php
slides.body: Create a new file. `abort()` is used here, so `csrf.php` must be loaded after `helpers.php` (where `abort` is defined).

slides.title: Append to bootstrap.php
slides.body: `csrf_check()` runs right after `start_session()`: the session must be open to read the token, and it must block before any page handles POST.

slides.title: Embed the token in every form
slides.body: Add `<?= csrf_field() ?>` right after each `<form method="post">` tag in: `login.php`, `register.php`, `settings.php`, `index.php`, `post.php`, `edit.php`, `includes/post.php` (two forms: like and delete), `includes/header.php` (logout form). Search forms use GET, so do **not** add it there.

slides.title: Redraw the images in uploads.php
slides.body: Replace the `move_uploaded_file` step with read/write through GD. `match` picks the read/write function based on the image type determined from `finfo`.

slides.title: Result: forged requests are blocked

image.alt: The Nhịp page shows the message “Your session has expired or the request is invalid.” Reload the page and try again.
image.caption: Submit a POST form with a wrong token (or one from another page) → 419, and no action is performed.

slides.body:
Self-check with DevTools:

1. Open Network, click Post — you should see `_token` in the payload.
2. Change the `_token` value of a form to garbage text (DevTools → Elements) and submit → the page **419**.
3. `curl -d "id=3" http://localhost/nhip/delete.php` (no token, simulating a foreign page) → **419**, the 3 post stays intact.
4. Real Nhịp still works fully: post, edit, delete, like, follow — because every form now carries the token.

slides.title: Result: polyglot images are neutralized
slides.body:
Create a test file:

~~~bash
cp anh.jpg poly.jpg
echo '<?php echo "PWNED"; ?>' >> poly.jpg
~~~

Upload `poly.jpg` as the avatar. Then open the saved file in `uploads/avatars/`:

~~~bash
grep -a PWNED uploads/avatars/<tên-tệp>.jpg   # không còn kết quả
~~~

GD re-rendered the image from pixels, so the `<?php … ?>` segment at the end was not copied over. Combined with `.htaccess` that forbids running `.php` (step 14), the upload attack path is closed at two layers.

slides.title: Acceptance check for step 18
slides.body:
- [ ] Every POST form includes `_token`; a POST with a missing or wrong token → 419.
- [ ] `csrf_check()` runs once in `bootstrap.php`; no page checks it on its own.
- [ ] Token compared using `hash_equals`; generated using `random_bytes`.
- [ ] Heart reactions via fetch still work (FormData carries the token).
- [ ] Uploaded images are re-rendered by GD; polyglot files lose their embedded code.
- [ ] Session cookie has HttpOnly + SameSite; note to enable Secure on hosting.
- [ ] `SECURITY.md` marks CSRF (A01) and file download (A08) as complete.

o: Cookies are automatically sent with every request to the target, regardless of who initiated it
quiz.why: A foreign page cannot read anything, but it can still trigger actions because cookies are attached automatically.

quiz.q: Why does a CSRF token protect against CSRF?
o: A page from another origin cannot read the token, so it cannot fill the correct value into a forged form.
quiz.why: Only the genuine Nhịp page can embed the correct token.

quiz.q: With SameSite=Lax in place, the CSRF token is no longer needed.
quiz.why: Defense in depth: older browsers, a misconfigured setting… the token is an independent layer.

quiz.q: Why use hash_equals instead of === when comparing tokens?
o: Constant-time comparison, so timing measurements don't reveal how many leading characters were correct.
quiz.why: === stops at the first differing character, leaking timing information.

quiz.q: Which Nhịp forms need csrf_field() embedded?
quiz.why: GET doesn't change data, so it's not needed; every POST needs it.

quiz.q: Which line causes the CSRF check to miss requests?
quiz.why: Skipping only GET isn't enough — PUT/DELETE/HEAD… also slip through; check 'anything other than POST is skipped' or only run when the method is POST.

quiz.q: What can redrawing the image with GD block that finfo doesn't?
o: A file that is both a valid image and contains hidden code in its metadata
quiz.why: GD only copies pixels to a new file, discarding any unexpected data blocks.

quiz.q: Fill in the function that generates a cryptographically secure random token.
quiz.why: random_bytes is the cryptographically secure random source for PHP.

quiz.q: How should the Secure cookie flag be set on localhost (HTTP)?
o: false — because localhost doesn't have HTTPS yet, enabling it would drop the cookie
quiz.why: Secure makes the cookie send only over HTTPS; enable it on hosting (step 24).

o: FormData packages the hidden _token field inside the form wrapping the button

step18.title: 18. CSRF, login sessions, cookies and safe file uploads

step19.summary: Completing stage 4: rate limiting logins to stop password brute-forcing, an action log for traceability, a safe error page when debug is turned off, and a final review of all of SECURITY.md.

slides.title: Three final lines of defense
slides.body:
Blocked Injection, XSS, CSRF, and malicious file uploads. Three threats in `SECURITY.md` remain unaddressed:

- **Brute force**: trying thousands of passwords against one account. A slow `password_verify` helps little; you need **rate limiting**.
- **Repudiation**: "I didn't delete that post." You need a **log** of who did what, and when.
- **Information leakage through errors**: the PHP error page prints file paths and the SQL statement. You need a **safe error page** before going to hosting.

These three layers are less glamorous but are the standard for every real application, and they fill exactly the remaining three items in OWASP Top 10:2025 (A06, A09, A10).

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Limit failed login attempts per IP within a time window.
2. Store IPs compactly using `VARBINARY` and `inet_pton`.
3. Log **sensitive actions** (login, sign-up, post deletion). Never log passwords or tokens.
4. Install a **global error handler**: when debug is off, show a generic 500 page; real errors go to the server log.
5. Distinguish data that must be hidden from users but still recorded for administrators.
6. Review `SECURITY.md`: every item has a countermeasure; run a final attack test.

slides.title: Rate limiting
slides.body:
Each **failed** login, Nhịp writes one line to `login_attempts` (IP and time). Before checking the password, it counts that IP's failures in the **last 15 minutes**:

- Under 5: allow the attempt.
- At 5 or more: reject immediately, without checking the password, with a message saying to wait 15 minutes.

A **successful** login clears that IP's attempt history. This sliding window makes brute-forcing thousands of passwords infeasible in time, while still not bothering someone who mistypes once or twice.

slides.title: Log: who, what, when
slides.body:
The `activity_log` table records every sensitive action: `action` (type), `user_id` (who; NULL if not logged in), `detail`, `ip`, `created_at`.

When an incident happens, the log answers three questions:

- **Who** deleted the post 42? Look up `action = 'post_delete'`, `detail = 'post #42'`.
- Was this account **brute-forced**? Count `login_failed` per IP.
- **When** did it happen? `created_at`.

Golden rule: the log **never** contains passwords, tokens, or card numbers. Record "logged in", not "logged in with password abc123".

slides.title: A06, A09, A10 of OWASP
slides.body:
These three steps fill three entries of the OWASP Top 10:2025:

- **A06 Insecure Design** — lacking rate limits is a *design* flaw, not an isolated code bug; OWASP recommends building rate limits in from the design stage.
- **A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures** — failing to log, or logging with no one reviewing the logs, lets an attack continue undetected.
- **A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions** — a **new** entry in the 2025 edition: handling errors incorrectly (exposing details, or "failing open" when an error occurs) is a separate risk.

> OWASP Foundation (2025) *A09:2025 – Security Logging and Alerting Failures*; *A10:2025 – Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions*, OWASP Top 10:2025. Available at: https://top10.owasp.org/2025/
>
> OWASP Foundation (2025) *Logging Cheat Sheet*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html

slides.title: Defending Properly Against Password Guessing
slides.body:
The NIST SP 800-63B guidelines require the system to **limit the number of failed attempts** per account to resist online guessing, combined with throttling. A limit per **IP** stops a guesser against one account; a limit per **account** stops a guesser coming from many IPs (implemented in the finished project).

NIST also notes that you **should not** permanently lock an account just for entering wrong passwords, because attackers can deliberately enter wrong passwords to lock out other people's accounts (a form of denial-of-service attack). A time window that unlocks automatically, as Nhịp does, is a reasonable balance.

> National Institute of Standards and Technology (2024) *SP 800-63B-4: Digital Identity Guidelines*, §5.2.2 Rate Limiting (Throttling). Gaithersburg: NIST. doi:10.6028/NIST.SP.800-63b-4

slides.title: Three-Part Design
slides.body:
| Part | File | Table |
|---|---|---|
| Rate limiting | `includes/ratelimit.php` | `login_attempts` |
| Logs | `includes/log.php` | `activity_log` |
| Error page | `includes/errors.php` | — |

Two new tables were added to `database/schema.sql`. All three files are loaded in `bootstrap.php`. `login.php` calls the limit and the log; `delete.php` and `register.php` call the log.

IPs are stored as **`VARBINARY(16)`** (16 bytes is enough for IPv6) via `inet_pton`. This is more compact and faster to compare than a string. phpMyAdmin and MySQL read it back using `INET6_NTOA`.

slides.title: Getting and Storing the IP
Counting with a Sliding Window
Logging
slides.body:
~~~php
function log_action(string $action, ?int $userId = null, string $detail = ''): void
{
    db()->prepare('INSERT INTO activity_log (user_id, action, detail, ip) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)')
        ->execute([$userId, $action, mb_substr($detail, 0, 255), client_ip()]);
}
~~~

Call it at sensitive points:

~~~php
log_action('login', $userId);                      // đăng nhập thành công
log_action('login_failed', null, $login);          // thất bại (ghi tên đã thử, KHÔNG ghi mật khẩu)
log_action('register', $id, $input['username']);   // tạo tài khoản
log_action('post_delete', $me['id'], 'post #' . $id);
~~~

`detail` truncates to 255 characters to fit the column and to prevent someone from stuffing huge data into the log (a form of *log flooding* attack).

slides.title: SET NULL foreign key
slides.body:
The table `activity_log` links to `users` via:

~~~sql
CONSTRAINT fk_log_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
  REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE SET NULL
~~~

Unlike `posts`, which uses `ON DELETE CASCADE` (delete the person, delete their posts). Logs use **`SET NULL`**: deleting an account leaves its log rows **in place**, only the link to `user_id` is lost. Because logs are **evidence**, they must not disappear when the related person is deleted.

Choose the foreign key behavior by what the data means: content belongs to the person (CASCADE), evidence is independent of the person (SET NULL or RESTRICT).

slides.title: Safe error page
Expected errors vs unexpected errors
slides.body:
Two kinds of errors, two ways to handle them:

- **Expected** (the user mistypes, lacks permission, or something isn't found): handle it **in place** with `$error`, `abort(404/403)`, flash — with a friendly, specific message.
- **Unexpected** (lost database connection, programming bug): let the **exception** bubble up to the global handler → a generic 500 page.

Don't use `try/catch` to swallow everything and show "something went wrong" — that hides your own programming bugs. Only catch exceptions you **know how to handle** (such as a duplicate name at sign-up, step 12), and let the rest bubble up.

The **fail-safe** principle: when you hit an unclear error, the system must **close** (deny), not "just let it through".

slides.title: Two new tables
slides.body: Append to the end of `database/schema.sql`. `BIGINT` for the log id, since it grows very fast. Run this part again in the SQL tab of phpMyAdmin (only the part with the two new tables, not the whole file, to avoid losing data).

slides.title: log.php and ratelimit.php
slides.body: Two small files, loaded in `bootstrap.php`. The constants `LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS` and `LOGIN_WINDOW_MIN` are placed in one spot for easy tuning.

slides.title: errors.php and login.php
slides.body: The error handler is installed in `bootstrap.php` right after reading `$config`. `login.php` wraps all the logic in a rate-limit check.

image.caption: After 5 failed attempts from the same IP, attempt 6 is rejected immediately, without checking the password.

Self-test: enter the wrong password 5 times, then attempt 6 is blocked. Logging in **correctly** once clears the counter (row `clear_login_attempts`), so someone who mistyped and then entered the right password is not unfairly penalized.

In phpMyAdmin, the `login_attempts` table has rows with `INET6_NTOA(ip)` = `127.0.0.1` (or `::1`).

image.caption: activity_log records five failed logins with the attempted name and the IP. No password.

Each `login_failed` records the attempted username (`lan.code`) and the IP (`0x7f000001` = `127.0.0.1`), but **not** the password. A successful login or a deleted post adds the corresponding `login`, `post_delete` rows.

This is raw material for **security analysis** (step 23): count failed logins per IP to detect attacks, and count new posts per day to see growth.

Reopen `SECURITY.md`. The "Open risks" table of step 16 must now be **empty**:

Go back through the STRIDE table: each row has a "mitigation" column and a "done in step" column. Attack once more with every attack from steps 17–18. All of them must fail.

step19.title: 19. Access control, rate limiting and logging: security review of Nhịp

step20.summary: Reorganize Nhịp into a lean MVC structure: separate public/ as the web root, src/ holding logic and views, config kept outside the public area; a front controller + router for clean URLs; and put the project under Git with a .gitignore.

slides.title: From "it works" to "it's maintainable"
slides.body:
Nhịp is now safe and feature-complete. But the code is still flat: 12 `.php` files sit at the root, anyone who types `/config.php` can download the config file, and every link hard-codes `post.php?id=5`.

Stage 5 takes Nhịp from "it works" to "maintainable and worth using". The first step is **structure**: where each file goes, who can access what, and every request enters through **a single door**. This is the biggest refactor in the course. The features don't change, but the code is much cleaner.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Understand the **MVC** pattern and map it onto Nhịp (Model = `src/*.php`, View = `src/views/`, Controller = `src/pages/`).
2. Split out the **web root** so it contains only `public/`; move `config.php`, `src/` **outside** the public area.
3. Write a **front controller** (`public/index.php`) + a **router**: clean URLs such as `/post/5`, `/u/lan.code`.
4. Use `.htaccess` to route every request (except static files) to the front controller.
5. Build URLs with the `url('post', ['id' => 5])` function instead of hard-coding them.
6. Put the project under **Git** with `.gitignore` excluding secrets and user files.

slides.title: MVC in Nhịp
slides.body:
**MVC** splits code by **responsibility**:

- **Model** — data and business rules: `src/posts.php`, `users.php`, `likes.php`… (SQL statements, checks). Knows nothing about HTML.
- **View** — display: `src/views/header.php`, `post.php`, `footer.php`. Only prints HTML from the data it receives.
- **Controller** — coordinates: `src/pages/feed.php`, `login.php`… Reads the request, calls the Model, chooses the View.

In fact Nhịp already follows this spirit from step 11 ("the page does not write SQL, the function SQL does not print HTML"). This step only **renames and rearranges** things properly, and adds a router as the gatekeeper.

slides.title: A single entry point
slides.body:
Before: each page was a separate `.php` file accessed directly — `login.php`, `post.php`… Each file had to handle `require bootstrap` on its own, and any file that forgot was a vulnerability.

After: **every** request enters through `public/index.php` (front controller). It loads `bootstrap` **once**, then the **router** matches the path against the route table and calls the right controller in `src/pages/`.

Benefit: one place applies security (CSRF, sessions, headers) to everything; controllers sit outside the web root so they cannot be called directly; URLs are decoupled from file names.

slides.title: MVC and Front Controller
slides.body:
MVC originated in Smalltalk-80 (Reenskaug & Trygve, 1979) to separate the user interface from the data. **Front Controller** is a pattern from Fowler (2002): it funnels every request through a single entry point, centralizing dispatch and cross-cutting concerns (security, logging).

Every modern PHP framework (Laravel, Symfony) is built on exactly these two patterns: a `public/index.php` plus a routing table. Understanding Nhịp by hand helps you see what the framework does internally.

> Fowler, M. (2002) *Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture*. Boston: Addison-Wesley. (Front Controller, pp. 344–351)
>
> Reenskaug, T. (1979) *Models–Views–Controllers*. Technical note, Xerox PARC.

slides.title: Minimal web root and PSR
slides.body:
OWASP (A01/A05 Misconfiguration) recommends placing **only** the files meant to be served publicly in the web root; source code, configuration and libraries must be placed **outside** it. The `public/` + `src/` structure is the standard way to achieve that. If PHP "fails" (shows source code instead of running), an attacker still cannot see `config.php`.

The PHP community (PHP-FIG) standardizes how code is organized and autoloaded through **PSR** recommendations: PSR-4 for autoloading, PSR-12 for coding style. Nhịp follows PSR-12; autoloading is left for when Composer is used.

> OWASP Foundation (2025) *A02:2025 – Security Misconfiguration*. Available at: https://top10.owasp.org/2025/
>
> PHP Framework Interop Group (2013) *PSR-4: Autoloader*. Available at: https://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-4/

slides.title: New folder structure
slides.body:
~~~text
nhip/
├── public/              ← WEB ROOT (chỉ đây công khai)
│   ├── index.php        ← front controller
│   ├── .htaccess        ← chuyển mọi yêu cầu về index.php
│   ├── css/  js/  img/  uploads/
├── src/                 ← mã nguồn (NGOÀI web root)
│   ├── bootstrap.php  router.php
│   ├── db.php  posts.php  users.php … (Model + hạ tầng)
│   ├── pages/           ← Controller: feed, login, post…
│   └── views/           ← View: header, footer, post
├── config.php           ← bí mật, NGOÀI web root, .gitignore
├── config.sample.php
├── database/  SECURITY.md
├── .gitignore
~~~

On hosting (step 24), you point the domain's "document root" to `public/` — the rest is automatically out of the browser's reach.

slides.title: Routing table
slides.body:
~~~php
const ROUTES = [
    ['GET',  '/',             'feed',    'feed'],
    ['POST', '/posts',        'feed',    'posts.create'],
    ['GET',  '/post/{id}',    'post',    'post'],
    ['POST', '/post/{id}',    'post',    'post.reply'],
    ['GET',  '/u/{username}',  'profile', 'profile'],
    // …
];
~~~

Each route: **[method, path pattern, controller file name, route name]**.

- Same path, different method → different controller job: `GET /post/5` views the post, `POST /post/5` adds a reply.
- `{id}`, `{username}` are **parameters** — the controller reads them with `route_param('id')`.
- **Route name** (`post.reply`) builds URLs without depending on the specific path: changing `/post/{id}` to `/bai/{id}` edits only one line, and all links stay correct.

slides.title: Matching a request to a route
Building URLs by route name
slides.body:
~~~php
url('feed')                        // /nhip/public/
url('post', ['id' => 5])           // /nhip/public/post/5
url('profile', ['username' => 'lan.code'])   // /nhip/public/u/lan.code
url('feed', ['tab' => 'following']) // /nhip/public/?tab=following
~~~

`url()` looks up the route by name, replaces `{id}` with the value (already `rawurlencode`), and extra parameters become the query string `?...`.

`base_path()` infers its value from `dirname($_SERVER['SCRIPT_NAME'])`, so **do not hard-code** `/nhip/public`: it works in any subdirectory, and at the domain root when deployed to hosting. All `href`, `action`, `redirect` now call `url()`; static assets call `asset('css/style.css')`.

slides.title: Front controller and .htaccess
slides.body:
~~~php
// public/index.php — cả ứng dụng vào đây
require __DIR__ . '/../src/bootstrap.php';
dispatch();
~~~

~~~apache
# public/.htaccess
RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f      # không phải tệp thật…
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d      # …cũng không phải thư mục thật
RewriteRule ^ index.php [L]              # → đưa về front controller
~~~

Two `RewriteCond` for `css/style.css`, images, `uploads/` are served **directly** (fast, without going through PHP); all other paths (`/post/5`, `/login`) go into `index.php`.

The built-in PHP server (`php -S`) doesn't read `.htaccess`. During development, use `php -S localhost:8000 -t public` with a small router script that does the equivalent (see README).

slides.title: Controllers become much leaner
Git: history and secret safety
slides.body:
**Git** records the code's history: each `commit` is a point you can return to, `git diff` shows what changed, and teammates don't overwrite each other.

~~~bash
git init
git add -A
git commit -m "Nhịp: cấu trúc MVC, front controller và router"
~~~

But **not everything goes into Git**. The `.gitignore` file:

~~~gitignore
/config.php                       # mật khẩu cơ sở dữ liệu
/public/uploads/avatars/*         # ảnh người dùng tải lên
!/public/uploads/avatars/.gitkeep # giữ thư mục rỗng
/vendor/                          # phụ thuộc Composer (nếu có)
.DS_Store
~~~

`config.php` leaked to public GitHub is a classic **leak incident** (A04 Cryptographic Failures). `config.sample.php` is still tracked so others know what to fill in.

slides.title: Does Nhịp need Composer?
slides.body:
**Composer** is PHP's library manager: declare dependencies in `composer.json`, run `composer install`, and use **autoload** so you don't have to `require` each file.

Nhịp **deliberately uses no external libraries** — this suits the learning goal and reduces **A03 Software Supply Chain Failures** (every dependency is a risk you inherit). When the project grows and needs, for example, an email library or stronger image processing than GD, only then add Composer.

If you add it: `vendor/` into `.gitignore`, and use PSR-4 autoload instead of the `require` list in `bootstrap.php`. Principle: **add a dependency when the benefit clearly outweighs the risk**, not for fun.

step21.summary: Make Nhịp fast and easy to use for everyone: eliminate the N+1 problem, add indexes and read EXPLAIN, use keyset pagination, optimize images, and reach a 100 Accessibility score on Lighthouse.

slides.title: Working correctly isn't enough — it has to run well
slides.body:
Nhịp is correct and safe. But with 10 posts, every query feels "fast"; with 100.000 posts and thousands of users, sloppy code slows down and then crashes.

This step measures and fixes four things that decide whether a product is **worth using**:

- **Query count** — the N+1 bug turns one page into hundreds of database calls.
- **Indexes** — help the database find things fast instead of scanning the whole table.
- **Pagination** — never load all the data at once.
- **Accessibility and images** — so the page works for everyone and loads light.

The guiding principle: **measure first, fix after**. Don't optimize by feel.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Recognize and eliminate the **N+1 bug** (one query per list item).
2. Read **EXPLAIN** to see whether a query uses an index or scans the table.
3. Add **composite indexes** for the feed, and understand when indexes help or don't.
4. **Keyset** (cursor) pagination — fast on deep pages.
5. Optimize images: explicit dimensions, `loading="lazy"`, lightweight formats.
6. Reach **Accessibility 100** on Lighthouse and understand each criterion.

slides.title: The N+1 problem
slides.body:
Suppose the page renders 20 posts, each one separately asking "who is the author?" and "how many likes?":

- 1 queries to fetch 20 posts.
- + 20 queries to fetch the authors.
- + 20 queries to count likes.

= **41 queries** for one page. With 100 posts, that's 201. This is the **N+1 problem** — the query count grows with the number of items.

The fix: fetch **everything in one (or a few) queries** using `JOIN` and `IN (...)`. Nhịp already got this right from the start: its `FEED_SQL` `JOIN users` fetches the authors, and `mark_liked` uses a single `IN` for the whole list (step 15). This step **verifies** that.

slides.title: Indexes: a book's table of contents
slides.body:
Without an index, finding "posts by user 5" forces the database to read **every row** (full scan — `type: ALL` in EXPLAIN). On a large table, that is very slow.

An index works like a **book's table of contents**: a pre-sorted structure (B-tree) that points straight to the needed row. Searching becomes "look up the index" instead of "read the whole book".

But an index **is not free**: every write (INSERT/UPDATE) must also update it, and indexes take up storage. So only index columns that **often appear in WHERE, JOIN, or ORDER BY** — don't index every column indiscriminately.

slides.title: Optimizing queries by MySQL
slides.body:
The MySQL document describes `EXPLAIN` as the main tool for viewing the **execution plan**: which order the tables are read in, which index is used (`key`), how many rows are estimated (`rows`), and the flags in `Extra` such as `Using filesort` (needs an extra sort) or `Using index` (gets all the data straight from the index, very fast).

Composite indexes follow the **leftmost prefix** rule: the column order must match how the query filters and then sorts. MySQL also notes that a large `LIMIT … OFFSET` is slow because it must read and then skip many rows, which is the basis for keyset pagination.

> Oracle (2025) *MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: Optimizing Queries with EXPLAIN; Multiple-Column Indexes; LIMIT Query Optimization*. Available at: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/
>
> Winand, M. (2012) *SQL Performance Explained*. Vienna: Markus Winand.

slides.title: Accessibility: WCAG
slides.body:
**WCAG 2.2** of W3C is the international standard for web accessibility, built around four **POUR** principles: *Perceivable*, *Operable*, *Understandable*, *Robust* (compatible with assistive technologies).

Lighthouse (Google) automatically checks **some** of these criteria. A 100 score does **not** guarantee a perfect page. Many criteria (for example, whether the reading order makes sense) can only be checked by hand, but it catches every error a machine can detect.

Nhịp has followed WCAG since step 1: buttons ≥44px, `alt`, `aria-pressed`, `aria-label`, `label` for every input field.

> W3C (2023) *Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2*. Available at: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
>
> Google (2025) *Lighthouse Accessibility scoring*. Available at: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/accessibility/scoring

slides.title: Measure before fixing
slides.body:
The work order for this step:

1. **Measure the query count** of a page by temporarily counting (or enabling query logging). Confirm the feed does **not** have an N+1.
2. **EXPLAIN** the feed query, and see `Using filesort`.
3. **Add the index**, run EXPLAIN again, and see `Using index`.
4. **Keyset pagination** instead of loading everything.
5. **Lighthouse**, fix the remaining issues, then 100.

The golden rule of optimization (Knuth): *"premature optimization is the root of all evil"*. Only optimize what is **measured to be slow**. Don't guess.

slides.title: Check that Nhịp has no N+1
slides.body:
Temporarily enable query counting in `db.php` (for measurement only, remove afterward):

~~~php
// Sau khi tạo PDO, bọc để đếm — chỉ dùng khi đo
$pdo->setAttribute(PDO::ATTR_STATEMENT_CLASS, [CountingStatement::class]);
~~~

A simpler way: turn on the **General Query Log** of MySQL for a moment, load the feed, then count the `Query` lines. For Nhịp, loading the feed once generates only **a fixed small number of queries** (feed + mark_liked + session), **not** growing with the number of posts.

If you accidentally write a loop that calls `find_user_by_id($post['user_id'])` for each post, that is exactly N+1. `FEED_SQL` already `JOIN users` to prevent this.

slides.title: Reading EXPLAIN

image.alt: EXPLAIN result in phpMyAdmin: type ref, possible_keys idx_posts_parent,idx_posts_feed, key idx_posts_feed, rows 102, Extra Using where; Using index
image.caption: EXPLAIN of the feed query after adding the index: key = idx_posts_feed, Extra = Using index (no more filesort).

slides.body:
Put `EXPLAIN` in front of a `SELECT` to see the plan. The important columns:

- **type**: `ALL` = full table scan (bad); `ref`/`range` = uses an index (good); `const`/`eq_ref` = very good.
- **key**: the index actually used (`NULL` = none used).
- **rows**: estimated number of rows to read. The smaller, the better.
- **Extra**: `Using filesort` = needs an extra in-memory sort; `Using index` = all data is taken from the index, the fastest.

Before adding the index, the feed query is `Using filesort`: the database must sort all posts by time on every request.

slides.title: Composite index for the feed
slides.body:
The feed query filters by `parent_id IS NULL` and then sorts by `created_at DESC, id DESC`. The index matches exactly that order:

~~~sql
ALTER TABLE posts ADD KEY idx_posts_feed (parent_id, created_at, id);
~~~

Column order follows the **leftmost prefix rule**: filter columns (`parent_id`) first, then sort columns (`created_at`, `id`). After adding it, EXPLAIN changes from `Using filesort` to **`Using index`**: the database reads exactly the first 20 rows from the already sorted index, with no re-sorting.

Note: on a **very small** table (a few dozen rows), MySQL may ignore the index because a direct scan is still faster. The index pays off when the data is large.

slides.title: Keyset pagination
"Load more" button

image.alt: At the bottom of the Nhịp feed there is a rounded-outline Load more button
image.caption: Fetch 21 posts and show 20. If post number 21 exists, show the Load more button carrying the cursor of post number 20.

slides.title: Image optimization
slides.body: Images are usually the **heaviest** part of a page. Nhịp does four things: - **Clear dimensions**: every `` has `width` and `height` → the browser reserves space, so the page doesn't "jump" when images load (reducing *Cumulative Layout Shift*). - **`loading="lazy"`**: off-screen images only load when scrolled into view. - **`alt`**: a description for screen readers; decorative images get `alt=""`. - **Redraw + compress** (step 18): the avatar is re-encoded by GD at 85 quality — small and uniform. Going further (outside this course): generate multiple sizes (`srcset`) and use WebP/AVIF for large images.

slides.title: Passes Accessibility 100

image.alt: Lighthouse scores for Nhịp: Accessibility 100, Best Practices 100, SEO 100, Agentic Browsing 2/2
image.caption: Lighthouse (mobile) on the Nhịp feed: Accessibility, Best Practices, and SEO all 100.

slides.body: Run Lighthouse (DevTools → Lighthouse → Accessibility → *Analyze*). Two common errors and how Nhịp fixes them: - **Missing meta description** → add `` to `header.php` (also good for search — step 23). - **Label doesn't match the visible text** (the heart button has `aria-label="Thích"` but shows "♥ 0"): change it to a **hidden label** that matches the content — `Thích,0`, and `♥` flags `aria-hidden="true"`. A 100 score is a floor, not a ceiling: you should still **test by hand** with the keyboard (Tab through every button) and a screen reader (VoiceOver/NVDA).

slides.title: Indexes and Pagination
slides.body: Add `idx_posts_feed` to `database/schema.sql` and run `ALTER TABLE`. Fix `feed_posts` to accept the pointer `$before`.

slides.title: feed.php: Load more button
slides.body: Read the `?before` cursor (check the regex), fetch 21 posts to tell whether more pages remain, trim the result to 20, and show the button.

slides.title: Fix a11y for Lighthouse 100
slides.body: Meta description in the header, and the heart button uses a hidden label that matches its visible text. `app.js` updates the hidden label instead of `aria-label`.

slides.title: Measure and optimize exercises
slides.body:
1. Turn on the General Query Log of MySQL (`SET GLOBAL general_log = 'ON';`), load the feed, and count the `Query`. Turn it off again after measuring.
2. Deliberately write an N+1 loop (call `find_user_by_id` inside the `foreach` loop), measure again, then remove it. Observe the query count spike.
3. Run `EXPLAIN` search queries `LIKE '%…%'`. Why does it **not** use the index? (hint: `%` at the beginning). Look into `FULLTEXT`.
4. Add `srcset` for the avatar (two sizes) and observe the Network panel.
5. Run Lighthouse in mobile mode and read each criterion in the Accessibility section.

slides.title: Acceptance check for step 21
slides.body: - [ ] Confirm the feed has no N+1: the query count is fixed and doesn't grow with the number of posts. - [ ] Can read EXPLAIN; the feed query uses `idx_posts_feed`, no longer `Using filesort`. - [ ] Keyset pagination works: the "Show more" button carries the cursor, page 2 has the correct order, no duplicate or missing posts. - [ ] Every `` has `width/height/alt` and `loading="lazy"` on the image in the list. - [ ] Lighthouse Accessibility = 100 on mobile; you can Tab through every button. - [ ] Understood: add indexes only for columns used in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY, not indiscriminately.

quiz.q: What is the N+1 problem?
o: The number of queries grows with the number of items: 1 query for the list + 1 per item
quiz.why: Fix it with JOIN and IN to fetch everything in a few fixed queries.

quiz.q: What does type: ALL mean in EXPLAIN?
o: Full table scan (no index used), usually slow
quiz.why: ALL = full table scan; you want to see ref/range/const.

quiz.q: You should index every column to make sure it's fast.
quiz.why: Each index slows down writes and takes up space; only index columns used in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY.

quiz.q: What does Extra: Using filesort mean in EXPLAIN?
o: The database has to sort extra; an index in the right order would eliminate it
quiz.why: Index matching ORDER BY for Using index, no re-sorting needed.

quiz.q: Why is keyset pagination faster than OFFSET on deep pages?
o: Jumps straight to the right spot via the index, without reading and discarding many rows
quiz.why: A large OFFSET still has to read and skip every row before it.

quiz.q: Which section causes the N+1 problem?
quiz.why: One find_user_by_id query per lesson; use a JOIN in the query that fetches the lessons.

quiz.q: Which approach keeps images light and avoids layout shift?
quiz.why: BMP is uncompressed; use WebP/JPEG. The other three are all correct.

quiz.q: Fill in the column order for the feed index (filter, then sort).
quiz.why: Left-prefix rule: the equality-filter column (parent_id) comes before the sort column.

quiz.q: Does a Lighthouse Accessibility 100 mean the page is perfectly accessible?
o: No — only the criteria a machine can check; you still need manual testing with the keyboard and a screen reader
quiz.why: Many WCAG criteria can only be checked manually.

quiz.q: Why can't a regular index be used for LIKE '%keyword%'?
o: The leading % means the index can't be searched by prefix
quiz.why: A B-tree index searches by prefix; a leading % breaks that. Use FULLTEXT for full-text search.

step22.summary: Three features that connect users: hashtags group posts by topic, @mentions connect people to each other, and notifications cover every interaction. Creating a post with tags and notifications happens in one transaction, and text is turned into safe links.

slides.title: Keeping users coming back
slides.body:
Nhịp is already fast and lean. But a social network thrives on **interactions that get responses**: you like a post and the other person knows; you mention someone and they get notified; you tag a topic and people who care about it can find it.

The final three features of stage 5:

- **Hashtags** (`#php`) — group posts by topic.
- **Mentions** (`@lan.code`) — link directly to a person.
- **Notifications** — alert users when someone replies, likes, follows, or mentions them.

This is also where you actually use **transactions** (learned in steps 10–11) and the technique of **turning text into safe links**.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Extract `#hashtag` and `@mention` from the content using regular expressions (Unicode).
2. Store hashtags as a **many-to-many** relationship (`tags` + `post_tags`); the `/tag/{tag}` page.
3. Send **notifications** for four event types; the unread badge counts them.
4. Create the post **together with its tags and notifications in one transaction**: all or nothing.
5. Turn `#tag` and `@user` into links **after escaping HTML**, so the XSS vulnerability doesn't come back.
6. Mark notifications as "read" when the notifications page is opened.

slides.title: Hashtags are many-to-many
slides.body:
A post has many tags, and a tag belongs to many posts, so this is a **many-to-many** relationship and needs a **join table** (like `likes` at step 9):

- `tags(id, name)`: one tag per row, `name` **UNIQUE**.
- `post_tags(post_id, tag_id)`: composite primary key, one row per pair.

When publishing a post with `#php`: create the tag `php` if it doesn't exist yet (`INSERT IGNORE`), then link the post to each tag. The `/tag/php` page `JOIN` the reverse direction to fetch every post carrying that tag. This is exactly the pattern you built for "likes": reuse the knowledge, just rename it.

slides.title: Notifications: recipient and actor
slides.body:
Each notification answers: *who receives it, who caused it, what happened, and on which post*.

- `user_id`: the **recipient** (the author of the liked post, the person mentioned…).
- `actor_id`: the **actor** who triggered the action.
- `type`: `reply` / `like` / `follow` / `mention`.
- `post_id`: the related post (may be NULL for "follow").
- `is_read`: whether it has been seen, for the badge.

Rule: **don't notify yourself** (liking your own post, replying to your own post). Check `user_id === actor_id` and skip it.

slides.title: Unicode regular expressions
slides.body:
Tag and user names with diacritics are common in Vietnamese, so the regex must be **Unicode-aware**: the `u` flag and the `\p{L}` class (any letter), `\p{N}` (any digit). PCRE, the regex library of PHP, fully supports these Unicode property classes.

Hashtags use `#([\p{L}\p{N}_]{1,50})` so they can match `#bảomật`. Usernames are narrower (`[a-z0-9._]`) because Nhịp itself restricts usernames to unaccented characters (step 12).

> The PHP Group (2025) *PCRE — Regular Expressions (Perl-Compatible); Unicode character properties*. PHP Manual. Available at: https://www.php.net/manual/en/regexp.reference.unicode.php
>
> Unicode Consortium (2024) *Unicode Technical Standard #18: Unicode Regular Expressions*. Available at: https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr18/

slides.title: Escape first, link after
slides.body:
Turning `@lan.code` into links means **inserting HTML** (`<a>`) into user content, which is exactly what XSS exploits (step 17). It is safe only if you follow this order:

1. **Escape all** of the content with `htmlspecialchars` first (every `<`, `>`, `&` becomes an entity).
2. **Then** find `#tag`/`@user` in the **escaped** string and wrap `<a>` around them.

After step 1 there are no live HTML characters left, so step 2 only adds the `<a>` tags we control. OWASP calls this the **context-aware, just-in-time encoding** principle.

> OWASP Foundation (2025) *Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet — Output Encoding*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html

Sending notifications
slides.body:
~~~php
function notify(int $userId, int $actorId, string $type, ?int $postId = null): void
{
    if ($userId === $actorId) return;        // không tự thông báo cho mình
    db()->prepare('INSERT INTO notifications (user_id, actor_id, type, post_id) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)')
        ->execute([$userId, $actorId, $type, $postId]);
}
~~~

Call it at the exact point where the event happens:

- `like.php`: after a heart reaction → `notify(chủ bài, người thích, 'like', bài)`.
