step23.summary: Product analytics with SQL: define metrics (vanity metrics vs. actionable metrics), write statistical queries (by day, top items, engagement rate, security signals), and build a role-restricted /stats page with pure CSS charts, respecting the CSP.

slides.title: What story does the data tell?
slides.body:
Nhịp runs and looks good. But how do you know whether it's **actually getting better**? Do users come back? Which topics draw interest? Is someone trying to brute-force passwords?

All of those questions **already have answers sitting in the database**. You just need to know how to ask. This step turns raw data into **metrics** and **charts** that help you make decisions: what to do next, what to fix, what to watch out for.

This is the final stage, "shipping the product". Analytics is the skill that separates someone who "wrote the app" from someone who can **actually run a product**.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Distinguish **vanity metrics** from **actionable metrics**.
2. Write statistics queries: overview, per day, top N, engagement rate.
3. Fill in **every day**, including days with no data (0), so the chart doesn't "skip" around.
4. Extract **security signals** from the log (`activity_log`).
5. Build a `/stats` page **with access control** (only the product owner can view it).
6. Draw a bar chart with **plain CSS**: no library, and **respect CSP** (no inline `style=""`).

slides.title: Vanity metrics vs. actionable metrics
slides.body:
- **Vanity metrics**: numbers that sound impressive but don't help you decide. "Total posts ever" only goes up; it never tells you whether you're doing well or badly.
- **Actionable metrics**: change with what you do and **suggest an action**. "New posts **per day**" dropping three days in a row means something is wrong, so investigate.

Tip for telling them apart: ask *"if this number changed, would I do something differently?"* If you can't answer, it's a vanity metric.

Nhịp tracks: posts/day, posters/day (DAU), engagement rate (likes per post), top posters, and failed logins/day (security).

slides.title: From raw data to decisions
slides.body:
The analysis chain:

1. **Events** are recorded as they happen: posts (`posts.created_at`), likes (`likes`), failed logins (`activity_log`).
2. **Queries** group them into metrics: `GROUP BY DATE(...)`, `COUNT`, `AVG`.
3. **Present** them as readable tables and charts.
4. **Decide**: when something looks unusual, act on it.

The important thing already done earlier: **record the timestamp** (`created_at`) for everything. Without timestamps you can't analyze over time, which is why every table in Nhịp has `created_at`.

slides.title: Actionable metrics
slides.body:
The concept of *actionable metrics vs. vanity metrics* was popularized by Eric Ries in *The Lean Startup*: a good metric must be **actionable** (clearly suggests what to do), **accessible** (easy to understand), and **auditable** (verifiable from the raw data). "Total page views" is the classic example of a vanity metric.

For measuring engagement, McClure's **AARRR** framework (Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue) is a common way to pick metrics for each stage of the user lifecycle. For a learning project like Nhịp, we focus on **Activation** (users publishing their first post) and **Retention** (coming back to post again).

> Ries, E. (2011) *The Lean Startup*. New York: Crown Business.
>
> McClure, D. (2007) *Startup Metrics for Pirates (AARRR)*. Available at: https://500hats.typepad.com/

slides.title: Grouping by time in SQL
slides.body:
The MySQL documentation describes the date functions `DATE()` and `DATE_FORMAT()`, which truncate timestamps into grouping units (day, week, month), and `GROUP BY`, which computes totals per group. One caveat: **time zones**. `DATE(created_at)` truncates by server time, so a product serving multiple time zones must decide which time zone to truncate by.

On security of analytics data: a statistics page that exposes aggregated information is also a form of **A01 Broken Access Control** if it doesn't restrict who can view it. So `/stats` must check permissions like any sensitive page.

> Oracle (2025) *MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: Date and Time Functions; GROUP BY Modifiers*. Available at: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/
>
> OWASP Foundation (2025) *Authorization Cheat Sheet*. Available at: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html

slides.title: Choosing metrics for Nhịp
slides.body:
| Metric | Query | Why |
|---|---|---|
| New posts / day | `GROUP BY DATE(created_at)` | Is activity growing? |
| Posters / day | `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)` | How many people actually use it? |
| Average hearts / post | `likes / posts` | Is the content getting a response? |
| Top posters | `GROUP BY user ORDER BY count` | Who are the core users? |
| Failed logins / day | `activity_log WHERE login_failed` | Is someone attacking? |

Save the queries in `database/analytics.sql` to run by hand in phpMyAdmin, and bundle a few key metrics into the `/stats` page.

slides.title: Overview query
slides.body:
Several subqueries inside a `SELECT` produce one overview row:

~~~sql
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users)                         AS users,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM posts WHERE parent_id IS NULL) AS posts,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM likes)                         AS likes,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM follows)                       AS follows;
~~~

Each subquery runs once and returns one value. With large tables, `COUNT(*)` on InnoDB has to scan, so if you need it often and in real time, people store a precomputed counter (trade-off: it must be updated on every write). With Nhịp, a direct count is enough.

slides.title: Per day, and filling in empty days
DISTINCT, AVG and top N
slides.body:
~~~sql
-- Người đăng bài mỗi ngày (một dạng DAU)
SELECT DATE(created_at), COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)
FROM posts GROUP BY DATE(created_at);

-- Tỷ lệ tương tác
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM likes) /
       NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM posts WHERE parent_id IS NULL), 0);

-- Top 5 người đăng nhiều nhất
SELECT u.username, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM posts p JOIN users u ON u.id = p.user_id
WHERE p.parent_id IS NULL
GROUP BY u.id ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 5;
~~~

- `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)`: counts **distinct people**, not the number of posts.
- `NULLIF(x, 0)`: avoids **dividing by 0** when there are no posts yet. Dividing by NULL gives NULL instead of an error.

slides.title: Security signals from logs
slides.body:
The logs (`activity_log`, step 19) are not only for tracing incidents. They are also a source for **security analysis**:

~~~sql
SELECT DATE(created_at) AS ngay, COUNT(*) AS lan_sai
FROM activity_log
WHERE action = 'login_failed' AND created_at > (NOW() - INTERVAL 7 DAY)
GROUP BY DATE(created_at);
~~~

When one day suddenly shows hundreds of `login_failed` from a few IPs, that is a sign of password guessing. This is exactly the kind of "detection" that **A09 Security Logging** targets: logging is not enough, you must **look** at the logs. The `/stats` page shows this number and flags it when it exceeds the threshold.

slides.title: The /stats page has access control
Pure CSS charts, and CSP

image.alt: The Nhịp Statistics page shows six number cards (6 users, 103 original posts, 6 replies, 17 likes, 10 follows, 0.17 likes per post) and a bar chart of new posts over the last 7 days, with columns 0,0,0,1,29,41,38
image.caption: /stats: metric cards and a bar chart drawn with plain CSS, with no charting library.

slides.body:
Draw the chart without a JavaScript library (remember A03 Supply Chain: every library is a risk). Each column is a `<div>` whose height is proportional to its value.

**But** the CSP of Nhịp (`style-src 'self'`, step 17) **forbids inline `style=""`**, so you **cannot** set `style="height: 80px"` on each column. The way to respect the CSP: predefine **height classes** in `style.css` (`.bar-h-0` … `.bar-h-100`) and have PHP pick the class by ratio:

~~~php
$pct = (int) (round($d['n'] / $peak * 20) * 5);   // làm tròn về bội số 5
echo '<div class="bar bar-h-' . $pct . '">';
~~~

The security policy in stage 4 shapes how the interface is written in stage 5. Security and architecture are tied together.

slides.title: Analysis exercises
slides.body:
Add to `analytics.sql` and run:

1. **Retention**: how many people posted in **both** this week and last week? (hint: use two subqueries `user_id IN (...)`).
2. **Trending topics**: the top 5 most-used hashtags (`post_tags JOIN tags GROUP BY`).
3. **Prime time**: which time slot do the posts concentrate in? (`GROUP BY HOUR(created_at)`).
4. **Silent users**: how many accounts have **not** posted anything? (`LEFT JOIN ... WHERE p.id IS NULL`).
5. Add a "hashtags per post on average" metric to the `/stats` page.

- [ ] The posts-per-day chart fills in all 7 days, and empty days show 0.
- [ ] The page does not violate the CSP (clean Console): use a CSS class, not `style=""`.
- [ ] Distinguish vanity metrics from actionable metrics using the numbers on Nhịp itself.
- [ ] Extract at least one security signal from `activity_log`.

quiz.q: Why do you need to fill in empty days (0) when plotting a chart by day?

step24.summary: Put Nhịp online for free: choose hosting PHP+MySQL, standardize the production configuration (debug off, Secure cookie, HTTPS), create a remote database, upload code via FTP with the web root set to public/, and test after deployment.

slides.title: From localhost to the world
slides.body:
Nhịp is fully working on your machine. But "running on localhost" means **only you** can access it. This step deploys Nhịp to a real server on the Internet so **anyone** can open it with a link.

Deployment is more than "copying files up". A production environment differs from localhost in three vital ways: **configuration** (a different database host, real passwords), **security** (debug off, HTTPS, Secure cookies), and **limits** (hosting resources are finite). Getting any one of these wrong leaks secrets or takes the site down.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Understand the difference between **localhost and production** and what must change.
2. Choose a free **PHP + MySQL** hosting that suits learning.
3. Standardize the production configuration: `debug = false`, the **Secure** cookie flag, **HTTPS**.
4. Create a remote database and import `schema.sql` through the hosting's phpMyAdmin.
5. Upload the code via **FTP**, set the web root to `public/`, and keep `config.php`/`src` out of public access.
6. **Post-deployment testing** against a fixed checklist.

slides.title: localhost vs production
slides.body:
| | localhost | production |
|---|---|---|
| Address | `localhost` | a real domain name, **HTTPS** |
| DB host | `127.0.0.1` | the hosting's own database server |
| DB password | empty (root) | a real strong password |
| `debug` | `true` (shows errors) | **`false`** (hides errors) |
| Cookie `Secure` | `false` (HTTP) | **`true`** (HTTPS only) |
| `X-Powered-By` | on | off (`expose_php`) |

All of these differences sit in **one configuration file** (`config.php`) plus a few headers. That is why, back at step 11 Nhịp, we split the configuration out separately.

slides.title: The web root is only public/
slides.body:
On shared hosting, the publicly served directory is usually named **`htdocs/`** or **`public_html/`**. The rule (step 20):

- The **`public/`** content of Nhịp → goes into the hosting's web root directory.
- **`src/`, `config.php`, `database/`** → go into the **parent** directory (outside the web root).

If the host does not let you place files outside the web root, put them in a subdirectory and block access with `.htaccess` (`Require all denied`). The invariant goal: **the browser must never be able to download `config.php`.**

slides.title: Free hosting and HTTPS
slides.body:
There are many free PHP+MySQL hosts (InfinityFree, AwardSpace…; 000webhost shut down in 2024). They run on **cPanel** or a similar control panel, offering FTP, phpMyAdmin, and **free SSL** certificates from **Let's Encrypt**, a nonprofit that issues TLS certificates automatically and for free, and has made HTTPS the norm for hundreds of millions of websites.

HTTPS is no longer optional. It encrypts the connection (preventing password and session cookie eavesdropping, which is Spoofing in STRIDE, step 16), and it is a prerequisite for the `Secure` cookie flag to work.

> Internet Security Research Group (2025) *Let's Encrypt — How It Works*. Available at: https://letsencrypt.org/how-it-works/
>
> Mozilla (2025) *Transport Layer Security (TLS)*, MDN Web Docs. Available at: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Transport_Layer_Security

slides.title: Secure production configuration
slides.body:
The security documentation of PHP recommends for public servers: **disable `display_errors`** (errors go to the log, not the browser), disable **`expose_php`** (hide the PHP version from the headers), and use HTTPS for all sensitive data. Exposing detailed errors is a form of **A02 Security Misconfiguration** and **A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions** (OWASP Top 10:2025). Nhịp handled this with `debug = false` + an error handler (step 19).

> The PHP Group (2025) *PHP Manual: Error Handling and Security; php.ini directives (display_errors, expose_php)*. Available at: https://www.php.net/manual/en/security.errors.php
>
> OWASP Foundation (2025) *A02:2025 – Security Misconfiguration*. Available at: https://top10.owasp.org/2025/

slides.title: Pre-launch checklist
slides.body:
Do these **locally** before touching the hosting:

- [ ] Re-run `database/schema.sql` on an empty database to make sure it is complete and correct.
- [ ] Delete the `lab/` folder (vulnerable code, step 17).
- [ ] `config.php`: `'debug' => false`.
- [ ] `src/auth.php`: cookie `'secure' => true`.
- [ ] Back up the localhost database (phpMyAdmin → Export) to keep an original copy.

Put everything into `DEPLOY.md`, the project's deployment document, so next time (and for others) the setup can be redone without having to remember it.

1. Sign up (email only, no card).
2. Create a website with a **free subdomain** (for example `nhip.infinityfreeapp.com`), or attach your own domain if you have one.
3. Turn on **free SSL** for the domain — it can take a few minutes to a few hours for the certificate to be issued.

Other hosts (AwardSpace, 000webhost…) follow a similar process: create an account → create a site → enable SSL.

slides.title: Step 2 · Remote database
slides.body:
In the control panel → **MySQL Databases** → create a database. Record **four** pieces of information:

- **Host**: for example `sql123.infinityfree.com`. **Not** `127.0.0.1`! This difference is what trips up many beginners.
- **Database name**: usually has a prefix, for example `if0_12345_nhip`.
- **User** and **Password**.

Open **phpMyAdmin of your hosting** → select the database → **Import** tab → upload `database/schema.sql`. Sample data (`seed.sql`) is optional. This is exactly the Import step you did on localhost (step 10), just on a remote server.

slides.title: Step 3 · Upload code over FTP
slides.body:
Get the **FTP** details from the control panel (host, user, password) and use an FTP app (FileZilla) or the web **File Manager**.

1. Web root of the hosting (`htdocs/` or `public_html/`): upload the **contents of the `public/` folder** here: `index.php`, `.htaccess`, `css/`, `js/`, `img/`, `uploads/`.
2. **Parent** folder of the web root: upload `src/`, `config.php`, `database/`.
3. Make sure the `uploads/avatars/` folder exists and is **writable** (permissions 755).

If the hosting does **not** let you go outside the web root: put `src/`, `config.php` in a subfolder inside the web root, and add a `.htaccess` containing `Require all denied` there.

slides.title: Step 4 · Production config.php
slides.body:
Edit `config.php` **on the hosting** with the database details you just created:

~~~php
return [
    'db_host' => 'sql123.infinityfree.com',   // host CSDL hosting
    'db_name' => 'if0_12345_nhip',
    'db_user' => 'if0_12345',
    'db_pass' => '••••••••',
    'debug'   => false,                        // QUAN TRỌNG: tắt trên production
];
~~~

`config.php` does not follow Git (`.gitignore`, step 20), so the production copy is separate. You fill it in directly on the hosting. `[1045] Access denied` or `[2002] Connection refused` errors (step 11) are usually caused by the wrong host or password here.

slides.title: Step 5 · Enable the Secure flag and HTTPS
slides.body:
In `src/auth.php`, the session cookie enables `Secure` so it is sent **only** over HTTPS:

~~~php
session_set_cookie_params([
    'httponly' => true,
    'samesite' => 'Lax',
    'secure'   => true,     // production có HTTPS → bật
]);
~~~

Note: if you enable `secure` but access the site via **HTTP** (no SSL yet), the browser drops the cookie and **you cannot log in**. So only turn it on once SSL works, and ideally **force a redirect from HTTP → HTTPS** using `.htaccess`:

~~~apache
RewriteCond %{HTTPS} off
RewriteRule ^ https://%{HTTP_HOST}%{REQUEST_URI} [L,R=301]
~~~

slides.title: Post-deployment testing
slides.body:
Run exactly this checklist on every deploy:

- [ ] `https://<tên-miền>/` shows the feed, with the HTTPS padlock.
- [ ] Register a new account, post, like, follow, mention a name. Everything works.
- [ ] Open `https://<tên-miền>/config.php` → **404/403** (outside the web root).
- [ ] Trigger an error (e.g. a wrong URL) → the **generic 500 page**, with no path exposed (debug=false).
- [ ] DevTools → Application → Cookies: `nhip_session` has **Secure** + **HttpOnly**.
- [ ] Upload an avatar → it saves (the `uploads` folder is writable).

If any line fails, **fix it and re-run the whole checklist from the beginning**. Don't leave the site "half working".

slides.title: Limits of free hosting
slides.body:
Know these so you aren't surprised:

- **Limited resources**: caps on CPU, RAM and queries per day. Enough for learning and demos, not for heavy traffic.
- **No background processes**: heavy cron jobs, workers and bulk email are usually banned.
- **May be shut down**: violating the terms takes the site offline. **Back up** your database regularly (Export).
- **Inconsistent performance**: you share the machine with many other sites.

When the project grows, move to a **VPS** (a full virtual machine) or a **PaaS** (Railway, Render…). The configuration, security and web-root principles in this step stay the same.

slides.title: DEPLOY.md
slides.body: Write the project's deployment document. With it, the next deploy just means following the steps, and anyone who clones the repo can get it online too.

slides.title: Standardize production
slides.body: Two changes are required before going live, and the rule forcing HTTPS in `.htaccess` of `public/`.

slides.title: Deployment exercise
slides.body:
1. Create a free hosting account, upload Nhịp, and send the link to a friend to try.
2. Deliberately leave `debug = true` on and trigger an error to see what it reveals. Then turn it off again. (Understand why it must be off.)
3. Try opening `/config.php` and `/src/db.php` in the browser. Confirm they cannot be downloaded.
4. Export the database from the hosting to your computer (a one-time backup).
5. Change one CSS line on your computer, redeploy only that file, and confirm the change appears on the site.

slides.title: Step 24 acceptance
slides.body:
- [ ] Nhịp runs on a real domain through **HTTPS**.
- [ ] Someone else (not you) can open and use it.
- [ ] `config.php` uses the hosting's database host, `debug = false`. Opening it directly → 404/403.
- [ ] The session cookie has the **Secure** flag. HTTP automatically redirects to HTTPS.
- [ ] Errors show the generic 500 page, with no details exposed.
- [ ] `DEPLOY.md` is enough to redo everything from scratch. Database backed up.

quiz.why: The database usually lives on a separate server, not on localhost as on your machine.

o: Detailed errors expose paths, versions and SQL to attackers
quiz.why: Exposing errors is a Security Misconfiguration (A02).

quiz.q: You should enable the Secure cookie flag even if the site only runs on HTTP (no SSL yet).
quiz.why: Secure means the cookie is only sent over HTTPS. On HTTP the cookie is lost and you cannot log in.

quiz.q: Which Nhịp folder is uploaded to the hosting's web root?
quiz.why: Only public/ is public. src, config and database are outside the web root.

quiz.q: Who usually issues a free SSL certificate?
quiz.why: Let's Encrypt issues TLS certificates automatically, for free.

quiz.q: What must you check after deploying?
o: Session cookie has the Secure flag
Triggering an error must show the generic 500 page
Set debug = true to make fixing easier
quiz.why: debug must = false on production.

quiz.q: If the hosting doesn't let you place files outside the web root, how do you protect config.php?
o: Place it in a subfolder with an .htaccess file containing Require all denied
quiz.why: Block HTTP access to the folder holding source code and secrets.

quiz.q: Write the directive in .htaccess that forces HTTP to HTTPS.
quiz.why: 301 is a permanent redirect, which is correct for forcing HTTPS.

quiz.q: What are the typical limits of free hosting?
o: Usually can't run cron jobs or background workers
May be shut down if the rules are violated

step24.title: 24. Free deployment: put PHP + MySQL on the Internet

step25.summary: Write documentation so that strangers (and your future self) can install, understand, and use Nhịp: README following the Diátaxis framework, Markdown syntax, installation instructions that run command by command, and deployment and security documentation.

slides.title: Code does not explain itself
slides.body:
Nhịp is live on the Internet. But if a stranger (or you, six months later) opens the repository, they will ask: *What is this? How do I install it? How do I run it? Where do I edit it?* Source code does **not** answer those questions by itself.

Documentation is the most neglected part of the work, yet it determines whether the project can be **reused**. This step writes documentation for Nhịp so that **a stranger can install and use it using only the text you write**, as the final stage requires.

Writing documentation is also a **design test**: if a feature is hard to explain, it is usually because it was designed in a tangled way.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Understand the four types of documentation under the **Diátaxis** framework and write the right type for each need.
2. Write **README** thoroughly: description, features, requirements, installation, structure, deployment, license.
3. Use **Markdown** proficiently: headings, lists, code blocks, tables, images, links.
4. Write **installation instructions that work**: every command copied runs, no steps missing.
5. Link documentation: README → `DEPLOY.md`, `SECURITY.md`.
6. Treat documentation as a **living document**: update it whenever the code changes.

slides.title: Four Types of Documentation (Diátaxis)
slides.body:
The **Diátaxis** framework organizes documentation by the reader's needs:

- **Tutorial** — *learning*: walks a newcomer step by step through finishing a first task. ("Install Nhịp and publish your first post.")
- **How-to** — *doing*: steps to solve one specific problem. (`DEPLOY.md`)
- **Reference** — *looking up*: precise, dry description. (Route list, database schema.)
- **Explanation** — *understanding*: why the design is this way. (`SECURITY.md`, the "research" slides.)

Common mistake: mixing them, such as putting theory into installation instructions. Each document serves **one** need.

slides.title: README — the project's front door

image.alt: The README.md of Nhịp renders GitHub-style: a title marked Nhịp, a one-line description, a banner image, a Features section with a bulleted list, and a Requirements section.
image.caption: README.md renders GitHub-style — the first thing people see when they open a repository.

slides.body:
README is the project's **cover page**. On GitHub/GitLab it appears automatically on the repository's home page. Readers skim it in 30 seconds to decide whether to use the project, so order matters:

1. **Name + one sentence** describing it (what it is).
2. Image/demo (what it looks like).
3. Features (what it can do).
4. Installation (how to get started).
5. Deeper links.

slides.title: Documentation standards
slides.body:
**Diátaxis** (Procida) is a documentation framework adopted by many large projects (Django, Gatsby…): it splits content into four types along the *learning/doing* and *theory/practice* axes.

**Markdown** (Gruber, 2004) is a lightweight markup language, standardized as **CommonMark**. GitHub uses the **GitHub Flavored Markdown** variant (adds tables, checklists, syntax-highlighted code blocks). It is the default documentation format of code repositories.

> Procida, D. (2017) *Diátaxis documentation framework*. Available at: https://diataxis.fr/
>
> MacFarlane, J. et al. (2019) *CommonMark Spec*. Available at: https://spec.commonmark.org/
>
> GitHub (2025) *Basic writing and formatting syntax*. Available at: https://docs.github.com/get-started/writing-on-github

slides.title: What a good README includes
slides.body:
The *Make a README* page summarizes what a README should include: **name, description, installation, usage, contributing, license**. Its key principle: write for **someone who knows nothing** about the project.

Installation instructions must **actually work**: every copy-paste command runs, with no hidden steps assumed ("of course you already have MySQL…"). The best test: give the project to someone who **has never seen it** and have them follow the steps. Wherever they get stuck is where the documentation is missing.

> Guo, D. (2023) *Make a README*. Available at: https://www.makeareadme.com/
>
> GitHub (2025) *About READMEs*. Available at: https://docs.github.com/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-readmes

slides.title: Documentation map of Nhịp
slides.body:
| File | Diátaxis type | For whom |
|---|---|---|
| `README.md` | Overview + setup (tutorial/how-to) | Newcomers opening the repository |
| `DEPLOY.md` | How-to | Deployers |
| `SECURITY.md` | Explanation | Security-minded readers |
| `database/schema.sql` (annotated) | Reference | People who need to understand the data |
| `database/analytics.sql` | Reference | Analysts |

The three `.md` files at the root link to each other. Don't rewrite the same content in several places: each fact lives in one place, and the others **link** to it.

slides.title: Markdown basics
slides.body:
~~~markdown
# Tiêu đề 1    ## Tiêu đề 2    ### Tiêu đề 3

**đậm**   *nghiêng*   `mã trong dòng`

- Danh sách      1. Danh sách có số
- gạch đầu dòng   2. ...

> Trích dẫn / ghi chú nổi bật

[Chữ liên kết](DEPLOY.md)      ![Mô tả ảnh](docs/feed.png)
~~~

A blank line separates paragraphs. Markdown is deliberately **simple**: it stays readable even unrendered, so it works as both a document and plain text.

slides.title: Code blocks and tables
slides.body:
Code blocks use three backticks followed by the **language name** for syntax highlighting:

~~~markdown
```bash
php -S localhost:8000 -t public public/router-dev.php
```
~~~

Table (GitHub Flavored):

~~~markdown
| Tệp | Vai trò |
|---|---|
| public/ | web root |
| src/ | mã nguồn |
~~~

Task-list checkboxes `- [ ]` / `- [x]` are useful for acceptance checklists (you've seen them at the end of every step). Use the correct **language name** (`php`, `sql`, `bash`) so readers know what they're looking at.

slides.title: Installation instructions that actually work
slides.body:
The most important part of README. Principles:

1. **List requirements first** (PHP 8.2+, MySQL, `pdo_mysql` extensions, `gd`…).
2. **Number each step**, with a clear purpose for each.
3. **Commands that can be copied and pasted**, with no vague abbreviations.
4. **State the expected result**: "Open http://localhost:8000, sample account `lan.code`/`nhip-demo-2026`".

~~~bash
cp config.sample.php config.php          # rồi sửa thông tin CSDL
mysql -u root -e "SOURCE database/schema.sql"
php -S localhost:8000 -t public public/router-dev.php
~~~

The `config.sample.php` (step 11) exists precisely so that the line "cp config.sample.php config.php" can run.

slides.title: Screenshots, demos and links
slides.body:
- **Screenshot**: one screenshot of the feed at the top of README is worth a thousand words of description. Store it in `docs/`, reference it with `![alt](docs/feed.png)`. `alt` describes the image (accessibility + shown when the image fails to load).
- **Live demo**: if deployed (step 24), add a link "Try it: https://nhip…".
- **Cross-links**: README **does not** repeat all of `DEPLOY.md`; instead it **points to**: `Xem [DEPLOY.md](DEPLOY.md)`.

Each fact is written in only one place. Duplication is the source of "drifting" documentation: fix one spot and forget the other.

slides.title: Documentation is a living document
slides.body:
A **wrong** document is worse than none: it makes readers lose trust and wastes their time. So:

- Add a feature → update the Features section in README.
- Change an install step → fix the instructions right away.
- Change the database schema → fix the comment in `schema.sql`.

Tip: treat documentation as **part of "done"**. A feature without documentation is **not done**. Many teams set a rule: a pull request that changes behavior without changing the documentation cannot be merged.

slides.title: README.md
slides.body: Write `README.md` at the project root. This is a version of Nhịp — adapt it to what you have actually done.

slides.title: Installation guide
slides.body: Installation steps must run one command at a time. `router-dev.php` is the router for the PHP built-in server (emulating .htaccess) during development.

slides.title: Documentation writing exercise
slides.body:
1. Give README to someone who has **not seen** Nhịp, and ask them to install it by following the guide. Record every point where they get stuck → that is where the documentation is missing. Fix it.
2. Write a short **tutorial**: "Publish your first post on Nhịp" (5–7 steps, with screenshots).
3. Write a **Reference** section listing every route (`GET /`, `POST /posts`…) and what each one does.
4. Add a **Contributing** section: how to report bugs, commit conventions.
5. Take real screenshots of the deployed Nhịp and replace `docs/feed.png`.

slides.title: Acceptance for step 25
slides.body:
- [ ] `README.md` has: a one-sentence description, screenshot, features, requirements, installation, structure, links.
- [ ] Installation instructions run one command at a time (a stranger can complete them alone).
- [ ] Markdown is correct: headings, lists, tables, code blocks with a language name.
- [ ] README links to `DEPLOY.md` and `SECURITY.md` without repeating content.
- [ ] Can distinguish the four Diátaxis document types.
- [ ] Understands: a feature without documentation is not done.

quiz.q: According to Diátaxis, which type does DEPLOY.md (the steps for putting the project on hosting) belong to?
quiz.why: How-to: a guide to accomplishing one specific task for someone who already knows the basics.

quiz.q: What should appear first in README?
o: Project name + one sentence describing what it is
quiz.why: Readers decide within 30 seconds; they must immediately know what this is.

quiz.q: Installation instructions should assume the reader is already familiar with the project.
quiz.why: Write for someone who knows nothing; every command must run, with no implicit steps.

quiz.q: What should a Markdown code block include so it is highlighted correctly?
o: Language name (php, sql, bash) after the triple backticks
quiz.why: ```php, ```sql… tells the renderer how to highlight it.

quiz.q: What sections should a good README include?
o: Paste the entire source code into
quiz.why: README describes and points the way; it does not copy the code.

quiz.q: Why should README link to DEPLOY.md instead of copying the content into it?
o: One source of truth; copying invites drift when one place gets updated and the other is forgotten.
quiz.why: Duplication is the root cause of inaccurate documentation.

quiz.q: What is the alt attribute of an image in Markdown (![alt](...)) for?
o: Describes the image for screen readers and displays when the image fails to load.
quiz.why: Accessibility and a fallback when the image fails to load.

quiz.q: Fill in the Markdown syntax that creates an unchecked checklist item.
quiz.why: - [ ] is an unticked box; - [x] is a ticked box (GitHub Flavored).

quiz.q: What is the best sign that the setup instructions are complete?
o: A person who has never seen the project can follow them without getting stuck.
quiz.why: The spot where a newcomer gets stuck is exactly where the documentation is missing.

quiz.q: Why should documentation count as part of 'done'?
o: A feature nobody can understand or use is not truly finished.
To make the repository look nice
quiz.why: Docs live alongside the code; changing behavior means changing the docs.

step25.title: 25. Write documentation: README, setup and usage instructions

step26.summary: Capstone project: turn the Nhịp template into your own product with at least 5 new features and 3 linked pages, following the rubric; then present, document, and defend it to earn Hugo Studio completion recognition.

slides.title: From lessons to your own product
slides.body:
You have completed all six stages: from a static HTML to a social network that is **safe, fast, documented, and running for real on the Internet**. Nhịp is now yours to turn into a product with your own stamp.

**The capstone project** is the final and most important part of the course: you add **at least 5 new features** and **3 linked pages** to Nhịp, applying everything you have learned — database design, security, performance, MVC, documentation.

This is not a copy-along exercise. This is your chance to prove you can **build a web product yourself** from start to finish.

slides.title: Goals
slides.body:
1. Understand the **minimum requirements**: ≥ 5 new features, ≥ 3 linked pages.
2. Choose features by value and set a **scope** you can manage.
3. Apply **every course standard** to each new feature: secure, documented, accessible.
4. Use **transactions, indexes, authorization checks, CSRF** where they belong.
5. **Present** the product: demo, feature list, screenshots.
6. **Defend** the project: explain why you built it that way, and point out its strengths and limitations.

slides.title: How Nhịp exceeded the standard
slides.body:
The Nhịp you build from this course **already** includes many features beyond the basic CRUD framework. Use them as reference models for your own features and pages:

**Features** (≥5): follow · like with Fetch · nested replies · hashtags · mentions · notifications · search · statistics.

**Linked pages** (≥3): `/u/{username}` (profile page) · `/post/{id}` (detail + replies) · `/tag/{tag}` (hashtag) · `/notifications` · `/search` · `/stats`.

The capstone project is about **adding your own** on top of that foundation. It is not about counting to fill a quota. It is about making Nhịp a product you want to use.

slides.title: Lifecycle of a feature
slides.body:
Every new feature goes through exactly the steps you have learned:

1. **Data design**: what new tables or columns are needed? What relationships? (phase 2)
2. **Model**: a parameterized SQL function, in `src/`. (phase 2–3)
3. **Controller + routes**: read the request, check permissions. (phase 5)
4. **View**: accessible HTML, escape output. (phase 1, 4)
5. **Security**: CSRF for POST, input validation, STRIDE. (phase 4)
6. **Documentation**: add to README, update SECURITY.md. (phase 6)

Skipping any step is technical debt. Completing all six steps for **one** feature is better than half-finishing five.

slides.title: Capstone projects in education
slides.body:
**Capstone projects** are a comprehensive form of assessment widely used in technical education. Instead of testing isolated pieces of knowledge, learners **integrate** everything they have studied into a real product. Harvard's CS50 ends with a *final project* that students choose and build themselves, which is exactly this spirit.

The value of a capstone lies in three words: **integration** (combining all skills), **ownership** (making your own decisions and taking responsibility), and **demonstration** (proving competence through a product, not through theory).

> Malan, D.J. (2025) *CS50 Final Project*. Harvard University. Available at: https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/project/
>
> Association for Computing Machinery and IEEE-CS (2023) *Computer Science Curricula 2023 (CS2023)*. New York: ACM.

slides.title: Scope and quality
slides.body:
A common lesson in the software industry: **scope creep** kills more projects than missing features do. Choosing **fewer** features and finishing them **properly** (safely, documented, working correctly) is better than having many half-finished features.

The **MVP** (Minimum Viable Product) principle: build the smallest version that is **actually usable** first, then add more. For a capstone, get 5 features + 3 pages to **working and safe** first, and polish afterwards if time allows.

> Blank, S. (2013) 'Why the Lean Start-Up Changes Everything', *Harvard Business Review*, 91(5), pp. 63–72.

slides.title: Choose your feature
slides.body:
Suggested new features to add to Nhịp (choose ≥5, or come up with your own):

| Feature | Touches |
|---|---|
| Edit / delete comments | CRUD, permission checks |
| Save posts (bookmark) | many-to-many join table |
| Followers / following lists | queries, pagination |
| "People you may know" suggestions | follow graph 2-step traversal |
| Dark mode | CSS variables, saved to localStorage |
| Report posts | new table, moderator permissions |
| Trending hashtags discovery page | GROUP BY, ORDER BY COUNT |
| Personal stats (posts, likes received) | aggregate queries |

Every feature must **actually work**, not be an empty button.

slides.title: Scoping the 100%
slides.body:
Before coding, write a **scope document** (a single `SCOPE.md` file or an item in README):

- An **exact** list of the features you will build (no vague "and more").
- For each feature: which tables or columns it needs, which routes, and who can use it.
- The three linked pages: their addresses and their jobs.
- **Out of scope**: state explicitly what you will NOT do, so the project doesn't bloat.

Lock the scope before you start. Changing scope midway is fine, but do it **deliberately**: update the scope document rather than drifting aimlessly.

slides.title: Adding a Feature the Right Way
slides.body:
Example "save post" (bookmark), going through all six steps:

1. **Data**: join table `bookmarks(user_id, post_id)`, composite primary key (like `likes`).
2. **Model** (`src/bookmarks.php`): `toggle_bookmark`, `bookmarked_posts` — prepared statements.
3. **Routes**: `POST /bookmark`, `GET /saved`.
4. **View**: save button on the post card, `/saved` page.
5. **Security**: the button in `<form>` has `csrf_field()`; `require_login()`.
6. **Docs**: add a line to README; if it receives new data, add it to the entry-point table of `SECURITY.md`.

Reuse every existing pattern: bookmark works exactly like "like", and the `/saved` page is modeled on `/tag`. **Do not reinvent.**

slides.title: Every Feature Passes STRIDE
slides.body:
For **every** new feature, ask the six STRIDE questions again (step 16):

- Any new entry points? → add them to the `SECURITY.md` table.
- Receiving data from users? → validate/escape (SQL parameterized, `e()`).
- Write operations? → POST + CSRF + ownership check.
- Displaying user content? → `e()` / `render_body`.
- Uploading files? → check content + image processing (GD) + rename (step 14, 18).

A feature that "works" but opens a vulnerability is **not done**. The security standard of the 4 stage applies to everything you add.

slides.title: Keeping Quality as It Grows
slides.body:
As the project grows, keep three habits:

- **Consistency**: write new features in the same style (PSR-12, function names, file structure) as the existing code, so the code reads as if one person wrote it.
- **Reuse**: when you catch yourself copying a block a second time, extract it into a shared function.
- **Measure before optimizing**: if a feature is slow, `EXPLAIN` it first before adding an index (step 21). Don't guess.

And use **Git** (step 20): each feature gets its own series of commits with clear messages. Your commit history is the story you tell when defending the project.

slides.title: Presenting the Product
slides.body:
When finished, prepare the **presentation** (demo of 3–5 minutes):

1. **One sentence** describing your Nhịp, and how it differs from the original.
2. **Live demo** of the deployed version: walk through 5 new features and 3 pages.
3. **What you're proud of**: a good design decision, a vulnerability you patched.
4. **Limitations and next steps**: what isn't built yet and what you'll do next.

README is the product's "static presentation" (step 25); the demo is the "dynamic presentation". Both tell the same story: *I built this, and I understand it.*

slides.title: Defending the Project
slides.body:
“Defending” your project means **being able to explain your choices**, not being on the defensive. Be ready to answer:

- *Why use a join table for feature X?* → many-to-many (step 9).
- *How does this guard against XSS?* → output escaping, CSP (step 17).
- *What if there are 100.000 users?* → indexes, keyset pagination, N+1 limits (step 21).
- *What if someone edits another person's post?* → authorization checks in SQL (step 13).

Being able to answer these means you **truly understand** the material rather than copying it. That is what Hugo Studio recognizes in you.

slides.title: Grading criteria table
slides.body:
A finished project passes when:

| Criterion | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Features** | ≥ 5 new features, **actually working** |
| **Pages** | ≥ 3 pages with their own URLs, linked together |
| **Security** | Every entry point validates input; POST has CSRF; no SQLi/XSS vulnerabilities |
| **Quality** | Clean MVC, prepared statements, no clear N+1 bugs |
| **Accessibility** | Lighthouse Accessibility ≥ 90 |
| **Documentation** | README + DEPLOY + SECURITY updated; installable by following README |
| **Deployment** | Running for real on the Internet via HTTPS |
| **Understanding** | Able to defend every design decision |

slides.title: Update README for your project
slides.body: The Features section of README must accurately reflect what YOU added. This is the first place graders look to see whether you reach ≥5 features and ≥3 pages.

slides.title: Project task list
slides.body:
In order:

1. Write `SCOPE.md`: list exactly 5 features + 3 pages you will build, and what is out of scope.
2. For each feature: data design → Model → routes+controller → view → security → documentation.
3. Run `EXPLAIN` for any heavy new query; add indexes if needed.
4. Run Lighthouse, fix until Accessibility ≥ 90.
5. Attack every new entry point yourself (SQLi, XSS, CSRF, IDOR).
6. Update README, DEPLOY.md, SECURITY.md.
7. Deploy to hosting and check against the post-deployment checklist (step 24).
8. Prepare the demo + defense answers.

slides.title: Project completion sign-off
slides.body:
**Complete source code:** [download nhip-hoan-chinh.zip](/downloads/coding/nhip-hoan-chinh.zip) — unzip it to compare with your work (code and course material are in sync).

- [ ] ≥ 5 new features, each actually working.
- [ ] ≥ 3 pages with their own URLs, linked to each other.
- [ ] Every new feature: input validation, POST has CSRF, authorization checks; no vulnerabilities.
- [ ] No clear N+1 bugs; heavy queries are indexed.
- [ ] Lighthouse Accessibility ≥ 90.
- [ ] README/DEPLOY/SECURITY updated; installable by following README.
- [ ] Running for real on the Internet via HTTPS.
- [ ] Able to defend every design decision.

Pass all of these → **4.000 JOY** and be recognized by Hugo Studio as having completed the course. You have become someone who can build a complete web product on their own.

slides.title: Closing words
slides.body:
Looking back: you started from a static HTML page and finished with a real social network — able to design a database, write secure PHP, defend against the most common vulnerabilities, optimize performance, organize clean code, and ship the product to the world.

More important than any line of code: you learned how to **think like** a programmer — measure before optimizing, don't trust user input, documentation is part of being done, and always ask “What could go wrong?”.

Nhịp is only the beginning. Every web application you encounter later is built on these same principles. Congratulations on completing the Coding course — **Exclusively by Hugo Studio**.

quiz.q: What is the minimum number of new features and linked pages a finished project requires?
quiz.why: ≥ 5 new features and ≥ 3 linked pages, all actually working.

quiz.q: Shipping several half-finished features is worse than shipping fewer that are fully done.
quiz.why: Scope creep kills a project; fewer features, but solid, safe, and documented.

quiz.q: Adding a 'save post' feature: how should the data be stored?
o: A single string column in posts
A junction table bookmarks(user_id, post_id), for a many-to-many relationship
quiz.why: Same as likes: a many-to-many relationship needs a junction table.

quiz.q: What security work does every new feature need?
o: Skip it, since CSP is already in place
quiz.why: CSP is one layer; it cannot replace input validation and authorization.

quiz.q: Why must every new feature go through STRIDE?
o: Missing even one entry point can open a security hole.
quiz.why: A feature that runs but opens a security hole is not finished.

quiz.q: A new feature's query is running slowly. What do you do first?
o: Run EXPLAIN to understand it before deciding
quiz.why: Measure before optimizing — don't guess (step 21).

quiz.q: What does 'defend the project' mean?
o: Defending yourself, arguing with the examiners
Explaining why you chose that design
quiz.why: Show that you understand it, including the product's limitations.

quiz.q: Fill in the names of the files you should write before coding to lock down the project scope.
quiz.why: Locking the scope prevents bloat; if you change it, update it deliberately.

quiz.q: What is the minimum Lighthouse Accessibility score for a completed project?
quiz.why: ≥ 90 — the base Nhịp scores 100; keep that standard as you add features.

quiz.q: What is the core value of a completed capstone project?
o: Integrating all skills, taking ownership, and demonstrating competence through a product
quiz.why: Integration, ownership, demonstration.
